Today, Motorola has shared a whole lot more info on its brand-new Signature 27 — packing the new Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 I tested and a retina-searing 12,000-nit display. But not only will it test your eyes, it will test the limits of your wallet.

This is a $1,599 phone. Yowzers. Pre-sales will go live on November 16.

Motorola, the company that has spent the last decade charming us with accessible mid-range and affordable phones, has jumped straight into the ultra-flagship pool. And to justify this phone compared to the iPhone 18 Pro Max, it built a device with a spec sheet that's absurdly overpowered.

If you’re going to charge $1,600 for a slab phone in this economy, you have to throw the kitchen sink at it. Turns out Motorola chucked the entire plumbing system in there for good measure — packing it all into a rather suave, slimline design.

Let’s start with the screen — a 1.5K Extreme AMOLED Duo tandem display that peaks at a bonkers 12,000 nits of brightness. For context, Motorola says users can “comfortably view” this “on a sunny afternoon,” but it’s closer to being able to read a map on the surface of the sun.

And for when you do want to flashbang your eyeballs with TikTok, there’s Bang & Olufsen-tuned speakers, too!

Under the hood is that Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, which as you know from my testing is an absolute monster. This is kept from melting your hands by an ArcticMesh cooling system with a massive vapor chamber.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

And to keep that silicon running, Motorola’s crammed in a gargantuan 7,000 mAh silicon-carbon battery that supports 90W wired charging and 50W wireless charging.

To further justify that astronomical price tag, Motorola strapped a camera block to the back of the phone that is bordering on clinical insanity. I’ll be real with you, it does look a bit weird to me. But I promise it’s functions are crazy.

The main shooter is a 50MP Sony sensor with a massive f/1.6 aperture designed to suck in as much light as physically possible. Next to it is a 50MP ultrawide, but the real flex is the 200MP periscope sensor capable of 100x Super Zoom Pro.

Need to take a selfie? That’s also a 50MP sensor, capable of shooting full 4K video.

But the wildest addition in my eyes is the industry’s first dedicated EVS “Action Sensor.” It’s not a camera; it’s a dedicated piece of hardware whose sole job is to detect pixel-level light intensity changes to freeze fast-moving subjects without blurring. Think of it like the equivalent of having a super fast shutter speed — something that’s a rarity in smartphones.

Pair that with Dolby Vision support and an AI video enhancement engine that optimizes dynamic range in real-time, and you effectively have a full camera rig in your pocket.

The Signature 27 is explicitly designed to run Gemini Intelligence and the brand’s own Qira AI ecosystem. To run the multi-step AI agents locally, Motorola needed to boost the RAM, which they’ve done in a rather clever way.

In silicon, you’ve got up to 16GB LPDDR5X, but with the RAM boost feature, that can be scaled up to a staggering 24GB of memory — utilizing some of the on-board storage.

This paves the way to a clever hybrid system where Gemini handles the super complex generative stuff, but local model work is entirely possible too. However, it does explain why the retail price has been driven into the stratosphere.

The Motorola Signature 27 is looking set to be a gorgeous, hyper-capable device that will likely outspec almost everything else released.

But it is also a 12,000-nit warning sign. Between Apple’s price hikes and Motorola’s $1,599 super slab, the era of an “affordable flagship killer” is behind us. If you want top-tier specs in this market, there’s quite the premium to pay.

#3259. AI super PACs lost their biggest general election bet of the midterms

AI super PACs spent $79M across 68 seats this cycle. Leading the Future, the biggest network, ends it with just over $20M left, and most Republicans backed by either camp lost.

United States Capitol, First Street Southeast, Washington, DC, USA

The AI industry’s biggest bet on a competitive general election race lost on Tuesday. Two super PACs linked to Leading the Future spent $4.8M backing Republican Darline Graham in South Carolina’s Senate race. She lost to Democrat Annie Andrews, who had called her “Data Center Darline”.

Most Republicans backed by either side of the AI industry’s spending fight lost, Fortune found in its tally of the closest races. It was the same night voters rejected AI data centres in 40 of 41 ballot measures. AI super PACs spent $79M across 68 House and Senate seats this cycle, according to Tech Influence Watch, a tracker run by writer Molly White.

The money comes from two networks. Leading the Future wants light regulation and a single national AI rulebook that overrides state laws. Andreessen Horowitz co-founders Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz gave it $25M each, according to filings reviewed by Fortune. OpenAI president Greg Brockman and his wife, Anna, are also among its biggest donors.

Public First, which has significant backing from Anthropic, wants stronger safeguards. Both networks run one arm for each party.

Leading the Future launched in August 2025 with a war chest of around $100M, WIRED reported. It ends the cycle with just over $20M in the bank. In October, OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman said AI money in politics was clearly not working.

The biggest fight came in June, in the Democratic primary for New York’s 12th District. Leading the Future spent more than $8.1M against Assemblymember Alex Bores, a co-author of the state’s RAISE Act. Public First spent about $15M backing him. Bores lost, finishing second to Micah Lasher, who also campaigned on AI safety.

Leading the Future then spent about $10M in the general election, mostly on safe seats, WIRED reported. Its Republican arm, American Mission, spent $590,428 backing Aaron Flint in Montana’s 1st District and $509,067 behind Laurie Buckhout in North Carolina’s 1st. Both conceded. Its Democratic arm, Think Big, backed Florida Rep. Jared Moskowitz, who won.

Public First’s Republican arm had a similar night. Defending Our Values spent $1.49M backing Carlos De La Cruz in Texas’s 35th District and $974,908 behind Rhett Marques in Alabama’s 2nd. Both lost. It also spent $857,426 backing Scott Singer against Moskowitz. Its Democratic arm, Jobs and Democracy, backed two winners in Ohio and Pennsylvania.

A conservative AI group, Alliance for a Better Future, spent just over $1M backing Mike Rogers in Michigan and $810,000 behind Susan Collins in Maine, Molly White wrote. Both lost.

Guardrails Alliance, a tech worker group pushing for stricter rules, spent more than $1M each against Flint and California Rep. Jimmy Gomez, TechCrunch reported. Gomez lost to Angela Gonzales-Torres.

Groups pushing for stronger rules claimed the result.

“Voters in both parties delivered the same verdict tonight. This is a crushing blow to the AI industry’s anti-regulatory efforts to buy a Congress that would look the other way.” Brad Carson, Public First Action, to WIRED

“Allying with the worst parts of the AI industry is just kryptonite for a campaign, and the results tonight double down on that.” Alex Bores, to Politico

Charlie Blaettler, Guardrails Alliance’s political director, told TechCrunch that Leading the Future held back in close races because its money would have become a liability for its candidates.

“Our goal is to make AI money politically toxic.” Charlie Blaettler, Guardrails Alliance, to TechCrunch

Before the vote, Leading the Future told TechCrunch that primaries are a better use of its money, because spending there builds name recognition and helps candidates set AI agendas. It said it would keep spending in 2028. It also leaves the cycle with dozens of winning candidates from both parties, WIRED noted, most of them in safe seats.

A Republican lobbyist pointed to the party’s message on AI.

“It’s proven to be incredibly unpopular, and ‘beat China’ did not resonate at all in places that it really needed to.” Greta Joynes, Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck, to Politico

Bores is already preparing for the next round. His new nonprofit, Who Decides, aims to raise $30M before 2028, Fortune reported.

#3258. Guarding the Gates of Knowledge

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

AI can fake a plausible paper at the push of a button. Can detection tools and peer review keep up?

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.

A recent scroll through social media got me thinking about trust. About half my feed was filled with AI slop that astute users would call out as being machine-generated, often to the embarrassment of the rube who unknowingly spread it and sometimes to the delight of the poster who shared it deliberately because they found it amusing or useful for sowing confusion.

Remember the good old days of GPT-3 when we could ask the chatbot anything and it would almost instantly and very confidently spit back a plausible but false answer? That’s when the word “hallucination” as applied to AI answers entered the lexicon. Six years and several versions of a few different chatbots later, I still can’t trust the answers I get, even though Claude or Gemini often do useful work for me. That’s the thing about current AI: Trust but verify. And verify you must.

Apply that maxim at scale to maintain the integrity of the scientific record and you get an idea of the challenge facing publishers of peer-reviewed scholarship. In “I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper,” freelance writer and doctor of applied mathematics Benjamin Skuse tells the story of the human gatekeepers trying to beat back the rising tide of AI slop by attempting to get his own AI-generated papers past IEEE’s defenses.

“He basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper.’ And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it.” —Eliza Strickland

As features and AI beat editor Eliza Strickland told me, Skuse was surprised at just how effortless it was to generate a paper that was more or less plausible and more or less science. For one of his experiments, “he basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper,’” she said. “And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it. He just launched it into the maw of the publishing engine.”

Skuse discovered that the combination of IEEE’s human-review processes and research-integrity checker programs are currently keeping pace in what amounts to a cat-and-mouse game against people using free tools. But the more advanced LLMs are no longer making the same dumb mistakes the free versions do. That leaves publishers locked in an arms race between increasingly plausible slop and the systems aimed at detecting it.

Scholarly publishers aren’t the only ones trying to hold the line against slop. So is that global depository of human-generated knowledge, Wikipedia. For this month’s Five Questions, Strickland interviewed Ellia Lebleu, a founding member of WikiProject AI Cleanup, a volunteer effort to detect and delete AI-generated material from the platform. Lebleu’s team is confronting the same problem as commercial publishers, but with fewer people and fewer tools.

“Wikipedia is known as a repository of human-generated information, and they want to hold on to that,” says Strickland. “Who knows how long they’ll be able to do that.”

If we can’t collectively assume that the scientific record is trustworthy or that basic facts about the world are accurate, then our understanding of what is real unspools into uncertainty. Perhaps that delights quantum scientists and the grifters who thrive in an information environment where there is no shared reality. But that uncertainty ultimately undermines trust in the institutions that exist to curate the corpus of human knowledge and to promote the advancement of science and technology for the benefit of humanity.

Or maybe in a world where AI is doing the science and writing the papers, it won’t matter whether or not humans trust the outputs. As Strickland put it, “Doesn’t it just feel crazy that we’ll have AI writing for other AIs at some point? We’ll just get left out of the loop.”

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.

#3257. Follow today’s midterm election results with the Apple News Live Activity

With votes now being counted in the US midterm elections, the Apple News app offers a convenient way to follow the results in real time. Here’s how it works.

Today is Election Day in the United States, with all 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 Senate seats up for election.

And with polls now closing and results starting to come in, Apple News is once again offering an easy way to keep track of the vote count, as it has done in recent elections.

As a refresher, Live Activities provide real-time updates from apps directly on your iPhone’s Lock Screen and, on supported models, in the Dynamic Island. This means you can keep track of information without having to constantly open an app.

U.S. users can open the Apple News app and then tap on the “Follow the 2026 midterms live” banner at the top of the screen.

Once enabled, the Live Activity will display election results as they become available, with updates throughout the vote count. This makes it possible to follow the election throughout the evening, even while using other apps on your iPhone.

For users who’d rather follow the results on their computers, Live Activities from your iPhone can also appear in your Mac’s menu bar through iPhone Mirroring, a feature introduced in macOS Tahoe 26.

You can also open Apple News for additional coverage and analysis of the 2026 midterm elections.

#3256. Musk’s midterm candidates lost almost everywhere, Texas included

Elon Musk gave at least $446 million to Republicans for the midterms, and most of his candidates lost. Tesla and SpaceX shares fell nearly 4% as the wider market rallied.

Elon Musk at the “New Golden Age” summit in Washington on 8 October 2026

Elon Musk was the biggest donor of the US midterms, and almost all of his money went to Republicans who lost. Texas, his adopted home and the base of Tesla and SpaceX, elected a Democratic senator and governor. On Wednesday, shares in both companies fell by nearly 4% as the wider market rallied.

The totals differ by outlet. Business Insider puts Musk’s donations at at least $446 million. A CNBC analysis of campaign finance records counts at least $474 million, as The New York Times does. Of that, $224 million went to Texas. Axios estimates $445 million. Before Tuesday’s vote, his record midterm donations were still a bet. Now they are a result.

America PAC, Musk’s super PAC, spent nearly $87 million across 44 federal races, CNBC found in filings with the Federal Election Commission. By Wednesday morning, the Republicans it backed had lost 29 and won three. Another 12 races had no winner yet. More than $80 million, or 93% of that spending, went to races Republicans lost.

In Texas, Democrat James Talarico beat Republican Ken Paxton for the Senate seat, and Gina Hinojosa unseated Governor Greg Abbott. In September alone, Musk gave $158 million to Senate Republicans’ main super PAC, Business Insider reported. That money went on to a group backing Paxton. America PAC spent more than $47 million against Talarico on top of that.

Talarico did not name Musk in his victory speech, as Business Insider reported, but the target was clear:

“The richest man in the world, the most powerful man in the world, and the entire Washington D.C. establishment. David wasn’t as big or as strong as Goliath.”

Musk stayed quiet on X for most of election night. He posted just before 1:15am Eastern time, Axios reported:

“Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn’t work this time.”

In another post, he joked that data centres in space looked appealing now, a nod to a SpaceX goal. His election day post urging followers to vote red had gone from his account by Wednesday, The Times reported.

Tesla closed down more than 3% and SpaceX nearly 4%, The New York Times reported. Meta, Microsoft, Google and the wider market rallied. The drops had been steeper before the open. Investor’s Business Daily reported falls of up to 6% for Tesla and 8% for SpaceX in premarket trading. SpaceX opened below its $135 IPO price for the first time since August.

Investors are watching the planned SpaceX and Tesla merger. Kathleen Brooks of the broker XTB told The Wall Street Journal:

“While Congress cannot stop a merger between SpaceX and Tesla, they could slow it down via extra scrutiny.”

Musk’s companies rely on state decisions on power, water, permits and tax breaks. Hinojosa has called for a moratorium on new data centres and an end to industry tax breaks, CNBC reported. Republicans still control the Texas Legislature, which limits what she can change. Voters across the country also rejected AI data centres at the ballot box.

Tesla and SpaceX are also building a chip plant in Texas worth more than $100 billion. Senator Ed Markey of Massachusetts gave The Times a statement on how Democrats would use their new power:

“To hold Musk and Tesla accountable for the risk their systems pose to our families and communities.”

Some protections will stay. The Texas law that shields company managers from shareholder lawsuits has support from both parties. It is unlikely to change, University of Texas law professor James Spindler told The Times.

Not everyone reads the night as the end of Musk’s influence. Alex Keena, a political scientist at Virginia Commonwealth University, told Fortune that the money still shapes the agenda:

“He basically gets to steer a political party.”

Trump still controls the federal agencies and holds a veto, which limits how far Democrats can reverse policies that help Musk’s businesses, CNBC noted. Eric Berger of Ars Technica wrote that the result may speed up SpaceX’s growth in Louisiana, which remains Republican, where it is already planning a second Starbase.

The next big test is the 2028 presidential race. That gives Musk two years to decide whether Democrats in Washington and Austin are rivals to fight or partners to bargain with.

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

Siva Rama Krishna Varma Bayyavarapu is an IEEE senior member and secretary of the IEEE Computer Society’s Central Indiana Chapter.

To help engineers keep up with emerging technologies such as AI, cloud computing, and sustainable infrastructure, and learn how they can be applied in practice, the IEEE Computer Society’s Central Indiana Chapter recently launched its Tech Talk Series.

The live webinar series connects IEEE members, undergrad and graduate students, and engineering professionals from IEEE Region 4 with industry practitioners. The monthly sessions have covered AI governance and security, agentic systems, and related topics. The sessions featured speakers from Apple, software company Tavant, and cybersecurity concern Zscaler.

Upcoming sessions and registration details are available on the IEEE Region 4 virtual events calendar.

Rather than presenting on emerging technologies only at a conceptual level, speakers discussed the design decisions behind specific tools and systems, how the systems are structured, and implementation challenges. They also shared lessons learned from using the tools in their daily work.

Sessions also include technical walkthroughs and practical examples.

The live format allows attendees to discuss and compare their approaches when evaluating and implementing new technologies with those used by other organizations.

The organizers chose to make the series virtual so that chapter members and other attendees could participate in technical discussions with engineers from major technology companies and eliminate the need to travel.

For young professionals, the sessions connect what they’ve learned in a classroom with the realities of the workplace.

Technical programs such as the Tech Talk Series give professionals and students access to expertise, help create connections across career levels, and make important engineering discussions available to a broader community.

Attendees learn how practitioners approach projects such as system architecture, reliability, security, governance, and product delivery. For experienced professionals, the talks offer a forum to examine new ways of designing, securing, and operating software systems, and compare technical approaches. They can ask questions relevant to systems being evaluated or deployed within their organization.

The most recent webinar, Feeding and Fencing AI Agents: Engineering Governed Agentic Systems on Real-Time Data, featured Gajendra Babu Thokala, a senior engineering leader at Apple in Seattle.

The IEEE senior member explained how teams can move beyond adding isolated AI features to applications and instead build governed AI-agent systems that use real-time business data to complete multistep business workflows.

Another recent session, Building AI Native Products: A Playbook for Agentic Systems, explored how products built around AI agents differ from traditional software. It also covered how agentic systems can help users complete multistep tasks and workflows. IEEE Senior Member Sandeep Shivam, a product and technology leader at Tavant in Dallas, led the webinar.

Those two sessions illustrate the series’ purpose: helping participants understand what a technology can do and what is required to use it responsibly.

Future sessions are being planned on areas including enterprise AI, software reliability, and responsible AI usage. In addition to speakers from technology companies, the chapter also plans to invite speakers from startups, universities, and research organizations.

Upcoming sessions are expected to cover cloud platforms, enterprise integrations, and the responsible development of AI systems.

Technical programs such as the Tech Talk Series give professionals and students access to expertise, help create connections across career levels, and make important engineering discussions available to a broader community.

When Sonos tried a major app update two years ago, things did not go well. Much-loved features disappeared, older speakers experienced connection problems, and accessibility features were broken. That debacle saw the company’s CEO fired.

The company is taking a much more cautious approach as it moves into the AI era with a Sonos 27voice update, enabling natural-language voice control via Hey Sonos requests …

The whole mess started when Sonos launched the company’s first headphones, the Ace, intended to compete with AirPods Max. The app needed to be updated to support these, and the company decided to use it as an opportunity for a ground-up rebuild, launching a completely new app just ahead of the launch.

Customers responded angrily to the loss of key functionality, compatibility issues with older speakers, and accessibility problems. Sonos initially downplayed the complaints, but CEO Patrick Spence subsequently emailed customers to apologize, and provide a timeline for fixes, subsequently making seven promises. However, customers weren’t impressed, and called for Spence to be fired – later getting their wish.

This time around, Sonos started out with a modest update in the form of the Sonos 27 app, leaving the more substantial changes to a subsequent Sonos 27voice version. This will replace the more limited voice control available today, much like the update from old Siri to Siri AI.

Rather than pushing it out to all customers, Sonos is adopting a very cautious approach. First, you’ll have to request early access to the beta and be approved. The new features work in much the same way as Siri on HomePods.

You can use Sonos 27voice at any time by saying the wake word, “Hey Sonos.” While Sonos is listening, the white status light on your Sonos product will glow brighter and the volume will lower if any audio is playing. A confirmation tone will play after Sonos understands your request.

#3250. AMD expects to outsell Intel for the first time after a record quarter

AMD’s earnings show data centre revenue up 97% to $8.5 billion in a record $13.4 billion quarter. Gaming fell 40%, and free cash flow dropped by almost two thirds.

AMD CEO Lisa Su shows a 6th Gen EPYC “Verano” processor at the OCP Global Summit in San Jose on 12 October

AMD expects about $17 billion in revenue this quarter. If it gets there, it will sell more than Intel in a quarter for the first time. The forecast came with record third-quarter results. Its data centre business nearly doubled, while gaming sales fell by 40%.

Revenue rose 45% to $13.4 billion in the quarter to 26 September, AMD said on Tuesday. The Intel comparison first appeared in Tom’s Hardware. Intel expects $15 billion to $16 billion for the same quarter. That forecast sent its shares into their steepest fall in decades.

“We delivered a record quarter with revenue exceeding the high end of our guidance as Data Center segment sales nearly doubled year-over-year.” Lisa Su, AMD chair and CEO

Both numbers beat Wall Street. Analysts had expected $13.09 billion for the third quarter and $16.2 billion for the fourth. Those are LSEG estimates, cited by CNBC. Going into the results, AMD needed a big quarter after a week of AI chip selling.

Data centre revenue rose 97% to a record $8.5 billion, about 64% of the total. AMD credited demand for its EPYC server processors and the launch of its Instinct MI450 GPUs. The unit’s operating income rose to $2.9 billion from $1.1 billion a year earlier.

Anthropic, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI and Oracle are running workloads on AMD’s first Helios racks, the company said. Meta said last week that its racks were running, as AMD agreed to invest $1bn in Meta.

Su told analysts on the earnings call that she expects much more next year:

“We have said the overall company will grow greater than 80 percent, and for the data center CPU business, we will about double, and for the data center AI business, it will significantly more than double.” Lisa Su, on the earnings call

Chief financial officer Jean Hu said on the call that she expects data centres to make up more than 80% of revenue in time. Su also said AMD had secured the wafers, packaging, memory and other parts it needs for that growth.

The rest of the business moved the other way. Gaming revenue fell 40% to $773 million, which AMD put down to lower semi-custom and graphics sales. Semi-custom chips are the processors it supplies for game consoles. Su said on the call that AMD expected the drop at this stage of the console cycle.

Client revenue, mostly Ryzen PC processors, rose 7% to $2.9 billion on sales of mobile chips. Memory prices are squeezing the wider PC market. Su said she expects it to shrink by a double-digit percentage next year. Embedded revenue rose 29% to $1.1 billion.

Operating income more than doubled to $2.8 billion and net income rose 95% to $2.4 billion. Cash did not keep pace. Free cash flow fell to $554 million from $1.53 billion a year earlier, AMD’s tables show. Inventories took $3 billion, and capital spending more than doubled to $648 million.

AMD also expects its gross margin to narrow slightly to about 55% this quarter, from 56% in the third. The shares rose about 8% after hours on Tuesday, CNBC reported. They gave back part of the gain as US election results came in.

The Intel milestone depends on AMD landing inside its own forecast. The range runs from about $16.5 billion to $17.5 billion. Even the bottom of that range sits above the top of Intel’s.

Apple this week warned that memory costs will reduce its holiday quarter profit margins.

MindStudio shows that skipping the charger could speed things up

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

We all know that plugging in your laptop is supposed to make it faster, but new testing of an Nvidia-powered laptop found the exact opposite, with AI performance dropping by nearly 80% when running Linux.

The surprising discovery comes from MindStudio, which tested an MSI Prestige N16 Flip AI+ powered by Nvidia's RTX Spark platform. The team wanted to see whether Linux could run on the machine without sacrificing the performance available through Windows.

It could, but there was a major catch. When running OpenAI's GPT-OSS-120B model, the laptop generated 65.4 tokens per second on Windows. Running Linux directly on the same hardware while plugged into a charger brought that figure down to just 13.9 tokens per second.

That's a nearly 79% reduction in AI performance simply from changing the operating system. But even stranger, unplugging the laptop brought much of that performance back.

Nvidia's RTX Spark platform is designed to bring powerful AI capabilities to laptops. The MSI laptop tested by MindStudio supports up to 128GB of unified memory, allowing users to run large AI models directly on their devices instead of relying on cloud services.

However, MindStudio found that the laptop's AI performance varied dramatically depending on whether it was running Windows or Linux.

Here's how the same AI model performed across the tested configurations:

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

The performance gap showed up in other tests, too. Windows completed one AI workload in roughly eight minutes, while Linux took 37 minutes to finish the same task.

MindStudio initially considered whether overheating might be responsible, but temperatures stayed between 40 and 47 degrees Celsius. Instead, the team found that the GPU was running at much lower clock speeds under Linux.

On Windows, the GPU reached approximately 2.2 GHz. But when running Linux while plugged in, that speed dropped to around 780 MHz, helping explain the dramatic difference in performance.

The researchers traced the problem to an Nvidia component called Platform Controllers and Framework.

On Windows, this component manages how the laptop distributes power between its CPU and GPU. Linux doesn't currently have equivalent support for the system tested, leaving the GPU unable to reach its expected speeds when plugged in.

MindStudio tested that explanation by disabling the controller in Windows. Performance immediately dropped, and GPU clock speeds fell to approximately the same levels seen under Linux. Restoring the controller brought performance back.

The team also reported that the firmware's power-management information is encrypted, preventing Linux from accessing the settings needed to control the GPU properly. That helps explain the strangest discovery of all: when running Linux on battery power, the laptop produced roughly 61 to 67 tokens per second in separate testing. Plugging it in dropped performance to around 15 tokens per second. So, yea, the laptop actually performed substantially better when disconnected from its charger.

The good news is that users who want Linux-based AI tools don't necessarily have to sacrifice performance. MindStudio found that Windows Subsystem for Linux, better known as WSL, delivered almost identical performance to running Windows directly.

That's because WSL uses the Windows driver system, including the power-management components that allow Nvidia's GPU to reach its full speed.

There are some limitations. The researchers had to adjust WSL's memory allocation to accommodate larger AI models. Installing Linux directly also required additional workarounds for hardware support and memory configuration.

For now, WSL appears to offer the better experience on the tested hardware.

Keep in mind that these findings are from one study and do not mean that every Nvidia-powered laptop will slow down when running Linux. The testing focused on a specific RTX Spark system, and the results haven't been independently replicated across other laptop models.

It's also important to distinguish these laptops from Nvidia's DGX Spark desktop, which runs Linux and performed substantially better in the same benchmark.

Still, the results raise questions about software support for a new generation of PCs designed to run powerful AI models locally.

For consumers considering an RTX Spark laptop specifically for Linux-based AI workloads, the operating system could make an enormous difference to the performance they actually get.

Until Nvidia provides equivalent power-management support for Linux, buyers may find that keeping Windows installed is the fastest option.

Tom’s Guide has reached out to Nvidia for comment and will update this story if the company responds.

#3247. Claude’s share of UK AI subscription spending quadruples in seven months

A study of 14.2 million UK bank accounts finds adults spend £1.07bn a year on AI subscriptions. Claude users are 20 times likelier to pay for £80-plus plans.

Anthropic’s Claude took 29.4% of UK consumer spending on AI subscriptions in July. In December 2025, its share was 7.4%. ChatGPT’s share fell from 73.5% to 52.5% over the same seven months. The figures come from a new study of UK bank and card data, published on Thursday.

The working paper, Who Pays for AI?, is by three economists. Nikhil Datta and Peter John Lambert are at the University of Warwick, and Patrick Schneider is at Imperial Business School. They used de-identified records from 14.2 million UK accounts, supplied by a financial data aggregator.

UK adults now spend about £1.07 billion a year on AI assistants at July’s rate, the study found. In June, 5.1% of adults paid for one, about 2.8 million people. A year earlier, the share was 2.3%.

“The first thing that surprised me is just the sheer volume of everything.” Peter Lambert, University of Warwick, to Bloomberg

Lambert told Bloomberg it is “unheard of” for a paid consumer technology to reach millions of adults this fast.

The study counts only subscriptions people pay for themselves, not licences employers buy for staff. It counts accounts rather than people, and it estimates app store payments it cannot see directly. With those included, Claude’s share of spending in July falls to 22.8%.

The payers skew young, male, well paid and urban. Adults in their 20s were nearly five times as likely as those over 60 to have ever paid for one. That holds after adjusting for income, sex and region. Men were 27% more likely to pay than women.

London had the highest share of payers and the North East the lowest. By occupation, IT professionals led at 20.3%, while social care workers were lowest at 1.7%.

The study lands as both companies prepare to go public. Anthropic’s amended IPO filing shows $17bn in revenue. OpenAI president Greg Brockman said on Wednesday that his company should be ready for an IPO in 2027.

Brockman told the WSJ Tech conference that OpenAI had a “pretty rough” first half in coding, The Wall Street Journal reported. He said its new tools turned that around in the third quarter.

OpenAI is also pointing to the size of ChatGPT’s user base. ChatGPT now has 1.2 billion weekly users, up from 1 billion two months earlier. Adam Fry, its consumer product lead, gave the figure to Big Technology on Monday.

You can expect to see more ads in the Reddit app as the platform begins placing them in search results. The company says that it will be evaluating how users respond to the development …

Reddit’s announcement says that ads will be based on a range of factors, including the search query.

I’ll respond by blocking them like always.

The goal is to leverage search results pages with a “high purchase and search intent.” In other words, where the company believes that you are searching for advice on buying a particular type of product.

Reddit says this will initially involve a relatively small number of advertisers before a wider rollout.

#3245. I just tested Apple’s first touchscreen OLED MacBook — and I still can’t believe my eyes

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Unlock and manage exclusive Tom’s Guide member rewards.

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display impresses thanks to its astonishing touchscreen OLED display that’s the brightest we’ve ever seen on a laptop. On top of that, it has a thinner, lighter design, punchy speakers, and super-long battery life. Plus. Apple finally ditches the notch. While it’s very expensive, this marvelous laptop will floor you.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display ($2,899 to start) is the finest laptop I’ve had the pleasure of testing. There’s a lot of hype around Apple’s first touchscreen OLED MacBook, and I can tell you it far surpasses it. Though it commands a steep asking price, I’d argue that this laptop is worth every penny for the pros thanks to the excellent experience you get.

The tandem OLED panel is a stunner, delivering inky blacks and scorching bright whites. You instantly notice the 10 million-to-1 contrast ratio, which also makes colors pop. Then there’s the touch functionality, which is the most responsive I’ve used on any touchscreen laptop. Combine these features with the Dynamic Island (finally) replacing the notch, and you have the best display ever on a MacBook. This is especially true for models with the optional anti-glare nano-texture display.

Apple didn’t stop with the upgraded display, as this MacBook Pro also has a thinner, slimmer design than its siblings. The 14-inch MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display weighs just a little more than a MacBook Air! You also get nearly 17 hours of battery life, blowing away the Windows competition. The cherry on top with the new design is the return of the iconic glowing Apple logo on the lid. In short, Apple somehow perfected its already stellar MacBook design.

While the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is decidedly expensive with the same performance as the MacBook Pro laptops released in March 2026, it’s easily one of the best MacBooks and best laptops you can buy. If you can afford it, you won’t be disappointed. Find out more in my full review of the 14- and 16-inch OLED MacBook Pros.

14.2-inch PROLED XDR (3024 x 1986 pixels), 120Hz, multi-touch

16.3-inch PROLED XDR (3472 x 2266 pixels), 120Hz, multi-touch

M5 Pro (15-core CPU / 16-core GPU / 16-core Neural Engine)

M5 Pro (18 CPU cores, 20 GPU cores/ 16-core Neural Engine)

3 x Thunderbolt 5, 1 x HDMI, 1 x 3.5mm headphone jack, 1 x SD card reader, 1 x MagSafe 3

3 x Thunderbolt 5, 1 x HDMI, 1 x 3.5mm headphone jack, 1 x SD card reader, 1 x MagSafe 3

The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display offers a premium laptop experience, with a magnificent tandem OLED panel, elegant yet utilitarian design, and intuitive touchscreen controls. There’s a lot to love here.

MacBook Pros have used the same design since late 2021. Apple hasn’t radically redesigned the MacBook Pro OLED, retaining the sturdy, squared-off aluminum chassis with rounded edges. However, the new laptops are thinner and lighter than previous models—the 14- and 16-inch MacBook Pros weigh 0.5 and 0.7 pounds less, respectively, than their predecessors. If you use MacBook Pros as often as I do, you’ll feel the weight difference the instant you pick up either new laptop.

As before, you can open the lid with one hand. This is especially noteworthy because Apple redesigned the lids to better withstand constant tapping and swiping. The lid is also noticeably thinner yet remains very sturdy and doesn’t wobble. Apple has reduced the border size by 15%, resulting in thinner bezels. Lastly, the lid features the glowing Apple logo with a dedicated backlight, signaling to everyone that you’re using a PROLED MacBook Pro.

Sign up to the Tom's iGuide weekly newsletter with coverage on everything from product launches to software updates, this is your go-to source for the latest updates on all the best Apple content.

The keyboard looks and feels the same as on other MacBook Pros I’ve tested, which is great since they’re among the best laptop keyboards. Whether it’s the 14- or 16-inch model, the keyboard deck is spacious, and the keys are highly responsive, with excellent travel and just the right amount of resistance when pressed. The huge touchpad is also as great as ever, never failing to respond to my gestures. Speaking of touch, the Touch ID button is still here for easier logins. Unfortunately, Face ID is still not supported.

You get the same array of ports here, including three Thunderbolt 5/USB-C ports, an HDMI port, a 3.5mm headphone jack, an SD card slot, and a MagSafe charging port.

Pardon the cliché, but the panel on the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is a feast for the eyes. Even our lab tester, who tests the best TVs for a living, said he has never seen a lovelier display! I wholeheartedly agree.

The latest trailer for Dune: Messiah showcases what makes the PROLED’s panel such a marvel. The superb contrast renders nighttime scenes appropriately dark, while Arakis’ scorching sun makes you squint during daytime sequences. I’m also impressed by the level of detail on the characters’ dusty faces, thanks to the sharp resolution of both models.

549.8% (SDR) | 1949 (HDR, 10% of display)

Our lab tests confirmed what my eyes saw. Apple claims the PROLED MacBook Pros can reach 2000 nits of brightness, and our display benchmarks were just a hair under that mark. The brightest laptop displays we’ve tested topped out at 1600 nits, but Apple’s notebooks go well beyond that. It’s even more impressive when you consider that images remain clearly defined even when portions of the display are set to maximum brightness.

Color reproduction (sRGB and DCI-P3) is identical on the two PROLED laptops. Color accuracy (Delta-E) is slightly better than on most of the laptops I’ve tested. Combined with the 10 million-to-1 contrast ratio, you get truly exceptional display quality.

Moving away from benchmarks, let’s discuss the other major display upgrade—the removal of the notch at the top center. While I’ve never been too bothered by the notch, I’m not sad to see it replaced with the Dynamic Island, which makes it easy to access Live Activities. I like how the Dynamic Island expands when you’re playing videos and music, and how you can use the touchscreen to stop playback, fast-forward, and rewind.

The PROLED MacBook Pro with M5 Pro supports up to three external displays (up to 6K/60Hz or 4K/165Hz), or one display up to 8K/60Hz, 5K/120Hz, or 4K/240Hz paired with a second up to 5K/120Hz or 4K/200Hz. The M5 Max model steps this up to four external displays (up to 6K/60Hz or 4K/165Hz), or two displays up to 8K/60Hz, 5K/120Hz, or 4K/240Hz.

Both chips can power the laptop's built-in PROLED XDR screen at full resolution at the same time. Thanks to Thunderbolt 5’s native DisplayPort 2.1 bandwidth, you can connect three or four external monitors through a single port using compatible docks or daisy-chaining.

As we detailed in our 10 things you need to know about the MacBook Pro OLED, most laptops use a separate, distinct digitizer to support touch input. Apple found a way to integrate the touch silicon directly into these laptops’ tandem OLED displays. The result? A super precise touchscreen experience.

I’ve tested dozens of Windows touchscreen laptops, but none have felt as responsive or intuitive as on the MacBook Pro OLED. Because of that, tapping, swiping, and even pinch-to-zoom are as smooth and snappy as on an iPad Pro.

I’ve tested dozens of Windows touchscreen laptops, but none have felt as responsive or intuitive as on the MacBook Pro OLED. Because of that, tapping, swiping, and even pinch-to-zoom are as smooth and snappy as on an iPad Pro. I didn't notice any input lag. Menu bar items expand under your fingertip, and window controls get bigger, making things easier to see and interact with.

So far, I haven’t encountered any compatibility issues with third-party apps. Google apps, such as Docs and Drive, work well with touch based on my testing. And naturally, Apple’s own apps work seamlessly. I’ll keep testing to see if I run into any issues, but so far macOS seems like a natural fit for touch.

I don’t often use touch controls on laptops with touchscreens because they can feel clunky, but I found myself using the MacBook Pro’s touch controls more than I expected. That’s a testament to how well touch is implemented on these laptops.

MacBook Pros have always featured excellent speakers that deliver incredible sound, but even that experience didn’t prepare me for how amazing the speakers are on the new MacBook Pro OLED laptops.

Apple says the enhanced six-speaker sound system now delivers 50 percent deeper bass. And that’s not just marketing bluster. It was the first thing I heard, or rather, felt, when I fired up Tommy Johansson’s cover of Black Sabbath’s “Headless Cross.” The rumbling bass notes beneath the ripping solos and soaring vocals made it feel like a live performance—and no doubt annoyed my neighbors when I had the volume cranked up.

The movie trailer for the latest Godzilla Minus Zero also sounds spectacular on the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display. Explosions, screams, and Godzilla’s iconic roar all came through loud and punchy. And naturally, voices in dialogue-heavy content like the Triple K.O. podcast also sound impressive.

Speakers can almost feel like an afterthought on some laptops, but that’s certainly not the case here. Whether it’s the 14- or 16-inch MacBook Pro, your ears won’t be disappointed. The sound system on these laptops is every bit as impressive as the display.

Even if the M5 Pro and M5 Max chips in the new OLED MacBook Pros aren’t technically new like the Apple M6 chip, they’re still the most powerful M-series chips available for MacBooks. Since these are the same chips we’ve already tested on the 14- and 16-inch MacBook Pros from March, these laptops deliver comparable performance.

The 14-inch MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display Apple sent us (valued at $3,699 as configured) has an M5 Pro chip with an 18-core CPU / 20-core GPU, 48GB of RAM, a 1TB SSD, and a glossy display.

Meanwhile, the 16-inch model I reviewed (valued at $8,549) packs an M5 Max chip with an 18-core CPU / 40-core GPU, 128GB of RAM, a 4TB SSD, and a nano-texture display. Thanks to those specs, both laptops pack a serious performance punch.

Geekbench AI (Quantized Core ML/Neural Engine)

On the Geekbench CPU benchmark, both the 14- and 16-inch PROLEDs delivered strong single- and multi-core scores. They also scored well in Geekbench’s AI benchmarks.

As you can see above, OLED touchscreen competitors like the Dell XPS 16 (currently $2,469) and Lenovo Yoga 9n (currently $2,999) don’t come close in performance. For your reference, the XPS 16 packs an Intel Core Ultra X7 358H CPU, 32GB of RAM, and a 1TB SSD, while the Yoga 9n has an Nvidia RTX Spark N1X chip, 32GB of RAM, and a 1TB SSD.

Surprise, surprise, the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display also crushed it in our other benchmarks. Disk speeds are extremely zippy, and the same is true for video transcoding. In fact, the new MacBook was more than 2x as fast as the Dell XPS 16.

Apple’s MacBook PROLED laptops are also more than capable of handling tasks in Adobe creative apps like Photoshop and Premiere Pro. Again, the competition can’t keep pace with Apple’s notebooks.

3DMark Wild Life Extreme Unlimited (score / fps)

The PROLEDs aren’t slouches at gaming. On the 3DMark Wild Life Extreme Unlimited GPU benchmark, the laptops scored well, with the M5 Max model performing significantly better thanks to its beefy 40-core GPU. The RTX Spark-powered Yoga 9n didn’t do badly, but Apple’s Pro laptops still outclassed it in this benchmark.

For real-world gaming, I tested Cyberpunk 2077 on both PROLED models. With the “For This Mac” graphics setting, the game ran at 85 fps and 95 fps, respectively. Cyberpunk 2077 is a graphically demanding game that pushes even powerful PCs to their limits, so these results are very impressive.

MacBooks with M-series chips are among the longest-lasting laptops we’ve ever tested. But I wasn’t expecting this kind of endurance, since there appears to be no “power penalty” for Apple adding an OLED touchscreen.

In Tom’s Guide’s battery life test, which involves continuous web surfing over Wi-Fi with the display set to 150 nits of brightness, the 14-inch MacBook Pro PROLED lasted 16 hours and 56 minutes, while its 16-inch counterpart endured 21 hours and 24 minutes. The previous non-touch 16-inch MacBook Pro M5 Pro lasted 21:10. This is yet another test in which Windows laptops are handily outclassed.

We always run three battery tests to calculate an average time, but we could only run one test in time for this review. I’ll update once we’ve completed the full testing, but based on my experience, the final results will be just as epic.

The webcam on the new PROLED MacBooks is mostly the same as before, only with a new stabilization feature to prevent screen wobble if you’re actively using the touchscreen display. As before, the camera can record 1080p video and also has Desk View.

The 12-megapixel Center Stage camera is as great as ever. This photo I took in my apartment late at night captures all the details on my face, clothing, and even in my background. During a Google Meet session, colleagues on the call also said my video looked sharp.

The new MacBook Pros come with macOS Golden Gate installed. Like I said in my macOS Golden Gate review, this update isn’t a complete overhaul like macOS Sequoia, but it brings a slew of new and enhanced AI features and smoother overall performance that make using MacBooks feel more personal and streamlined.

macOS Golden Gate now includes a dedicated Siri AI app that works like a typical chatbot. In a dedicated chat window, you can ask Siri AI questions or talk to it about whatever’s on your mind. Siri is baked into the OS, so it can recognize what’s on your screen and do things like add items to your calendar or create shortcuts by speaking what you want instead of building them manually.

A new Liquid Glass UI slider lets you adjust the effect’s opacity more precisely. You’ll also notice that complex background visuals appear more diffused, improving text readability. Icon edges are more pronounced so they stand out more. This feature should have been in Sequoia, but at least it’s here now in Golden Gate.

Another highlight of macOS Golden Gate is Spatial Reframing, which is also available on iOS and iPadOS. Reframe lets you reframe existing photos and adjust the perspective to your liking. If you’ve taken a lot of photos with your iPhone or iPad, this feature is a great way to make them look exactly how you want.

macOS Golden Gate goes big on AI, especially with the new and improved Siri. If that doesn’t matter to you, you’ll still enjoy a smooth, stable macOS experience overall.

The new OLED MacBook Pros are easily the most impressive laptops I’ve ever tested, but all those amazing features come at a steep cost.

I wasn’t expecting the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display to be cheap, given all the high-end components it uses. That said, I can’t help but wonder how much these laptops would have cost without RAMageddon inflating electronics prices. I suppose that doesn’t matter, because in this reality, you’ll have to pay a premium for Apple’s high-end touchscreen laptop.

Tech enthusiasts or anyone who can be more productive with a touchscreen laptop will get their money’s worth with the PROLED MacBook Pros. If you want to save money on a MacBook Pro and don’t need the performance of the M5 Pro/M5 Max chips, or if an OLED touchscreen isn’t important to you, the new M6-powered 14-inch MacBook Pro starts at $1,999. That’s also expensive, but still $900 less than the entry-level MacBook Pro PROLED.

Since the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display uses the same M5 Pro and M5 Max chips as the regular MacBook Pros we’ve tested, performance gains are negligible at best. This matters if you're considering upgrading from those MacBook Pros to the new touchscreen laptops.

Geekbench AI (Quantized Core ML/Neural Engine)

3DMark Wild Life Extreme Unlimited (score / fps)

I selected some benchmarks I discussed earlier to show you how these MacBook Pros compare in performance. As you can see, the gains are minor at best. So unless you are set on owning a touchscreen OLED MacBook, it might be wiser to save your money for future iterations that deliver a substantial performance boost over what you currently own.

I thought the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display could be amazing, but it shattered and exceeded my expectations. The new tandem OLED display raises the bar for laptops in brightness and color reproduction. Smooth touchscreen controls, a lighter design, and booming audio take Apple’s new machine to the next level. Yes, it’s very expensive, but it’s a brilliant laptop that makes competitors pale in comparison.

Apple’s first attempt at a touchscreen MacBook is mostly a success, but I’m already curious to see what future iterations bring to the table. If this initial laptop is anything to go by, we’re in for some truly fantastic devices. For now, Apple has made good with these laptops. They truly are the best of the best.

#3244. With iOS 27.3, Apple will start checking iCloud public links for ‘harmful content’

iOS 27.3 adds lots of new iPhone features, and it also makes a change to how public iCloud links work with the aim of preventing harmful content from being shared. Here are the details.

This week Apple released the first iOS 27.3 beta, which adds Siri AI improvements, new Safari features, the all-new Apple Health app, and more.

Per a newly published support document on Apple’s website, iOS 27.3, macOS 27.3, and more also include a key change to how iCloud public links work.

Apple currently provides two main options when sharing photos, files, and more via iCloud. You can share with ‘People you choose’ or create a public link that works for ‘Anyone with the link.’

Starting with iOS 27.3 and companion updates, the ‘Anyone with the link’ option will start being checked by Apple for harmful content.

When you share content that’s stored in iCloud, such as a photo in iCloud Photos or a file in iCloud Drive, you can choose to Share a Link or Send a Copy of the item. If you choose Share a Link, you can either share the item with “People you choose” — only people you invite or approve — or with “Anyone with the link,” which makes it accessible to anyone who has the link, including Apple. Starting in version 27.3 or later of iOS, iPadOS, macOS, and visionOS, items shared using Anyone with the Link will be checked by Apple for harmful content.

If Apple flags the content you’re sharing as harmful, the support doc says it “reserves the right to move, refuse, modify, remove, or delete the content at any time.”

For anyone trying to upload harmful content, the company may “take action against your Apple Account, including blocking or disabling your Apple Account, blocking the ability to create a new Apple Account with the associated email address or phone number, or if necessary, involving law enforcement.”

As outlined above, choosing the ‘Anyone with the link’ option has always made it accessible to “anyone who has the link, including Apple.” That’s because it’s a public link.

What’s changing now, though, is that Apple says it will begin checking those public links for harmful content.

Do you use iCloud public links? What’s your take on this change? Let us know in the comments.

#3243. Living with Mom and trading on margin. The regular investor gets in on Wall Street's record stock borrowing binge

HOUSTON — During a late night at home in May 2021, Hy Luu, a 29-year-old engineering consultant, was researching how to obtain more capital to invest in shares of Tesla.

That's when he discovered margin investing: the act of borrowing money from a broker to buy securities such as stocks, while using existing investments as collateral. Borrowing would give him more buying power, and he could pay it back as the stock appreciated. The main risk would be a margin call, or having to deposit more money into the account, if its value fell.

It was all too good to be true, Luu thought.

Luu — who lives with his mother, Kim Nguyen, in a three-bedroom, two-bathroom house in Houston — decided to get her opinion on the topic, given that she used to work as an accountant and just so happened to still be awake that evening. The 66-year-old retiree found it interesting.

That was the reassurance he needed, and it wasn't long before he started using margin to invest in Tesla for the first time. A year or so later, he had amassed more than $100,000 of margin debt.

"I went really crazy," he told CNBC in an interview. "The stock was going up, and so I was like, 'There's no way I could lose.'"

After five years of margin investing — including a period in 2022 where he worried that further declines in Tesla could trigger a margin call — Luu is working to pay down his largest margin balance ever. In June, he exercised $165,000 on five Tesla call options and bought 500 shares at $330 per share. After accounting for the cash in his account, this drove his borrowing to more than $156,000.

Tesla swung from below $370 a share to more than $430 during that month.

Between his Tesla investments, his company stock and 401(k) — while subtracting his margin debt as well as other debt he's accumulated, such as his car loan and student loans — Luu's net worth has skyrocketed to more than $800,000 from negative territory seven years ago.

"I'm very close to becoming a millionaire," the investor said. He did stress, "What I'm doing is risky. I don't recommend anyone do it."

Yet, Luu has found himself part of a growing trend taking hold in the market.

Retail investors like Luu are borrowing more and more money to invest. Robinhood's margin book grew to a record $21.6 billion in the second quarter, up 127% year over year and a 332% increase from the $5 billion seen in Q2 2024. To margin invest on the platform, eligible users must have a portfolio value of at least $2,000.

"Robinhood has made a really concerted effort to go after customers that are actively using margin because they're the most active traders," said Devin Ryan, head of financial technology research at Citizens.

Brokerage firms can benefit from margin investing by collecting interest on margin loans, while highly active customers can also generate additional trading-related revenue.

"If you look at the offers that Robinhood has had in the market over the past couple of years, it's been targeting those customers with obviously transfer bonuses, but also very low margin rates, very high yields on their cash," Ryan said.

To be sure, other parts of Robinhood's business are also growing, including retirement assets — which have nearly quadrupled in the last two years.

Another factor fueling the rise in margin investing is easier access through smartphones, according to Ryan.

"Having very little friction in investing and having everything at your fingertips, and then having a really seamless mobile experience where it's not clunky, I think, plays a big part of that," he said.

A Robinhood spokesperson told CNBC its products are designed to appeal to a number of customers, saying that "we don't believe it's accurate to characterize" its transfer promotions as specifically targeting "active traders who are trading on margin or may trade on margin." The company said it tries to "meet users where they are," and they "reject any implication" that the company is "encouraging risky trading."

Robinhood's margin debt isn't the only one reaching records. Total margin debt hit an all-time high of around $1.5 trillion in June, per the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority, which incorporates data on both institutional investors such as hedge funds and retail investors.

Not all of that debt is driven by fresh borrowing due to new borrowing decisions. For example, as equities rise in value, an investor may need to cover a short position that's been marked to market, or valued at its current price.

Nonetheless, Sam Huszczo, chief investment officer at SGH Wealth Management, thinks the market's bull run — which has seen multiple record highs this year alone — is feeding a shift in investor psychology, and margin debt is one sign.

"That's greed," the founder said, adding that it's "not everywhere" in the market, but it's "certainly creeping into pockets."

"Margin, that's only the tip of the iceberg of what we can see," he continued. "Fear of missing out is just the emotion of jealousy with a brokerage account."

Huszczo considers the market to actually be "way healthier" than people think. Though he recognizes that increasing margin debt and the rise of risky assets such as leveraged ETFs inject more fragility in the system.

"People need to differentiate between what's a legitimate momentum growth investment and what's reckless chasing," Huszczo also said.

Huszczo shares the commonly held belief among financial advisors that investors' portfolios shouldn't be overly concentrated in one stock or even one sector.

Yet Luu has been zeroed in on Tesla ever since he bought his first share in late 2019. Earlier that year, he had started his current job — a time when he knew nothing about investing, he said. It wasn't until a co-worker told him to download Robinhood months later that he began looking into stocks and other assets.

"I started making money, and I quickly learned, 'Now I'm making money, what do I do with it?'" he said. "I started investing in index funds and even in crypto, and then I did the math. I looked at the returns, and I was like, 'This is very slow returns. I'm never gonna reach retirement, financial independence until like 65.'"

Little did he know that a decision he had made that summer would become his guiding light.

"I was choosing between a Honda Civic and a Tesla Model 3, and my friend, he scheduled a test drive for me to drive the Model 3," Luu said. "My plan was only to go into it just to test drive it. I wasn't going to buy anything. I wasn't going to put in any reservation. Long story short, after the test drive, I put in my reservation the same day, and I got the car like two weeks later."

Seeing the value the car provides in his life, Luu said he can envision a future where electric and autonomous vehicles are commonplace. Because of how much he believes in that future, he considers Tesla the "easiest" investment he's made, and over the course of seven years of investing in the company, he has generally held his shares.

However, things got a bit more difficult with his strategy when Tesla shares began falling in 2022, putting him in the vulnerable position of potentially receiving a margin call. 2022 was Tesla's worst year on record, with the stock finishing off the year at $123.18 after a roughly 65% decline.

In search of more capital, Luu made a serious financial decision with his mother's approval.

"I refinanced the house to get access to an extra $30,000 of capital, and I used that to pay down my margin debt," he said.

Luu understands the level of risk that accompanies trading with margin. Because he's been using margin for most of the nearly seven years he's been investing in Tesla, he has deemed his investing strategy "gambling with an asterisk."

For now, it has paid off. In the last five years, Tesla shares have risen more than 43% to $375. However, the volatile stock is about 25% off of its all-time high near $499.

"It's very easy to see it as gambling, because obviously all your money is in one stock, and that's inherently risky," he said. "But the reason why I say there's nuance to it is because it's a matter of investing temperament, financial discipline and time horizon."

With a time horizon of "many decades," a temperament he labels as "very calm and collected" and a "very high" conviction in Tesla, Luu believes he's "at no risk of panic selling," even when the market tanks.

Still, the situation points out another danger: Missing an opportunity to make an investment when an equity is undervalued. When Luu was scrambling to raise funds to meet his margin obligation, it reduced his flexibility to purchase more Tesla shares at the lower price.

Margin levels this high have been followed by risk-off periods in equities.

Whenever monthly margin debt has grown above 45% year over year since 1960, there were declines in the stock market five out of six times, data from Fundstrat Global Advisors shows. June's margin debt record came in at 49%, but the S&P 500 has still added more than 13% in 2026. A swing into the red by year-end in accordance with this historic pattern would be a dramatic move — one that would be considered highly unusual for the stock market.

The firm also found that the median performance for S&P 500 forward returns following a breakout of 40% year-over-year margin debt growth has been worse off 12 months later as opposed to one month after it. To be exact, the S&P 500's median 12-month forward return is a 4.2% decline, while the median one-month return is a drop of 2.2%.

In essence, the more rapidly margin debt rises, the worse it is for S&P 500 returns over 12 months.

While margin debt doesn't necessarily cause S&P 500 declines, it can exacerbate existing moves to the downside if there's a significant amount of leverage in the market, said Hardika Singh, economic strategist at Fundstrat.

"The premise of gains beget gains, it turns into losses beget losses, and that's what's troublesome," Singh said. "You have these losses, they keep piling up, and then the stock gets sold, and everyone's starting to close out their position, and it becomes this huge train wreck that's very hard to stop, and it adds a lot of volatility to the market."

Then again, Singh sees why investors like Luu are leaning into such a risky strategy. "No one ever got rich by diversifying," she said.

Luu, who said he's been a "hobbyist" from an early age, has folded in investing as one of his many hobbies, which include activities like climbing and playing guitar. It's become such a hobby that he's created his own social media account detailing his investing journey.

Even if Luu reaches his financial goals, he "wouldn't ever stop investing," he said. Instead, he said he "would probably start investing in SpaceX."

It's not just Luu who views trading as a hobby.

Fundstrat's Singh explained that American traders, particularly younger ones, feel they have to take bigger risks to get ahead. She said it's part of a broader trend dubbed financial nihilism, in which young investors grappling with a tough job market and high inflation turn to less-stable investing tools.

"It makes a lot of sense why individuals, specifically retail investors, keep gravitating towards this margin debt," the economic strategist added. "This is like a drug, and I think people just can't get enough of it in this economy."

Kevin Davis, a 59-year-old retail investor who made a living as a rapper in the 1980s and '90s before becoming a stock broker, believes the risks with leveraged trading outweigh the rewards.

"It's gambling. You're borrowing money you don't have, and so if it goes the other way, now you have a clock on your money, and it's ticking," said Davis, who owns an investing technology platform. "The market's not going to save you. It never does."

"Don't play the margin game," the Florida resident warned.

Luu became an engineering consultant because his father, who died of lung cancer in 2012, exposed him to computing. His mother said that between her two sons, Luu most resembles his father not only in terms of his features but also his character.

Reflecting on what her late husband might have thought about Luu's investing pursuits, Nguyen paused for a moment, holding a slight smile.

She then said, "He would've said he's proud of him."

— CNBC's Charlotte Morabito and Deena Zaidi contributed to this report.

#3240. Security Bite: The record $6.3B Binance heist started with a fake Homebrew install on Mac

9to5Mac Security Bite is exclusively brought to you by Mosyle, the only Apple Unified Platform. Making Apple devices work-ready and enterprise-safe is all we do. Our unique integrated approach to management and security combines state-of-the-art Apple-specific security solutions for fully automated Hardening & Compliance, Next Generation EDR, AI-powered Zero Trust, and exclusive Privilege Management with the most powerful and modern Apple MDM on the market. The result is a totally automated Apple Unified Platform currently trusted by over 45,000 organizations to make millions of Apple devices work-ready with no effort and at an affordable cost. Request your EXTENDED TRIAL today and understand why Mosyle is everything you need to work with Apple.

Last week, news broke that hackers had stolen $6.3 billion from wallets on Binance, the most popular cryptocurrency exchange in the world. The company was able to freeze about nearly $3 billion of it, but the attack quickly made headlines, and rightfully so, as the largest financial heist in human history.

At the time, I suspected, along with security researcher Christopher Lopez and plenty of others, that this could have very well started on a Mac. As Lopez pointed out, the $1.5 billion Bybit heist last year also began on a developer’s Mac. On top of that, Macs are hugely popular among DevOps engineers and crypto folks, and they’ve been on the receiving end of a steady stream of malware and social engineering campaigns over the past few years.

I can now say any suspicions that this heist originated on Mac were right. I’m still in a state of shock. Dazed not by the amount stolen, but how the said hackers did so using the same ol’ social engineering tricks they’ve been using for years. No sophisticated multi-milllion dollar underground zero-day here.

Yesterday, Binance published a more detailed breakdown of the attack. The company never actually says “Mac,” but the malware it published targeted /opt/homebrew, which is where Homebrew lives on Apple silicon Macs. In other words, this was almost certainly an M-series MacBook.

The attack basically transpired in two steps.

According to Binance, in June this year, a DevOps engineer working on Wallet searched for an AI coding tool and downloaded a malicious clone of the Homebrew installer in Google Search. Binance claims it caught it early and stopped any damage. However, what it didn’t know was that it allowed the attackers to learn which employees worked on its wallets. This was phase 1.

Fast forward a few months to September, a different engineer who, you guessed it, worked on wallets for Binance, was lured into a fake job interview. As these sort of social engineering attacks normally go, they told to run a coding “assignment” on their work computer. This was not caught by Binance security, and on October 29, the world learned that hackers (now widely speculated as North Korean hackers) walked off with billions.

Of course, most of what we know so far comes directly from Binance, so if you’re looking for more details on exactly how this happened, you’ll likely be left empty-handed.

It’s important to note here though, none of these two attack vectors are new. Back in early 2025, I wrote about fake Homebrew ads at the top of Google Search pushing Atomic Stealer to Mac users. Binance only says the engineer found his installer through “a search engine.” Of course, I can’t confirm it was a sponsored ad, but if history tells us anything…

This is a rather uncomfortable situation for Apple to be in. The largest financial heist in history happen on Mac last week, though to be fair, there’s no security feature that can stop a developer from running a script he wants to run.

Sure, the Terminal paste warnings introduced in macOS 26.4 could have helped here. But realistically, if someone’s convinced they’re doing a coding test for a job they really want, a warning pop-up probably isn’t going to stop them.

I’m having Christopher Lopez (@L0Psec) a professional macOS reverse engineer back on the Security Bite Podcast this week to talk about the Binance situation with me. Follow the show so you don’t miss that.
