#3165. REITs Usually Underperform When Interest Rates Are Rising. Not This Year. Here's Why.

Fundamentals are driving REITs higher despite rising interest rates.

Real estate investment trusts (REITs) typically perform worse when interest rates are rising. In fact, there's a rule of thumb many investors have used for this asset class: rates up, REITs down.

REITs typically own and manage properties, and they often rely heavily on borrowing to expand their portfolios, so higher interest rates can hit them harder than many other businesses. In addition, real estate values tend to rise when interest rates fall. And REITs are dividend stocks -- they're legally bound to distribute 90% of their taxable income to shareholders as dividends -- so when interest income is harder to find in a low-interest rate environment, these stocks are more attractive to income investors.

That makes REITs an investment that does well when interest rates are low or falling.

That's not the case this year, however, as the Federal Reserve has been talking about raising rates for months, and it finally did so in September. Futures markets are pricing in two to three more quarter-point hikes by the end of 2027. So, interest rates are clearly heading higher.

Yet REITs are doing reasonably well this year. They were the best-performing asset class in October, as measured by the Vanguard Real Estate Index Fund ETF (VNQ +3.18%), which climbed 4.8%. The exchange-traded fund (ETF) holds various types of REITs, including data centers, healthcare, industrial, and retail REITs, among others.

Several REITs are doing much better than the group as a whole. Welltower (WELL +2.83%) is a REIT that focuses on senior housing and healthcare properties, and it's up 33% so far in 2026 (as of Nov. 3). Equinix (EQIX +3.91%), a large data center REIT, has climbed 28% this year. Iron Mountain (IRM +1.69%), which has a large portfolio of warehouses and storage units plus data centers, has soared 39% this year.

How are these REITs faring so well in an environment of rising interest rates?

Well, it turns out that REITs aren't driven by interest rates alone. In fact, the correlation of REIT performance with low interest rates is weaker this year, according to research by investment firm Cohen & Steers. Instead, fundamentals such as cash flow growth, real estate supply-and-demand dynamics, and valuations are driving returns in 2026.

Many of the post-pandemic headwinds that REITs faced in the 2022-2024 period -- businesses abandoning office space, high inflation and very tight financial conditions, stay-at-home work culture, and an imbalance between demand and new supply -- have faded.

And the U.S. economy is healthy. Third-quarter gross domestic product (GDP) increased at a 3.4% annual pace, and the unemployment rate, at 4.2% in September, remains near historical lows. That means businesses need warehouses, office space, data centers, health facilities, and many of the other properties that REITs own and manage.

In addition, the fact that the Fed didn't raise its target interest rate in October suggests to me that the Kevin Warsh-led Fed plans to go very slowly and deliberately on raising rates, taking the economy's pulse methodically before each rate move.

The best-performing REIT categories this year, through the first half, have been data centers, lodging and resorts, and healthcare. Residential REITs have lagged behind those sectors significantly, but I think that will change when the housing market eventually turns up.

REITs provide a steady stream of income to their shareholders. And when they're also providing returns, they become doubly attractive. If the economy continues to thrive, demand for all kinds of real estate will continue to grow. And sector-specific trends, such as the aging of the U.S. population and the growth of data centers, will affect the performance of certain types of REITs. Overall, this asset class strikes me as very attractive right now.

#3162. Bread as a Sponge for Oil Is the Best Kitchen Hack I Learned All Year

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Oily pans, stews and sauces are no match for the bread sponge trick.

If you want to degrease a pan or the top layer of an oily sauce without ruining a sponge, a single slice of bread could be your new favorite cleaning sidekick.

While we have vastly improved how we dispose of most things, excess cooking grease still presents a problem. Down the sink? Not advisable. Neither is the dishwasher—even the garbage bin can become a gnarly affair.

Getting the bulk of the grease out of a pan after cooking a batch of bacon or burgers is a good first step, but that greasy pan will either take down a sponge or half a roll of paper towels. What if a humble slice of past-its-prime sandwich bread was the all-natural solution for greasy pans you’ve been looking for?

It’s cheap and easy, and you can toss the used-up bread into a compost bin or countertop food waste processor without disrupting its yuck-free operation.

So, is it ever OK to pour excess grease or used cooking oil down the sink? Even if you run the hot water tap at the same time? Short answer: no. Long answer? Here’s an expert for the “no.” “When grease cools, it solidifies, coating the interior of the pipe,” says Jacylyn Basilone, chief operating officer of Brooks Plumbing. Even if you’re running hot water, the grease will eventually cool further down the line and cause future problems. “Over time, the solidified grease in the pipes can catch debris, thus making a partial clog grow larger and larger,” she says, reducing the pipe’s circumference little by little if you do this repeatedly.

Unlike a clogged shower drain, which you can usually clear easily, “a normal sewer machine or ‘snake’ can’t alleviate this type of stoppage,” says Basilone. “While grease solidifies, it can’t be captured by the claw head. Grease removal is best remediated with a hydrojetter, which tends to be more expensive than the traditional drain-cleaning services.”

Bread is the real answer, and I can’t believe I haven’t been doing this all along. (*Hangs head in shame, fully guilty of relying on the obviously very sketchy hot water method.*)

Bread has always been a superb grease-mopping tool; we usually think of it in a culinary context rather than for waste removal. Just as you’d drag a crusty baguette or hunk of ciabatta across the drippings on your plate, bread is an excellent sponge for all manner of oil, whether or not it is appealing to consume. Using bread to soak up excess oil essentially turns liquid food waste into a solid, making disposal much easier.

If it’s not obvious, this is also a great way to use bread that might otherwise go to waste: the ends of the loaf you can’t bring yourself to eat, or bread that’s gone stale or is starting to show the first mold spores. If you’re going to discard the bread anyway, at least put it to good use.

The bread trick comes in handy in almost endless ways. If there’s a pool of oil, it’s the mop for the job. I initially tried it after cooking bacon. A single, small slice of bread was enough to absorb what was easily four to six ounces of liquid grease left in the pan. I dragged the slice around the pan like a mop, but even after letting it sit a few extra moments, it kept working and eventually soaked up all the liquid grease. (If you’re feeling indulgent and used a fresh bread slice for this purpose, the temptation to make pretty epic croutons here is quite strong — another upside.)

If your air fryer has space between the drawer and the basket, you can place the bread there to soak up grease while cooking. Even for oily, slow-cooked proteins like pork shoulder, you can press the bread onto the meat to soak up grease before serving.

Once the bread has absorbed the oil and needs discarding, responsible food-waste methods are much easier to manage. Depending on how much oil the bread has absorbed, you can safely put the soaked bread in the compost bin or countertop composter without risking a major oil spill and a mess to clean up later. Oil can slow decomposition, so composting large amounts isn’t recommended. Small amounts, such as a few tablespoons at a time, are safe.

Even if you have no other option but to throw it away — and if that is the case, please consider getting a small composting appliance — at the very least, you’re not involving an easily recyclable glass container.

For more home tips, learn this neat trick for reusing frying oil and learn the 10 worst things to pour down your drain.

#3159. Scientists Build Biocomputer That Runs on Bacteria to Solve Hard Problems

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

The study relied on the bacterium E. coli and V. natriegens to run the calculations.

Move over, microchips. The next generation of supercomputing might just run on living bacteria. For 20 years, an international team of scientists has been developing a biocomputer that uses bacteria to process information. Scientists from McGill University in Montreal announced their findings on Nov. 3 and published a paper detailing the results earlier this year in Nature.

Researchers from Canada, Europe, the United Kingdom and Australia contributed to this work, which combines biology with computer science and engineering. The researchers say the resulting biocomputer could be used to solve problems that give standard computers a hard time.

“Electronic (sequential) computers are not meant, or designed, to solve decision trees,” Dan Nicolau, a McGill bioengineering professor and senior author for the research paper, told CNET via email.

Nicolau noted that if electronic computers are to solve these types of problems, the computers will need a lot of RAM.

The study relied on the bacterium Escherichia coli and Vibrio natriegens to run the calculations. The researchers used E. coli because it moves through fluid in a predictable, measurable way and V. natriegens because it reproduces very quickly.

By using live bacteria rather than digital processing, the team says the biocomputer can solve big, complex problems at a small fraction of the memory and resources that regular computers require.

The researchers tested the biocomputer with a seemingly simple math problem called the Subset Sum Problem, which famously becomes exponentially harder as the number of inputs increases.

When the Subset Sum Problem inputs grow too large, the problem is known to give traditional computers issues, such as taking centuries, or even millions of years, to solve the problem.

The researchers translated the problem into a graph that branches off into each possible combination of inputs. Next, the team created a tiny physical structure that mirrored the Subset Sum Problem graph.

Inside the structure, they built a network of tunnels to mirror the graph branches. Each fork in the tunnels represents a decision point, and every possible route through the tunnels represents a different solution to the problem.

The researchers unleashed bacteria, which rapidly reproduce, inside the tunnels. The fast-growing bacteria moved through the tunnels, exploring many routes to the solution simultaneously.

Compared to digital processing, the bacteria are slow. But rather than tackling a problem sequentially, as traditional computers do, the bacteria can examine many solutions at once. And if you need more computing power, bacterial reproduction within the tunnels creates additional processing units to help solve the problem.

The team used automated image analysis to follow the bacteria through the correct tunnels. In this way, the researchers were able to tell which paths through the network satisfied the problem’s constraints.

The researchers were also able to adjust temperatures to prevent bacteria overcrowding while traveling through the network.

Enterprising fans have figured out how to run Doom, the groundbreaking 1993 first-person shooter video game, on everything from E. coli to a thermostat. Nicolau says Doom could probably run on the new system, with an important caveat concerning the biocomputer’s size.

“(The biocomputer) must be huge!” Nicolau said. Because bacteria make slow processors, you would need a massive biocomputer to host enough bacteria to run a video game.

But because no RAM is needed, Nicolau said biocomputing could help to solve the global RAM shortage, and even broaden our understanding of what a computer could be.

“A computer is a device which accepts (input) numbers and gets out (output) numbers. Full stop,” he said. “All other uses of the word computer (are) from our point of view, well, poetical.”

#3158. 3 High-Yielding Dividend Stocks That Investors Can Safely Buy and Hold for Decades

It might be time to make some philosophical adjustments to your portfolio's long-term allocation.

These are strange times for the stock market. Although the S&P 500 (^GSPC +1.58%) is technically more expensive than it's ever been and the AI stocks leading it higher are finally showing signs of vulnerability, we're also still within sight of the record highs reached early last month.

And that's despite consumer confidence remaining near multiyear lows. Lingering inflation doesn't seem to be weighing too much on investors' minds either, even though it's forcing the Federal Reserve to ratchet up interest rates, which seem likely to stay there for a while.

This might be a good time to rethink what your portfolio looks like for the indefinite future, focusing more on future cash flow and relying a little less on capital growth that may not materialize as much as previously anticipated.

In other words, it may be time to add some long-term exposure to higher-yielding dividend stocks. Here are three to consider.

Clorox (CLX +5.71%) hasn't exactly felt like a super-safe dividend stock to buy and hold lately. Although the consumer goods ticker rallied during and because of the COVID-19 pandemic, since its 2020 peak it's peeled back by 60%, making a new multiyear low just last month.

Thanks to a 2023 cyberattack that did some surprisingly long-term damage and a migration to a new ERP (enterprise resource planning) platform that's not gone as smoothly as hoped, the company's simply struggled -- with the shrinking sales and earnings to prove it. Never mind the fact that it just doesn't have the same benefit of scale that much larger rival Procter & Gamble enjoys. P&G did $87 billion worth of business last fiscal year, for perspective, while Clorox only did $6.7 billion, down 5%.

But with most of what was broken now fixed, the company's looking for respectable organic revenue growth of between 3.5% and 4.5% for the fiscal year that began in July, driving a similar improvement in per-share earnings. This turn likely does mark the beginning of longer-lived forward progress.

Lost in all the noise is the fact that Clorox has not only continued paying its dividend through this rough patch but has also continued growing it, now into a 49-year streak of annual per-share payment increases. You can plug into this long-term growth trend that's one year away from reaching Dividend King status while its forward-looking dividend yield stands at a frothy 5.7%, taking advantage of the overly aggressive sell-off that looks right past the fact that the company's been planning a smart turnaround for a while now.

Utility companies are usually great dividend payers for the obvious reason: Their customers make a point of keeping their power turned on by faithfully paying their monthly bills.

The business is getting trickier, though. Aside from being capital-intensive and increasingly regulated, growth typically comes only from geographic expansion, which adds complexity and eats away at efficiency.

Brookfield Renewable (BEPC +2.63%) is taking a different tack. Rather than never-ending expansion into adjacent geographic territories, Brookfield Renewable picks and chooses to back -- with capital -- smaller cash-generating utility projects all over the world, like its 38% stake in Colombia's hydropower company Isagen, or its recently acquired share of Canada's wind power specialist Boralex.

These aren't deals that would have been of much interest to a major U.S. utility outfit. Brookfield's management team understands smaller and foreign wind, hydro, nuclear, and solar power opportunities though, knowing when to buy in, and sometimes, when to sell. This is flexibility that more traditional utility outfits just don't have.

Perhaps more important, Brookfield Renewable is structured and invested in a way that prioritizes dividend payments and supports substantial dividend growth. While there is some capital appreciation to be reaped from the company's portfolio of revenue-bearing assets, built for income, the organization believes its distributions will grow between 5% and 9% per year indefinitely. Newcomers will start with a solid, forward-looking dividend yield of 5.4%.

Just make sure you're buying the right version of this stock. There's a limited partnership version that trades under the ticker BEP, but owning stakes in partnerships requires additional tax-filing forms that aren't always worth the trouble.

Finally, add Verizon Communications (VZ +2.06%) to your list of safe high-yielding dividend stocks you can buy and hold for the long haul, while you can plug into its yield of 6.3%.

Almost as much as they make a point of keeping their lights turned on and their water flowing, consumers keep their mobile phones connected to wireless networks. Many of them effectively feel like they have to, in fact. Data from Harmony Healthcare IT says the average American spends more than five hours per day staring at their smartphones' screens, suggesting addiction-level usage.

Mentally healthy or not, most consumers aren't apt to let go of the digital centerpiece of their lives now. That's a big reason Verizon's been able to raise annual per-share dividend payments for 20 consecutive years.

There's no great potential for capital gains here, for the record. With data from Pew Research indicating 98% of adults living in the United States already own a mobile phone (91% of which are smartphones), the market is pretty well saturated, with most of the major companies in the mobile telecom business simply swapping customers with one another. Any net growth will come only from population growth and price increases, which won't be much.

As a dividend-supporting cash cow, though, you'd be hard-pressed to find a better business than wireless telecom, and Verizon is one of its best.

Although the evolution of artificial intelligence (AI) has been the hottest trend in decades on Wall Street, it's not the only catalyst lifting the broader market. Investor euphoria for high-profile stock splits has also played an important role.

A stock split allows a public company to alter its share price and outstanding share count by the same factor without affecting its market cap or underlying operating performance. Within a span of just eight days, two historic AI stock splits were announced by Meta Platforms (META +1.44%) and Sandisk (SNDK -7.91%), which are set to undertake their first-ever forward splits, respectively.

Until recently, Mark Zuckerberg's Meta was the only member of the "Magnificent Seven" that hadn't split its stock. That changed with the company's Oct. 21 quarterly report, which unveiled the creation of a new class of stock.

Current Class A shareholders will receive a one-for-one Class C (non-voting) stock dividend after the Jan. 19 effective date. The unorthodox choice to create an entirely new share class will effectively act as a 2-for-1 split of the company's Class A shares. But with Meta stock oscillating between $500 and $750 for more than two years, something needed to be done to make its shares more accessible to retail investors who can't purchase fractional shares through their broker.

Although Meta generates the lion's share of its revenue from advertising on its family apps, including Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Threads, excitement is mounting regarding its AI ambitions.

Zuckerberg's company is already integrating generative AI into its ad platforms, enabling clients to create personalized static and video messages to improve click-through rates. The benefit for Meta is improved ad-pricing power.

Meta also recently introduced Muse, its agentic personal AI tool that's capable of multitasking on users' behalf. With a strong foundation of profitability built atop its social media platforms, Meta appears to be firing on all cylinders.

Just eight days after Meta announced its first-ever stock split, NAND flash storage specialist Sandisk declared its first split since being spun off from Western Digital (WDC -6.77%) in February 2025.

With its shares skyrocketing more than 6,000% at one point since its public debut, perhaps it's no surprise that Sandisk's board of directors approved an aggressive 8-for-1 forward split. The company's fiscal first-quarter report notes that its split, which becomes effective after the close of trading on Nov. 19, is designed to make its shares more accessible to retail investors and employees.

A split became necessary for Sandisk due to the overwhelming demand for memory and storage solutions in AI-accelerated data centers. This combination of strong demand and persistent supply shortages has afforded Sandisk otherworldly pricing power and pushed its gross margin to an almost unfathomable 85%.

Over the last 14 months, Sandisk's 2027 projected earnings per share have jumped from less than $10 to nearly $228!

While Sandisk is a screaming bargain on paper, history shows that memory and storage products are highly cyclical, with premium pricing power rarely having any staying power. Though Sandisk has reduced its near-term risk by locking in orders more than a year in advance, the prospect of an AI bubble-bursting event still looms large.

#3152. Social Security Trustees Project 22% Benefit Cut in 2032. This Change Would Cut Benefits by Only 17% Instead

There's a potentially less bad outcome, but it's not so clear-cut.

There are millions of older Americans today who rely on Social Security for retirement income. And without those benefits, many would be unable to afford basic living expenses.

Unfortunately, Social Security is facing a major financial crisis that could come to a head in just a few years. In fact, benefit cuts are something all retirees might need to brace for.

One potential solution could reduce the extent to which Social Security has to cut benefits. But it's not guaranteed to happen.

The reason Social Security faces benefit cuts boils down to a shrinking workforce. The program's main source of revenue is payroll taxes. But as older workers retire and a smaller share of replacement workers enter the labor force, Social Security will be under strain. The program is not expected to have sufficient incoming tax revenue to keep up with scheduled benefits once there's no trust fund to tap.

The Social Security Trustees, in their most recent report, projected that the program's Old-Age and Survivors Insurance (OASI) Trust Fund would run out of money by the fourth quarter of 2032. Once that happens, Social Security may face a 22% benefit cut.

The OASI Trust Fund is where Social Security's retirement benefits are paid from. But Social Security has another trust fund called the Disability Insurance (DI) Trust Fund, which pays disability benefits.

If the two trust funds were to be combined, Social Security would be able to pay retirement benefits in full for almost an extra two years. And from there, those benefits would only face a 17% cut.

The problem, though, is that Social Security can't simply combine the two funds. Congress would need to vote for that change.

Also, combining the OASI and DI funds doesn't prevent benefit cuts. It simply reduces them while slightly shifting the timeline.

It also puts the DI Trust Fund at risk of depletion much sooner than it would otherwise run out. The current projection by the Trustees indicates the DI Trust Fund could last at least through 2099 if left alone.

Of course, the main reason Congress might hesitate to combine the two Social Security trust funds is that a 17% benefit cut would still be catastrophic to millions of older Americans, not to mention future retirees. There's a good chance that if lawmakers make a change, they'll focus on one that can prevent Social Security cuts entirely.

#3151. Researchers asked people to use AI chatbots for election info – results were mixed

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Chatbots can skew election-related information and act as an intervening layer in a voter's search.

Most search tools now put a layer of AI between you and the information you’re looking for, especially Google.

Also: Tired of AI Overviews? I found 9 Google Search alternatives

In a new study, Yale researchers found that a third of users asked a chatbot to help them pick a candidate. Grok often recommended candidates on its own without any information from users, while ChatGPT recommended candidates most often overall, and twice as much as Claude.

The researchers asked nearly 2,500 people in 35 states with Senate races to query ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, or Gemini about the election. Participants in the study, which ran for a few weeks in October leading up to the Nov. 3 midterm elections, were adults who already use chatbots weekly.

Most users asked chatbots for basic facts about the election, including who was on the ballot. But 36% asked a chatbot to help them pick a candidate to vote for, often by describing their priorities and asking the chatbot to assess which candidates aligned with them.

The former query has slightly less room for error, because the internet has a ton of data on the basic facts of an election, such as who is running where. Chatbots interpreting candidate positions, on the other hand, is a bit more dicey, and relies significantly on the sources a chatbot uses (a statement from a candidate’s own website, for example, is more reliable than a social media clip of an opponent characterizing them in a certain way).

Also: How to keep your chatbot conversations as private as possible

In one example, a user asked ChatGPT to give them the “pros and cons” of each candidate in Virginia, an inherently subjective question.

When it came to recommending candidates, chatbots varied widely.

“When users asked who to vote for but had not yet said anything about themselves, only Grok regularly recommended a candidate, in 14% of chats,” the researchers wrote. “Once users shared their views, ChatGPT recommended a candidate in 79% of chats and Claude in 40%, with Grok and Gemini in between.”

Pew Research found that 42% of US adults surveyed use chatbots to search for information. That’s a broad umbrella that can include election information — but Pew also found that only 8% of US adults reported using chatbots to find election-related information in this year’s election.

What those users are looking for matters, though. Pew found that of that group, 76% were inquiring about where candidates stand on certain issues, and 71% were fact-checking information they’d heard about candidates or issues.

Also: OpenAI will merge ChatGPT’s chat and work tabs

Given that chatbots are still not reliable summarizers, the nature of these questions poses a misinformation risk if users don’t also check a chatbot’s linked sources. An overwhelming majority of users don’t, at least when it comes to Google’s AI Overviews. At least one study found AI platforms gave users “outdated or inaccurate” information that could mislead voters in some cases by missing a deadline or failing to mention a step about voting logistics.

This election cycle was particularly plagued by AI-generated deepfakes and misinformation as tools have become much more sophisticated since the 2024 election. OpenAI and Anthropic reportedly set up election “war rooms” to monitor misuse and information accuracy, according to exclusive reporting by Politico and Semafor.

While an August study from the Brennan Center for Justice found that chatbots did push back surprisingly well against certain falsehoods related to election disinformation campaigns, it also found that AI models easily generated “misleading election-related images and video” when asked.

“Many of their safeguards for preventing this were ineffective, inconsistently applied, or functionally absent,” noted the study, which tested ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok, Meta AI, Runway, and Flux.2.

Also: 50 AI agents tried to build a thriving Minecraft civilization – it didn’t end well

Apart from these factors, however, there is a broader theme in AI use that is equally consequential for civic engagement: cognitive offloading. The political media landscape can already be dense and hard to parse for a voter trying to stay informed. Layering a chatbot — which has opaque training data sets, filters, and other settings determined at the discretion of AI labs — on top of that information search process can further muddy the waters while appearing like a convenient and neutral summarizing tool.

While some studies test how AI chatbots respond to election questions by using standardized questions, this approach let users themselves engage with chatbots as they normally would. While the Yale researchers’ queries and standardized study queries show a lot of similarities, the distinction is valuable for evaluations.

“This is a small step toward evaluations that measure AI’s political influence on the questions users actually ask,” the researchers noted.

Outside of users self-reporting what they asked a chatbot, only AI labs have records of what users are really asking about elections. In October, Anthropic analyzed 250,000 conversations with Claude and determined people “rarely ask Claude whom or what to vote for,” finding that “0.51% of all conversations are specifically about elections or voting,” though it expected election-related queries to increase closer to Nov. 3.

Also: 6 AI agent workflows I use to hand off everyday tasks

“More often, we observed people asking Claude questions that could help them reach their own conclusions, like where candidates stand on a particular issue. Requests that violated our election integrity policies were even less common, appearing in about 0.002% of conversations,” Anthropic’s report said.

The Yale researchers said the next step for a study like theirs is determining how accurate and unbiased models are in their responses, as well as what models learn about users, and whether their recommendations actually match users’ needs.

“In multi-turn chats, users often answered the chatbot’s questions, and those answers led to its recommendations. The questions a model asks shape what users tell it and what it recommends,” the researchers explained.

#3149. CoreWeave credit default swaps hit distress levels as investors sour on AI debt

CoreWeave's credit stress continued to spiral on Thursday amid a broader sell-off in AI-related names.

CoreWeave — a so-called neocloud company — has taken on more than $51 billion of debt and obligations to finance its AI infrastructure build-out. It's now facing a rebellion from stock and bond investors as concerns mount about AI overspending and debt levels.

Yields on CoreWeave debt have continued to climb, with the yield to maturity on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 reaching 15.78%. Bond yields move inversely to prices. Meanwhile, the spread on its five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default, at one point soared above 1,140 basis points. It last stood at nearly 1,038 bps — a 16% week-over-week jump and 164% higher than a year ago.

Credit concerns are spreading into AI equities too. CoreWeave's stock dropped during trading Thursday before recovering and closing 5.94% higher. The moved followed Wednesday's 15.5% nosedive.

Other neocloud stocks were under similar pressure. Nebius also sank before climbing higher to close 1.29% and and Iren ultimately ended the day down less than 1%.

Anxiety about AI overspending is also spreading. For instance, shares of Micron Technology and Advanced Micro Devices sold off following a big sell-off in South Korean chip stocks. Micron closed up 1.87%, while AMD fell 1.5%.

While AI debt worries have been rising steadily, investors have suddenly grown skittish about the underlying finances of companies borrowing heavily to buy chips, build data centers, and rent out computing power.

Coreweave's credit default swaps are one place to see that stress.

Credit default swaps are contracts where buyers pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. The spread widening in CoreWeave's CDS means investors view the debt as riskier.

The market is "basically saying 'no mas' to AI debt without operating cash flow support," the Evercore ISI trading desk said.

A spread level of 1,000 basis points or above is generally a sign of credit distress, said Gavan Nolan, executive director of fixed income pricing at S&P Global Market Intelligence.

No one is questioning whether demand for CoreWeave's services is real, since the company has contracts with all the big hyperscalers, Nolan said. The question is whether the cash flows will ultimately arrive.

"It's obviously heavily negative free cash flow at the moment, and it needs that cash flow to arrive really to justify all the capex that it's spending," Nolan said.

CEO Mike Intrator dismissed the market moves on Wednesday, according to a memo obtained by CNBC.

"When you are building a new type of technology company there will be periods of time when the market misunderstands and acts irrationally," he wrote. "We are confident in our backlog which more than supports all of our debt obligations."

The backlog is over $100 billion, with around two-thirds of it with investment-grade counterparts including Microsoft, Meta, IBM and Caterpillar, Deutsche Bank said in a note Thursday. The firm reiterated its buy-rating on the stock Wednesday, calling the dislocation a buying opportunity.

"The problem is this kind of concern can prove to be a self-fulfilling prophecy, and risks triggering broader issues in other AI-related names," said Jim Reid, global head of macro and thematic research.

Domino effects may already be happening. Oracle's five-year CDS spread also spiked this week. It was last at 282 basis points, a roughly 10% increase in one week.

"A downgrade from its BBB rating would risk pressuring IG-only investors into forced sales," Reid said.

#3148. 2 Bank Stocks to Buy After Their Third-Quarter Earnings Reports

With the third-quarter earnings season well underway, most banks have now reported.

Largely speaking, bank profits have continued to climb, as most banks take advantage of higher interest rates and a steep yield curve, in which lower-maturity bonds yield less than higher-maturity ones, an environment that most banks tend to benefit from.

Banks typically borrow money at short-term rates and lend it out at longer-term rates, which is why banks benefit from a steeper yield curve. Still, it's not all roses. Banks are also grappling with higher funding costs, while investors wonder whether a real credit cycle will ever show up.

Here are two bank stocks to buy after their third-quarter earnings reports.

For investors just starting to look at bank stocks, or who simply want a little exposure, JPMorgan Chase (JPM +4.18%) is an easy place to begin. It's the country's largest bank, with more than $5 trillion in assets, and is run by Chief Executive Officer Jamie Dimon, whom many regard as the best leader in banking.

JPMorgan Chase is good at many different banking businesses, from credit card lending to investment banking to wealth management and payments.

So you've got a bank that can benefit from a steep yield curve like other traditional banks, but JPMorgan will also benefit from large initial public offerings like the one planned for artificial intelligence (AI) company Anthropic, which only a handful of the country's largest investment banks can say. This gives JPMorgan revenue diversity that few banks have.

JPMorgan actually missed Wall Street estimates for both earnings and revenue in the third quarter, which is rare for the bank. The undershot came from weaker fixed-income trading revenue and higher expenses.

However, JPMorgan raised its full-year outlook for net interest income (NII), the spread revenue the bank makes on its loans and bond holdings after covering its funding costs for the deposits and other interest-bearing liabilities that fund those assets.

Management provided a forecast of $107 billion for NII in 2027, representing roughly a 10% increase over its projected 2026 NII. While JPMorgan trades at a premium valuation of roughly 3 times its tangible book value (TBV), or its theoretical liquidation value, it has earned this premium during two decades of excellence.

Investors should ignore the third-quarter earnings miss and buy the stock for the long haul.

Raleigh, North Carolina-based First Citizens BancShares (FCNCA +0.41%) has total assets of roughly $241 billion, putting it at a fraction of the size of JPMorgan Chase, but still one of the larger banks in the country.

First Citizens has delivered a masterclass in growth through acquisition, particularly by purchasing distressed banks or those on the brink of failure.

For instance, First Citizens acquired the struggling CIT Group in 2022, which traded at a significant discount to its TBV. As a result, the deal was 38% accretive to First Citizens' TBV, which is a huge increase. Most bank acquisitions dilute TBV and take two or three years to earn back the dilution.

First Citizens struck again when it acquired all of Silicon Valley Bank's deposits, loans, and branches after the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) took over during the banking crisis in 2023, of which Silicon Valley Bank was at the center.

Shares of First Citizens soared about 40% after announcing the acquisition. Furthermore, First Citizens had a loss-sharing agreement with the FDIC on loans, as well as other protections that made the deal even more appealing.

After its third-quarter earnings on Oct. 23, First Citizens' stock rose nearly 8% after adjusted earnings per share of $55.37 easily topped estimates of $45.89, according to FactSet. The bank's board also approved a $1.2 billion share repurchase plan through next year.

First Citizens is a proven acquirer, and I suspect it will continue to grow in this manner.

#3146. Tomato Paste, Mayo and 5 More Foods You Can Use for Cleaning

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

A potato to lift rust from cast iron, plus more edibles that do double duty as cleaning agents.

For every spill, splatter or spot, there seems to be a specific product promoted to make you believe nothing else could possibly handle the job. We already know that’s false, right? Pantry heroes such as white vinegar, baking soda and club soda are already staples in our regular rotation when we’re not sure which of the dozens of bottles under the sink to grab.

Many other kitchen staples, however, can also handle certain types of dirty work. None of these are exactly an all-purpose cleaner (as may be obvious with staples such as tomato paste, below), but for specific jobs, in the absence of the perfect product, or to spite the industrial cleaning complex that would have you believe there is a perfect product, the solution or anecdote may already be lurking in your cupboards.

Using that which you already have on hand is a win-win-win. You’ll feel like a mastermind, save money and avoid the tyranny of more and more plastic. “The most sustainable cleaner is usually the one already in your kitchen, says Julian Silva, founder of Plastno nontoxic cleaners, “because you skip buying another single-purpose bottle.”

To use pantry products for cleaning and polishing, “It’s helpful to figure out why a certain product or method works in order to better determine other applications,” says Sofia Martinez, cleaning expert and owner of Sparkly Maid Austin. She also cautions, however, “Disinfecting is not the same as cleaning. Just because a product or method removes soil, provides shine or covers up odor doesn’t mean that the surface has been properly disinfected.”

Silva, Martinez and other cleaning experts below explain why and share seven kitchen staples you probably already have on hand that can clean or polish.

Polishing and disinfecting are far from the same thing, but the kitchen staple you might have sitting right next to your stove can also add shine.

“Olive oil can make fingerprints on stainless-steel appliances much less noticeable, because it creates an ultra-thin coating that changes how light reflects off the surface and disguises smudges,” says Raquel Perez, owner of Karen’s Green Maids in Chicago.

You’re not going to want to use large quantities of oil to clean up the oil and other foodstuffs that spatter during cooking, obviously. “Only use a tiny drop,” Perez advises. “Rub it onto a microfiber cloth, and always test on a small, hidden area first. Too much will make it feel greasy.”

Tomato paste isn’t exactly something like baking soda, where you might confidently apply it to whatever and see if it works. “I would describe tomato paste as a very limited tarnish removal option, not an all-purpose cleaner,” says Martinez. In other words, don’t rub deeply colored, concentrated tomatoes on your cutting boards and countertops.

However, it might do the trick for polishing stainless steel, copper pots and pans, or brass fixtures. “Its acidity can help loosen some oxidation,” she says, “while its thick consistency helps the paste stay in contact with the surface.” As with just about everything here, try a small amount on an out-of-the-way spot first.

Soaking up excess oil with bread is the kind of hack that deserves its own headline. (See here.) You can also use it in place of a broom when something shatters.

“Soft bread is great for broken glass because the crumb grabs the tiny shards a broom misses,” says Silva. “Carefully pick up the big pieces first, then press a slice over the area and toss it right after.” Make sure to press, not rub, as rubbing can cause bigger problems and small scratches. Disposing of it right away, and deep in the trash, is also crucial so nobody (including pets) mistakes it for something they could eat as a snack or croutons.

Your sink may be the basin you use for rinsing and cleaning, but grime and soap residue can build up in certain places and require cleaning. For a quick fix that requires less elbow grease and leaves your stainless steel sink shiny, turn to your baking supplies.

“Sprinkle a little flour over a clean, dry sink and rub it around with a soft, dry cloth or paper towel to remove residual grime and give it a polished look,” says Sham Zemichael, owner and operations manager of Costina Cleaning Services. Conditions must be right in order to begin here, though. “Note that this can backfire if you do it over a damp sink,” he says. “You’ll be left with a flour slurry and more grime than there was before. I use it as a finishing touch on washed and completely dried sinks, and I also recommend keeping the flour away from the drain to avoid it clumping in there.”

Cream of tartar might be one of those baking supplies that sits in the back of your cabinet for years (decades?) because it’s used only for highly specific baking projects. If you’re not regularly stabilizing egg whites in your kitchen or using it as a baking soda sidekick, try using it up before the best-by date by giving it another purpose.

“Most of those gray ‘scratches’ on ceramic plates and sinks are actually metal left behind by forks and knives, since the glaze is harder than the cutlery,” says Silva. “Cream of tartar mixed into a paste with a little water is a gentle, mildly acidic abrasive, so it rubs that metal off without hurting the glaze.” It won’t fix a true scratch, but it will give old ceramics a smart look when they just need a little glow-up.

Seasoning cast iron is a process unto itself, giving its heavyweight, heat-retaining base what is essentially a nonstick surface. Even if you consistently give your cast iron the white-glove treatment in care and cleaning, little rust spots can still appear here and there. You don’t always have to start over with the full seasoning process when this happens, however.

“My favorite way of cleaning light surface rust on cast iron is dipping a half-cut potato in baking soda and rubbing it over the rusty patches,” Zemichael says. “The small amounts of oxalic acid inside potatoes help loosen rust buildup, and the baking soda acts as a mild abrasive for a cleaner finish,” he says. “It doesn’t work for stubborn rust, though. I simply use it for new spots when they appear.”

For kitchen tables or coffee tables that have been begging you to use coasters, you may be able to minimize water rings with what you have on hand for sandwiches. “Mayonnaise can help with water ring stains in some types of wood,” says Perez. “Before trying this solution, find out what type of wood finish your table has and how deep the water-ring stain goes,” she says, whether it’s just in the finish or goes deeper. “That will affect how you should try to remove it and avoid making the situation worse.”

The vegetable oil in full-fat mayonnaise can help displace the moisture that’s locked inside the finish. Apply a thin coating to the ring and let it sit for at least 15 minutes or overnight, covered with plastic wrap. Wipe with a clean, dry cloth after the mayo has absorbed the moisture.

White or hazy rings are worth trying this on, but darker rings might be beyond help. “The mayo can affect the appearance of the stain, as opposed to removing it,” says Perez, and you could be left with a greasy area around the stain if it’s not completely removed.

#3145. Linux Mint 27 arrives next month, and I like it already: New features and other upgrades to expect

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Linux

It starts with a surprise version number: Linux Mint 27 instead of 24. But the next release brings far more changes than that.

Linux Mint, my favorite Linux desktop distribution, is ready for a fresh start.

Its lead developer, Clement “Clem” Lefebvre, announced earlier this year that the team behind it was considering slowing Mint’s release cadence because the old twice-a-year release cycle was time-consuming and constrained their ability to make major changes. So it is that the next release, Linux Mint 27, will appear in your Christmas stocking.

Also: 5 premium Linux distros absolutely worth paying for in 2026

The developers officially changed the designation on Oct. 13th when Mint changed both its release cadence and its numbering. Clem’s happy about the change: it “was a tough decision to make, but we’re really starting to see it pay off. We’re taking on projects and implementing changes which would previously have been considered too large or ambitious.”

The new Mint will use Ubuntu 26.04 Long Term Support (LTS) as its base. As before, it will offer Cinnamon, Xfce, and MATE desktops.

Earlier development snapshots had been labeled Mint 23 “Alfa.” That title was explicitly a placeholder while the team decided its release strategy. Its final name is Adrien. Moving ahead, release numbers will be based on the upcoming year. Clem said, “We’ll no longer use point releases, so the release after that will be 28. You’ll upgrade from 27 to 28 to 29, and so on.” Instead of girls’ names, Mint will use boys’ names for distro titles.

On Halloween, Clem announced the top changes in Mint 27. It starts with Mint bringing hibernation back into its supported desktop configuration through a dedicated Sleep Modes page in its System Administration tool. The page is intended to make enabling and configuring hibernation easier, including addressing its swap-space requirements.

It may not sound like much, but Clem explained it’s actually rather a big deal. “When you close the lid of your laptop, it goes into a sleep mode called “Suspend”. This mode is very useful… but it has a major limitation: It uses power.” People often forget it’s not really off and that your laptop will eventually run out of power. When that happens, “the outcome is worse than a normal shutdown. The session is gone, and the battery is empty.”

Also: Linux Mint vs. RefreshOS: I compared the two best distros for new users

That’s where “Hibernation comes into play. It saves the session to disk and completely shuts down the computer. No power is used. When you reopen the lid, the session is as it was, and so is the battery.”

Another new feature is Superlight. This fresh system-monitoring application replaces the older GNOME System Monitor. It comes with CPU, RAM, swap, GPU, network, disk I/O, temperature, and fan-speed graphs. It also includes per-application and per-process resource views. Battery-equipped systems also get charge and power-flow history.

Its storage analysis is particularly interesting: it can break down disk usage into files and folders, Steam games, and Flatpak applications. That brings several common troubleshooting tasks — “What’s using the CPU?” and “Where did my disk space go?” — into one interface. I’ve been checking it out on a Mint virtual machine (VM), and I like it already.

The Nemo file manager is getting a media preview pane, toggled with F7 or a status-bar button. It supports pictures, audio, and video, and displays associated information — for photographs, that can include the capture date and camera model. I like this feature a lot. I’ve always done a lot of work from file managers going all the way back to the classic Norton Commander and its Linux successor, Midnight Commander.

I’ve said it before, I’ll say it again. You don’t need to ever touch a Linux shell via a terminal to use Mint. But if, like me, you’re an old-school Linux user and you like using the terminal, Velocitty, Mint’s new terminal application, looks interesting. Its announced features include:

The point is to make recurring projects and SSH sessions easier to find and reopen. If you like other terminal programs, my latest fave is the Rust-based WexTerm; you don’t have to use Velocitty.

Unfold is a new archive manager for viewing, creating, and extracting archives. It uses 7-Zip and 7zip-RAR and supports the encryption formats those backends handle, including password-protected archives. Its design goal is simplicity rather than a sprawling feature set.

The new Mint uses Ubuntu 26.04 LTS as its foundation. Mint is also moving from Ubiquity to the Linux Mint Debian Edition live installer for installing the operating system. This fresh installer comes with support for OEM bulk-produced installations, installation on both BIOS and EFI PCs, support for Secure Boot, and LVM/LUKS configurations.

Also: Linux Mint vs. Zorin OS: I’ve tried both Windows alternatives, and here’s my winner

For the Linux kernel, Mint 27 will use version 7.0. Which one exactly? Good question. We’ll see closer to Christmas.

Wayland compatibility remains the goal, but X11 isn’t disappearing. As Clem said in June, “In an ideal scenario, we manage to make Wayland work just as well as X11.” But they’re not there yet.

The central change is a cleanup of existing code. Mint’s longer cycle gives developers room to overhaul several parts of the desktop together, rather than squeezing individual improvements into six-month windows. As Clem put it in the September newsletter, “I don’t think I’ve ever seen so many changes and new features implemented for a single release.”

What that means for you and me will be better laptop power management, more capable built-in utilities, and a more complete collection of everyday desktop applications. For example, I expect the updated Mint will ship with GIMP 3.2.2 as its default photo editor, instead of Mint 22.3’s years-old GIMP 2.10.

#3144. Palantir Just Made Company History. Is the Stock a Buy?

Palantir's business is booming, but I'm concerned about the stock.

Palantir (PLTR -2.11%) just did something for the first time during its third-quarter earnings report: Its U.S. commercial revenue surpassed U.S. government revenue.

That's a big deal, because Palantir got its start selling its AI-powered software to the government. As Palantir transitions to this new paradigm, is that a good thing for the company? Or is it a concern?

I think it's a good thing, as the company is spreading its customer base out among different clients that wouldn't be affected by a government spending crackdown. But does that make the stock a buy overall? Let's take a look.

Palantir continues its streak of crushing expectations and outperforming where both management and the analyst community thought results would be. Outperformance is becoming the expectation, as management has consistently underguided and overdelivered every quarter (which isn't a bad thing).

In Q3, Palantir's revenue reached $2.3 billion, up 96% year over year. At the end of Q2, management told investors to expect $2.16 billion in revenue, so this was a sizable beat. Another factor Palantir has going for it is that its net income margin remained strong. It posted a 49% profit margin in Q3, making it one of the more profitable companies on Earth.

If that's the only perspective you have on Palantir's stock, it's easy to conclude that the stock is a strong buy. These results are simply incredible, and doubting Palantir's business isn't a smart move.

However, investing in the stock is a different story.

The price you pay for a stock matters, and even the most impressive company bought at the wrong price tag can lead to underperformance or even negative returns. Palantir's stock (which the company has no control over) is toeing that line.

Palantir's stock trades for a very expensive 110 times this year's earnings estimates and 76 times next year's.

PLTR PE Ratio (Forward 1y) data by YCharts

Somehow, among the broad AI sell-off, Palantir's stock has remained highly valued. Companies on the infrastructure side are trading for less than 20 times next year's earnings, and even the AI hyperscalers are trading in the low 20s. This showcases just how expensive Palantir's stock is, and its day of reckoning could be coming.

I don't think the stock is a buy here, as it's just too expensive compared to some of the other AI investments available. While I'm a huge fan of Palantir, the business, I'm much more concerned about Palantir's stock. As a result, I think it's one to stay avoid.

#3143. Safer Water at Home: New Water Heater Tech Aims to Kill Bacteria in the Tank

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

I asked the inventor about his design and when consumers might see the tech in their homes.

One challenge of current water heater designs is staying hot enough to kill harmful bacteria like Legionella pneumophila, which can cause Legionnaires’ disease. A new water heater design, developed and patented by researchers at the National Institute of Standards and Technology, aims to raise tank temperatures to 160 degrees Fahrenheit, which spells instant doom for Legionella bacteria.

Legionella bacteria love warm water, so while they struggle to survive in a water heater tank set to 120 F, they’re more than comfortable elsewhere in a home’s hot water pipes. It’s technically possible to achieve sufficient temperatures with existing water heaters, but those temperatures are also likely to scald human skin whenever you turn on the faucet.

The biggest innovation of this new design is how it finds a new use for heat exchangers, the same technology behind air conditioners, heat pumps, furnaces and refrigerators. I wanted to know more, so I reached out to David Yashar, a NIST mechanical engineer behind the new design.

As Yashar and his team researched ways to kill Legionella bacteria, they needed to figure out how to make tank temperatures around 160 F safe and practical for humans. They ultimately landed on the concept of using cold water entering the water heater to cool the hot water leaving the tank with an unmixed heat exchanger that contains the water inlet and outlet.

The principle behind unmixed heat exchangers—where the fluids don’t mix—is that incoming cold water gets a heating boost from the hot-water outlet while cooling the water to safe levels for people. As a result, the tank can maintain the high temperatures required to prevent pathogen growth behind illnesses like Legionnaires’ disease, which has a fatality rate of around 10%, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Beyond the safety benefits, the process recaptures some waste heat and can improve heating efficiency for the cold water, since it enters the tank warmer.

I’ve covered various heating, ventilation and air conditioning tech over the years, so I immediately recognized similarities between the new design’s unmixed heat exchanger and those used in HVAC and refrigerators. For example, air conditioners use a heat exchanger for the refrigeration cycle (also called the Carnot cycle) to pull heat from air inside your home (evaporator coil) and push it outside (condenser coil) without pulling in outside air. Additionally, heat pumps may use a heat exchanger for defrosting ice buildup when in heating mode.

When I asked about the similarities, Yashar noted that it wasn’t a coincidence that his patent took inspiration from HVAC and refrigeration tech. Yashar said, “My background is in HVAC&R, and it is very common to use unmixed heat exchangers like this to manipulate the bounds of the Carnot cycle to achieve some specific condition. I came up with the idea when I first learned about Legionella and the existing mitigation strategies.” He goes on to explain that using an unmixed heat exchanger “across the inlet and outlet was a very simple, effective, and inexpensive way to push the water temperature up to that condition and back down.”

It’s fitting that Yashar discovered better ways for heat exchangers not only to kill pathogens, but also to improve energy efficiency. Finding new applications for existing technology is certainly an underrated aspect of invention.

As exciting as this tech is, a patent doesn’t necessarily mean it will hit the market immediately. Yashar notes that while his research “proved the concept using a 60-gallon tank,” it depends on when manufacturers license the technology and get their engineers working on designing consumer products suitable for homes. This process could happen quickly or take several years.

It may be years before we see consumer heaters that use the promising new technology.

Because Yashar’s concept essentially modified an existing water heater, I asked if it would be possible to retrofit products in people’s homes. He notes that NIST’s project started with the intention of modifying the tank’s hardware and controls. “The steps we took might not be simple tasks for an existing application,” said Yashar. “It really depends on a lot of things, so it is best if people learn how this works and understand how to achieve it within their existing application.”

He brings up one important consideration: Retrofit tanks will need extra insulation to be worth it. It’s “absolutely necessary for a retrofit because the tank temperature will be about 40 degrees hotter than what the existing system was designed for. If this isn’t done, the standby losses would be very large.” Without appropriate insulation, any efficiency gained by the heat exchanger would be lost to heat loss in standby mode.

So, while a retrofit might be possible, it seems more likely to engineer a product from the ground up based on this design, especially if consumers want to keep utility costs manageable.

For more tips, see the best temperature to set your thermostat this winter and learn how to find air leaks in your home for more efficient heating.

#3142. Could Archer Aviation Stock Make You a Millionaire by 2036?

A multitrillion-dollar opportunity in aviation, an eVTOL that ferries passengers in the sky: Could Archer mint new millionaires?

The 2030s could become one of the most momentous decades of recorded history, for more reasons than one. Those years could be the first full decade in which we have artificial general intelligence (AGI), or something close to it. That would not only accelerate the pace of scientific and technological breakthroughs, but quite possibly shift the economic foundations on which society is based (e.g., robots in the workforce).

Another change in the next decade could come to transportation: Indeed, if Archer Aviation (ACHR -0.24%) has its way, by 2036, a large portion of travelers and commuters will be flying in air taxis instead of driving cars.

But can Archer make and certify eVTOLs at scale by 2036? And better yet, could its stock, currently trading almost 60% lower since last year, rebound and make investors millionaires?

In a nutshell, Archer is in the business of making eVTOL (electric vertical takeoff and landing) aircraft. Today, that business is mostly nonexistent (or rather, it exists in a pre-commercialization form). Indeed, no eVTOL is flying commercially right now in the U.S. But by 2036, this industry could be at a breakout point, one that transforms eVTOLs into a multibillion-dollar commercial market.

Morgan Stanley, for instance, projected in a 2021 report that the global total addressable market (TAM) for urban air mobility, a broader industry that includes eVTOLs, could grow from $55 billion in 2030 to $255 billion in 2035, before reaching a staggering $1 trillion by 2040. Morgan Stanley even went so far as to project a $9 trillion market by 2050.

Of course, this doesn't mean that Archer will grow into a $1 trillion company by 2040, or that it will even capture a large portion of that growing market. Indeed, Morgan Stanley's forecast encompasses several markets -- like cargo and military -- not just passenger transportation.

But since Archer is also developing military aircraft through its partnership with Anduril, and has plans to acquire a defense business (Insitu) from Boeing, its growth opportunity could well exceed ferrying passengers around cities.

Here's a thought: If Archer doesn't have a flying taxi business in 2036, can it survive as a company?

I think so. With its planned acquisitions from Boeing, it could lean more heavily on defense. It could also find opportunities selling autonomous aircraft for other purposes, like transporting cargo or carrying out military missions. But without a successful air taxi business, I doubt Archer will grow large enough to make millionaires out of investors buying shares in 2026.

Still, just because Archer doesn't mint millionaires doesn't mean it's off the table as a growth stock. But just know what you're buying -- a company with a lot to prove -- and understand the risks of investing in a speculative aviation company before you do.

Apple gave its pro iPhones a crucial camera and battery boost this year. As a frequent traveler, these upgrades had me stoked for the iPhone 18 Pro Max, so I took it with me to Japan. Going vintage watch hunting through the streets of Tokyo to 6 a.m. hikes in Kyoto’s Fushimi Inari and the Shinto shrines, I used the new phone as my main camera. It made me rethink my shots, pushed me to experiment more with my perspective and surprised me in the most unexpected ways.

The variable aperture, manual camera controls and new Photographic Styles make the iPhone 18 Pro the most fun camera system from Apple, even if they are just minor upgrades from the 16 Pro and 17 Pro. The starburst effect in f4, grain in Photographic Styles and adjustable shutter speeds add drama, depth and more personality to even the most mundane shots.

From my time landing in Osaka to landing back in Delhi, the iPhone 18 Pro Max had me experimenting for two weeks. Here’s what I shot and how the new upgrades made an impact on my first trip to Japan.

The iPhone 18 Pro has manual controls baked into the Camera app. I can adjust the focus, choose the lens aperture from four stops, pick a shutter speed and select the white balance without needing to install a third-party app. The variable aperture is the main attraction here, letting me experiment with lighting as I visited various shrines.

You can go from f/1.48 to f/4 on iPhone 18 Pro’s main camera to adjust the amount of light hitting the sensor. Apple has programmed the f/4 (its narrowest) setting to give you a starburst effect with bright light sources, which showed up as light blobs on older iPhones. I used f/4 to get starbursts from the reflections of sunlight hitting a shrine:

Not every photo needs this effect, but starbursts add a unique style that you won’t find on any other phone. I was busy framing my shots to get the most reflections and the cameras didn’t disappoint.

Combine this with adjustable shutter speeds (takes a bit getting used to) and it leads to endless new possibilities. On the night I landed in Osaka, I went out for a stroll near my hotel, and took about 250 shots at a red light. I only got a few decent light trails, but it forced me to get more creative with my photography

After a few days I finally got the shot of a moving car stabilized with a blurred background. The trick? Finding the right shutter speed (1/15 in this case) through trial and error and moving my iPhone at the same speed as the car. At night, I stuck to 1/2s for moving vehicles with handheld stabilization. I’m happy with the results.

From light trails at night to a speeding car in daylight, the iPhone 18 Pro Max cameras create an effect that was previously only possible through third-party apps. This is different from simply taking a live photo and tapping Long Exposure in edits. You can track a subject to focus and the rest of the movement creates visual effects like the ones in my photos.

Apple’s manual controls are all about getting creative with your frames. You can then personalize these with the new film look and grain in Photographic Styles. These are like simulations that you’d find on the Fujifilm X100 series or Ricoh GR cameras.

For example, I edited this cyclist shot in the Photos app. I used the Dramatic + Film Style because I liked the blue tint in the sky and background, while keeping the skin tone intact. It gave my shot a moody look without editing the colors on my subject, like a regular filter would.

For these two nature shots, I brought all three aspects: adjustable shutter speed, f4 aperture and new Photographic Styles into a single frame. I love the grain, film and glow effects on the iPhone 18 Pro this year. They make the iPhone cameras exciting again.

However, there are a few things I’d like to change about this software.

The grain and film look are nice additions but I’d have loved to adjust the intensity of grain, much like my Vivo X300 Ultra. The current look is good for photos shot in bright light, but anything dim starts looking too artificial. The grain is too aggressive for most situations.

As much as I appreciate the new manual controls, I’m not fond of their placement in the Camera app. I missed a slow shutter shot of the Shinkansen because I was busy finding the manual control. These bullet trains are just too fast!

The new manual controls can be added to the top of the viewfinder or accessed through the six-dot settings menu at the bottom-right corner. In both positions, they aren’t made for one-handed use. It’d also be nice if I could adjust the position of certain toggles in the six-dot menu on the viewfinder. I need the aperture and shutter speed on the rightmost side, but I can’t edit it. The two icons aren’t instantly recognizable up on top. I believe that if I could change their positions in the bottom menu, I’d recognize them faster and remember their positions for a more reliable shooting experience.

Then comes the Camera Control. It doesn’t support any of the new manual controls. So, you can’t adjust the shutter speed or choose an aperture. If I have an extra button dedicated to the camera, I’d ideally like to use it for manual controls. It’d allow faster access to the new features.

In my opinion, Apple should also let us assign two separate Photographic Styles on the front and back cameras. On my trip, I had set a Fuji-like look for street photography, which seemed great for my surroundings but not for my selfies. You can always edit these photos in post, but if I’m out with new friends and sharing these photos with them, it’d be easier if I could set two different Photographic Styles for the front and back cameras.

During my trip, I didn’t have to top up my iPhone 18 Pro Max more than once a day. I left it on charge overnight as my mornings were reserved for breakfast and figuring out the train connectivity through Google Maps. (Seriously, I don’t know how I’d travel without this app.)

Japan is a unique mix of next-gen technology and decades-old systems. While it has a Suica card for public transport, I couldn’t add it to my Apple Wallet. Most stations don’t accept Visa contactless payments. I had to run to the nearest 7/11 to get cash and purchase train tickets. Some markets are also cash-only, so my iPhone was constantly running Maps, Music and Camera for a healthy 6 hours a day.

It lasted me through long photography sessions and constant navigation without any issues. In my experience, this is a huge upgrade over my iPhone 17 Pro Max, which required two charging instances if I was pushing it with Camera and Maps usage. The new model also doesn’t get as warm as its predecessor. I noticed the heat dissipates quicker when using the iPhone 18 Pro Max without a case. I’ve tried three cases so far and each one traps heat, making it warm to touch. If you can, going caseless is a good idea on the new pro iPhones.

The added battery life is a fantastic addition to this year’s model, and will be appreciated by anyone who travels regularly. This is in line with CNET’s tests, where the iPhone 18 Pro Max emerged as the longest-lasting battery life of any iPhone Apple has ever made. I just wish it was lighter. At 248 grams, it is one of the heaviest phones on the market and if you put a case on it, the iPhone 18 Pro Max becomes bulky and hard to use with one hand. I hope Apple finds a way to give us an even better battery life in a lighter form next year.

On the front, you also get a smaller Dynamic Island, which can expand to show up to three live activities (up from two) simultaneously. However, some apps aren’t yet fine-tuned to accommodate the change. On one occasion, when I ordered food through Uber, while running Spotify and Maps navigation, the Live Activity cut the “2” in 27-minute ETA for the order. So I had the next direction, music and an incorrect ETA as glanceable info on top of my screen.

Japan was one of my bucket-list locations and I’m glad I took the iPhone 18 Pro Max with me. This is the most fun I’ve had with an Apple camera system in a long time. From the shrines in Kyoto to the riverside walk along the Sumida River in Tokyo, these cameras invited me to get more experimental. The film-like Photographic Styles, new manual controls and variable aperture helped me get more creative with my perspectives.

It took me more than 250 shots at a crossing in Osaka before I figured out which shutter speed was ideal for what occasion. Similarly, I experimented with my frames to find the best angles for the starburst effect in f/4. Then came the film simulations in Photographic Styles to stylize my shots within the Photos app. All of these new iPhone camera features give me a more analog feel, and I’m here for it.

The iPhone 18 Pro Max, thankfully, has the battery life to support my curiosity and slow learning pace. Through my trips last year, I had to carry a power bank with me, but the iPhone 18 Pro Max changed that. I’m more confident it will last through the day. While none of those camera features would appeal to casual users, the battery life enhancements and improved heat dissipation are tangible upgrades that would benefit everyone.

#3140. Motorola’s $1,600 Signature 27 Is Throwing Every Ultra-Level Phone Feature Together

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Motorola's new Signature 27 has one of the fastest wired charging speeds we've seen for a US phone.

After teasing it during Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Summit in September, Motorola’s $1,600 Signature 27 phone will be unveiled on Thursday, and it clearly wants to make a big impression for that high starting price.

Even with the ongoing RAM shortage leading to higher prices for most phones, it would be understandable to think a $1,600 candybar-style phone sounds extravagant. It is. But it’s actually priced competitively against the 512GB model of the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra (also now $1,600 following its own fall price increase).

The Signature 27’s biggest feature could be its 200-megapixel periscope telephoto camera, which is capable of a 3x optical zoom and what Motorola calls a 100x Super Zoom Pro. That camera is joined by a 50-megapixel wide camera, a 50-megapixel ultrawide camera and a 50-megapixel front camera. An Event-Based Vision action sensor will also be included to assist with photographing fast-moving subjects.

But particularly eye-opening to me — as someone who’s constantly tracking how quickly phones can recharge — is that the Signature 27 will have 90-watt wired charging. For context, the Galaxy S26 Ultra and the iPhone 18 Pro Max charge at 60-watt speeds, with both phones being among the fastest we’ve tested. The Signature includes a 7,000-mAh silicon carbon battery, which is a newer battery technology that’s able to pack more capacity into less space.

The phone will have a 6.8-inch 1.5K-resolution display that runs at a 120Hz refresh rate, but has an absurdly high 12,000-nit peak brightness. By comparison, many phones we’ve tested lately have included 2,000- and 3,000-nit brightness levels that make it easy to see the screen in sunny environments.

Powering it will be Qualcomm’s new Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 processor, which Qualcomm says will be particularly helpful for gaming at high-graphics settings, recording video at 8K resolution as well as 4K at 60 frames per second and for on-device AI tasks. The phone’s audio system is created with a partnership with Bang and Olufsen, which we’ll have to hear but should help tune the phone well for music and movies.

The Signature also gets several Android 17 features that debuted on Google’s Pixel 11 series, including Rambler for voice transcription that uses AI to remove “umm”s from the text as well as understanding commands. There will also be a Create My Widget feature for having Gemini create personalized homescreen widgets, and the ability to use American Sign Language for texting. Motorola’s own Qira AI assistant will also be available on the Signature 27, which Motorola says will work across Lenovo devices.

Like the Razr Fold, the Signature 27 will get seven years of software and security updates — which brings Motorola firmly in line with what Google and Samsung provide to their flagship Pixel and Galaxy phones. The Signature will come in two Pantone colors: the dark coal smoke and the green capulet olive. I am interested in feeling both phones because the coal smoke model is described as having a “tactical weave finish” akin to materials used for cars while the olive is said to have a textile-inspired finish that may be closer to the vegan leather backings we’ve seen on the Razr line.

The Signature 27 may be expensive, but I do see where there may be an audience. With the recent retreat of OnePlus from the US phone market, fans of that brand may be looking for a new gamer-friendly phone alternative with both a high-end processor and fast phone charging. The Signature 27 is also arriving after years of growth for Motorola’s Razr line of foldable phones, which itself has included a number of luxury-minded variants such as Razr phones that include Swarovski crystals.

The Signature 27 will release first in the US, going on preorder on Nov. 19 before going on open sale Nov. 26. Both the coal smoke and capulet olive models will come with 512GB of storage and 12GB of memory.
