#3138. Brian Sullivan: Why the 'real' price of oil is likely $30-$40 higher than where it is now

Oil, in reality, is $125 per barrel or higher.

That's the real cost of a barrel of oil because buying the physical commodity is a very different story from a number on traders' screens.

Oil futures are just that: paper contracts indicating a price today, tomorrow, next month or further out.  If you want to buy the physical commodity, it may be a totally different story — and price.

As I've reported, prices for oil delivery have skyrocketed. Last week, a VLCC (aka a "supertanker" in non-shipper parlance) was chartered from the U.S. Gulf Coast to China for $76 million. Another very large crude carrier went for $77 million from the U.S. to South Korea. That's 10 times more than the price of the same trip less than one year ago.

Assuming these ships hold about 2 million barrels of oil, that charter price means each barrel on the ship costs about $38 over the price of the oil itself.

I'm certainly not saying to avoid looking at oil futures prices, but you need to know that the price on the CNBC screen or CNBC.com isn't always the full price being paid. These days, any company that needs oil shipped by sea, rail or truck will pay a hefty premium over the price of the oil itself. So, while the volume of oil moving through Hormuz is closing in on pre-war levels, costs are not. And there's no sign that they're going anywhere but up.

You know what else is up? The stocks of the shipowners. Look at their moves this month and this year.

On a more serious note, I want to express my condolences for the awful attacks on the airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. The cowardly strike on civilians—some of whom were religious pilgrims—took the lives of at least 14 people and injured more than 300.

The airport was attacked at least three times as travelers and energy industry professionals from around the world were flying into Riyadh for the World Petroleum Council conference. I was scheduled to fly in on Saturday, but the trip was canceled because of the strikes. The WPC went on as planned — here's one panel that took place Tuesday — and I look forward to seeing all my global energy friends again soon.

Thanks for reading—and watching. Be safe in these crazy and often scary times.

The supercap oil and gas stock to watch right now is Shell (SHEL). Shell is not a shell of its former self. It's back to being what energy investors wanted: a major player in global energy, focused on what it does best. Shareholders are being rewarded.

Shell hit a new high this week. While analysts remain bullish, the stock is getting close to its target price.

Shell may be underappreciated for its huge liquefied natural gas business. With HH broadly unchanged throughout the summer, export margins have increased to the widest levels seen since 2022, on our estimates nearly double the level in 2Q26 (~$13/mmbtu vs. $7/mmbtu)."

Borkhataria expects Shell and other companies with huge U.S. LNG positions — TotalEnergies (TTE) and BP (BP) — to benefit from wider margins on exports to Europe.

Speaking of RBC and energy, the firm lists ConocoPhillips as one of its top 30 global stock ideas. He loves its "global and diverse" asset base and management's clear "investment propositions." Hanold has a $152 target on COP. That's more than 20% upside.

#3137. It’s Possible You’ve Been Making Coffee All Wrong: 6 Mistakes a Pro Says to Avoid

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Avoid these brewing blunders for coffee that tastes like the stuff baristas make.

I make coffee every morning, almost without fail. I haven’t always used the same method, and because I bounce between processes to test and experiment with coffee makers, beans and, yes, even K-Cups, I’m open to the idea that I might not always get it right.

According to Sarina Prabasi, the founder of Buunni micro-roastery in New York City, I’m in good company.

Prabasi serves on the board of the Specialty Coffee Association and assures me I’m probably making one or two common coffee-brewing mistakes, like everyone else. Coffee is nuanced; it’s easy to fall into habits—often passed down from family, and often bad.

Whether you brew your morning coffee with a pour-over, French press or espresso machine, here are six coffee mistakes to avoid.

Even the slightest film of soap residue can taint your next cup.

Ditching the soap for your coffee pot and pour-over immersion brewer might seem like dubious advice. In reality, your coffee equipment doesn’t need a scrub down every time you use it. Even small amounts of residue from fragrant dish soap detergent will leave you with a sudsy, subpar pot of coffee.

“It really stays in there; it can mess with the flavor, and so, usually, a good rinse with super hot water is enough for black coffee,” Prabasi said. Oils from the beans may build up over time, so fragrance-free dish soap comes in handy for occasional deep cleaning. A simple rinse with hot water will more than suffice for daily use, however. Save yourself time and avoid any unwanted “soap scum” notes that might interrupt the notes of your single-origin Sidama natural roast.

Coffee beans are one pantry staple you shouldn’t buy in bulk.

Buying in bulk can save time and money at the grocery store, but it can disappoint coffee drinkers. Buying smaller quantities of beans helps you avoid stale, flat coffee, especially for average drinkers and households with one or two people. Probasi told us that you’ll know coffee has gone stale because it “can taste like a shadow of itself.”

The roaster recommends checking the coffee label for a roast date within one month, ideally within two weeks. (Keep in mind, the “best buy” date is different and isn’t an indicator of freshness.) If you don’t like grinding at home, the roast date should be on the fresher side.

But you needn’t panic about the declining flavor in your cupboard like a ticking time bomb. “Every day post-roast doesn’t mean it’s losing freshness, but after two weeks, I’d say it starts to go down,” Prabasi said. Store coffee in an airtight container but avoid the humid fridge with its plethora of smells that can stick to the beans.

You can find tutorials online recommending brewers, scales, tampers, water filters, grinders and miscellaneous techniques to make the perfect cup. Experimentation is key to crafting your favorite brew but only if you start with the basics. “So just adjust only the water in the beginning,” Prabasi said.

If you don’t have a kitchen scale, the roaster told us the rule of thumb is to start with two tablespoons of ground coffee per cup of water. The finer the grind, the stronger your coffee will taste, so adjust the grounds-to-water ratio accordingly. If that seems too weak or too strong, then adjust by adding more or less coffee at the same grind level.

Beyond the basics, you can get creative. “If your coffee is too sour, it’s maybe that you prefer a dark roast,” Prabasi said. Coffee too bitter? You can adjust the roast type by buying a level down, such as dark to medium or medium to light. “ If you got a coffee from East Africa, maybe try one from South America, you know, like switch [it] around,” she said. Changing one element at a time ensures you know which step affected the result, for better or worse.

Filling your coffee pot with tap water will yield less-than-ideal flavors. For most of us, filtered water will make a big difference in your coffee’s final flavor. Tap water often contains by-products that a home water filtration system can easily remove.

Almost all tap water in the US is disinfected with low levels of chlorine. This chemical helps keep drinking water safe as it leaves treatment centers but can alter the taste and smell of tap water. Chloramines can also strip lead and copper from pipes, by-products that can affect even the most carefully prepared coffee.

Smell can be a dead giveaway that your coffee has gone stale. Prabasi explains that you should immediately open a bag of beans or ground coffee and smell the roasted coffee scent. Aroma is a key indicator of flavor. No aroma means a serious lack of taste.

Prabasi said stale coffee can taste muddy or flat and lack any complex tasting notes that a bag might list on its label. “ That’s why I think for in the coffee profession, so much of what we do is tasting coffee,” she said. “From the farm to the coffee shop, every step of the way coffee gets tasted or cupped, in our vernacular.”

Old coffee isn’t likely to make you sick, so there’s no need to toss it. You might, however, want to shift from taking your coffee black. Making iced coffee is a simple way to mask the lack of tasting notes. An immersion brewer also lets you steep the grounds longer to add a bit more flavor after the coffee has dulled.

Don’t skimp on organic coffee even if it costs a few bucks more.

The multitude of coffee brands at the grocery store can feel overwhelming. To help sift through the masses, Prabasi explains the organic coffee label is a sign of quality that’s important for coffee.

“If you can, then I think for coffee and tea, organic is really important because coffee and tea crops, especially from large farms, tend to get really over-sprayed,” Prabasi said. Pesticides are sprayed right onto the coffee cherries, and coffee is unlike an apple that you can wash or a banana that you peel before eating. Tea leaves go through a similar process, and anything left on the leaves then steeps into your mug.

The coffeehouse owner made it clear that she doesn’t believe coffee needs to be expensive to be considered “good.” Great coffee comes in a variety of price points. ” I think the care that goes into sourcing it, to roasting it, or just serving it, I would be looking for those things,” Prabasi said. The organic label is a helpful place to start.

#3136. Intrepid Potash: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Intrepid's 300,000-ton Trio goal was pulled forward from 2027, and its $152.3 million cash pile carries no debt.

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 4, 2026, Intrepid Potash (IPI +1.72%) announced an increase in its full-year production guidance for Trio, a specialty fertilizer containing low-chloride potassium, magnesium, and sulfate. Operational improvements across mining facilities are driving unit production costs lower. And increased output paired with cost discipline supports expanding margins across agricultural cycles. Three takeaways from management's commentary stand out for long-term investors.

Operating performance at the East mine resulted in a 19% year-over-year production gain for Trio during the third quarter. Management plans to invest $16 million in 2027 to add 30,000 tons of annual Trio capacity, with an expected internal rate of return of 30%, a metric that estimates project profitability.

Management is prioritizing high-return investments within its existing asset footprint to sustain output in muriate of potash, a potassium-rich crop nutrient. The company plans to allocate capital toward mine development projects that boost volume without increasing fixed overhead expenses.

The United States Department of Agriculture, or USDA, selected Intrepid's proposed Carlsbad facility for potential grant funding. The plant would produce 220,000 tons of sulfate of potash (SOP), a premium fertilizer, annually, expanding the company's specialty product portfolio.

A balance sheet with $152.3 million in cash and zero debt gives the company room for ongoing organic growth investments alongside opportunistic share repurchases. Management is aligning capital allocation directly with internal return thresholds to maximize per-share equity value over time.

#3135. Touch Macbook Pro OLED review: The first slam dunk of the Ternus era

MacBook users have been waiting a long time for this one: After many years, Apple has finally relented and released a touchscreen laptop. But what's really exciting about this new Apple machine is the incredible tandem OLED display, which Apple has dubbed the PROLED XDR Display. The internet is split on whether "PROLED" is cheesy or not, but what isn't the internet split about?

I'm still in the process of testing the new MacBook Pro, but I can tell you this: Apple has made an incredible laptop, and the company wasn't exaggerating when it promised a "groundbreaking" and "industry-leading" display.

Now, if you're a laptop nerd, you might be rolling your eyes. Touchscreen laptops have been around for ages, and virtually all of Apple's competitors have long offered a high-end OLED display. Well, it shouldn't surprise you that Apple's version of an OLED laptop goes hard in every possible way.

I'm loving this laptop so far, and I think it's the first true slam-dunk of the John Ternus era.

Apple hasn't just made an OLED laptop; it's made a genuine reference-quality display, designed to meet industry standards for video editors, photographers, animators, 3D artists, and color graders. The PROLED XDR display is also the brightest laptop display ever made, with 2,000 nits of peak brightness for HDR content, racing past the MacBook Pro's Liquid Retina XDR display, which tops out at 1,600 nits. The top Windows competition maxes out at 1,300 nits. For non-HDR content, the PROLED offers up to 1,000 nits of sustained brightness.

After spending just 72 hours with the PROLED, my eyes are hurting, and I'm genuinely worried the screen is too bright for my own good.

I'm not going to waste time explaining exactly how tandem OLED technology works; instead, you'll have to trust me that it means a brighter display that lasts longer. The blacks on the display are deep, the colors pop, and the shadows and highlights provide incredibly detailed contrast.

Previously, Apple reserved tandem OLED for the iPad Pro, and the M4 and M5 iPad Pros are famous for reference-quality displays. The iPad Pros also introduced Apple's ProMotion technology, powering an adaptive refresh rate up to 120 Hz. Tandem OLED combined with ProMotion is unmatched, and you don't really know what you're missing until you try it.

Now, ProMotion and tandem OLED finally, finally, come to the MacBook Pro.

This laptop absolutely slaps, and the incredible PROLED XDR display is the headline. It's stunning.

The bad news? I do recommend paying $500 more for the 16-inch model. You'll want the extra screen space. This is a maximalist laptop, and I think size matters here.

To be honest, I don't care about touchscreen. I think there's limited utility if your touchscreen laptop isn't a convertible that flips all the way around into tablet mode. The PROLED also lacks support for Apple Pencil and third-party styluses. So, after so many years talking smack about touchscreens, why has Apple given in?

Maybe it's because kids born today expect everything to be a touchscreen. There are also 3D artists and animators working in Blender who will be happy to pinch and zoom to their heart's content.

I tried out the touchscreen using software like Blender and Final Cut Pro. Some apps will have custom touchscreen interfaces and functionality, but it will take time for macOS developers to adapt to a touchscreen world. For now, anything you can do on the trackpad, you can do on the display. The touchscreen is responsive, and mostly works as you expect. I just don't really need or care about it.

If I were a betting man, I would wager that the touchscreen won't stick around forever. However, the OLED ProMotion display is going to make a lot of Mac users jealous. I wouldn't be surprised if it becomes available as an option, like the Nano Texture finish is with certain Apple products.

I did my best to stress-test this laptop, which runs macOS 27 Golden Gate, with the limited time I've had with it. Due to a shipping delay, I've only had three days with this laptop, so I haven't been able to conduct battery rundown tests or some of our other standard benchmarks.

But when you have to condense a week's worth of testing into three days, you really appreciate just how much modern laptops have to do. I've been busy testing local AI performance, speakers, cameras, multitasking, file transfers, video and photo editing, Siri AI, the new touchscreen display, and the new OLED panel. So far, I'm impressed across the board. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

Apple made stress-testing this machine difficult. My 16-inch review unit has 48GB of RAM and the M5 Pro chip, and it wasn't easy to slow it down. The high-powered M5 chips feature an 18-core CPU architecture, including six "super cores."

For my stress test, I opened complex Blender files. I made Final Cut Pro export large 4K video files while simultaneously applying local AI effects such as stabilization, color adjustment, and generating subtitles to an entire project. I watched 4K HDR YouTube videos, used Siri AI, opened a massive 15.5MB Excel spreadsheet (with 16,000 rows in some tabs), and asked Gemma 4 to compose a sonnet in iambic pentameter about the majestic manatee.* With my 48GB of RAM and the M5 Pro chip, I was able to run a large local AI model, Gemma 4 26B-A4B, and set it to coding applications and composing my sonnet.

Weirdly, the only task that really brought up the spinning wheel of death? That damn Numbers spreadsheet. Go figure.

I also ran the latest Geekbench 7 benchmark test, and it logged impressive results:

Mashable has tested over 90 laptops in the last couple of years, and the PROLED is now the top multi-core scorer in our entire database, handily beating other Macs and Windows laptops with the Qualcomm Snapdragon X2 Elite chipset.

If you're a superuser, you can also upgrade to the M5 Max chip and even more RAM. As we've noted before, a fully specced-out MacBook Pro PROLED will set you back $14,549.

As you'd expect from a high-end Apple laptop, the design is both familiar and impeccable. There's a reason the Windows world has been copying the best MacBooks for decades. However, there are some key hardware and software changes on this laptop (it's the first to bring Dynamic Island from iOS to macOS), aside from the display. The laptop is also lighter and thinner than its forebears. The 14-inch version is half a pound lighter, the 16-inch model is 0.7 pounds lighter, and Apple shaved off half a millimeter and a full millimeter, respectively.

Apple has also famously brought back the glowing Apple logo on the top cover, which dims and brightens as you adjust the brightness settings. That glowing apple has been missing since 2015, and it's a nice touch. Otherwise, this laptop feels a lot like other Apple laptops, with a familiar keyboard, trackpad, and Touch ID key.

For super-super users, this laptop has three Thunderbolt 5 ports and supports up to three external displays.

I'm simultaneously testing the latest MacBook Pro with the M6 chip, and I was in the middle of writing a note about how much I love the speakers when I decided to do a side-by-side test with the MacBook Pro OLED.

Apple enhanced the speaker system to provide deeper bass and better clarity, and you can hear the difference. This MacBook doesn't get quite as loud as I expected, but the sound it produces is incredibly clear and rich (it supports Dolby Atmos and spatial audio, of course ). Compared to the regular MacBook Pro, the audio just has more space to it.

The opening chords of Radiohead's "Everything in its Right Place" have an otherworldly quality, as they should, and bass-heavy tracks like "Billie Jean" really hit you. I also queued up Master and Commander and Masters of the Air on Apple TV, and the combination of the display and audio quality should make other laptops tremble in their aluminum chassis.

Unfortunately, I'm not enough of a "Pro" to require a laptop like this, but for creators, professionals, and early adopters who need (or just want) the best possible display in a laptop, I think this MacBook Pro justifies its high cost. I've done a lot of complaining about prices in my tech reviews this year, but I think Apple has put enough into this laptop to make it worth the investment. You can order it at Amazon, Apple, and other retailers.

The Apple touchscreen MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display launches on Nov. 6. The 14-inch model starts at $2,899, and the 16-inch model (the one I recommend for most people) starts at $3,399.

#3134. Geron: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Operating expenses fell 9% year to date, and $339 million in cash leaves Geron room to pursue hematology deals.

On its third quarter of 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 4, 2026, Geron (GERN +16.13%) announced that full-year net revenue will reach the mid- to high end of its guidance range of $220 million to $240 million. Growing commercial adoption of RYTELO (imetelstat), an enzyme-inhibiting drug approved for lower-risk myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS), a group of bone marrow disorders, provides expanding cash flow from community oncology practices. Three things management said stand out.

Community oncology clinics drive the majority of patient prescriptions, giving Geron a growing footprint in second-line blood disease treatment. Net product revenue reached $60.1 million in the third quarter, representing a 27% increase year over year.

An independent monitoring committee found the Phase III IMpactMF trial unlikely to hit its primary endpoint for overall survival, prompting management to stop the study. Ending the trial avoids future clinical trial spending and sharpens focus on existing commercial priorities.

Geron is launching RYTELO in Germany by the end of 2026 without spending heavily on international sales teams. This staged approach maintains drug pricing overseas while leaving room to sign regional distribution partners later.

Operational efficiency is helping reduce total costs, and management is openly pointing to improved expense controls. Operating expenses year-to-date fell 9% following earlier workforce reductions, while cash reserves reached $339 million. Management is watching commercial adoption rates, European reimbursement milestones, and disciplined capital allocation.

With a self-sustaining U.S. commercial footprint and substantial liquidity, management intends to leverage its existing infrastructure by acquiring additional hematology assets.

Apple has released another iterative update, equipping the 2026 MacBook Pro with the latest Apple silicon. And if you have a much older MacBook, the new model also runs macOS 27 Golden Gate and Siri AI, the latter of which is still a work in progress.

I'm not the first tech reviewer to complain about iterative updates. In recent years, many tech brands have been releasing new models on an annual release cycle. That means customers don't have to wait as long for new upgrades to come to market, but there are downsides, too.

In a world of iterative updates, your shiny new laptop or phone gets out of date much more quickly. I wish tech companies would focus more on making future-proofed models that stand the test of time. We already live in a world of overconsumption and high prices, and every annual release is another opportunity for trillion-dollar tech companies to increase prices even more.

The new $1,999 MacBook Pro is $300 more expensive than the 2025 version with M5 silicon. To be fair, Apple increased prices across the board in June due to the memory shortage, and this release doesn't include an additional price bump.

As I said in my latest MacBook Air review, I wish Apple had waited to release a new MacBook Air and stuck with the older, less expensive version a little longer, but that may not have been possible thanks to RAMageddon.

Testing the new M6 is a bit tedious. I have already thoroughly stress-tested the M5 Pro, and the M6 will inevitably deliver the same results with some improvements. And that's exactly what I found.

Apple promises the new "12-core GPU delivers up to 30 percent faster graphics and up to 25 percent faster AI workloads when compared to M5." Unsurprisingly, that matches up with my results.

Because of a shipping delay, I'm still performing some of our standard benchmarks on the new MacBook Pro, and I'll update this review after spending more time testing the M6 chip and battery. I The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

Like the M5, the M6 MacBook Pro passes the Cyberpunk: 2077 test, with some compromises. I didn't notice significant improvement in performance this time around. I originally tried loading the game with a 60-frame-per-second target refresh rate and MetalFX and ray tracing turned up to the max. I had just enough time to wipe out a gang of Tiger Claws before the game crashed.

At 30 frames per second and with some graphic settings tuned down, I was able to play the game without problems, and Night City still looks gorgeous. However, I had more fun playing the backrooms-inspired game Pools, recently adapted from its original virtual reality format. The spooky, atmospheric visuals looked great on the Pro.

Siri AI isn't unique to macOS 27 Golden Gate, and if you have a compatible Apple device, it's been available for a few months. I tried to use Siri AI on this new laptop, with mixed results. While Siri AI was able to answer many of my queries and draw on my personal data, it also struggled in disappointing ways.

At one point, I asked it to pull up photos from my time visiting Charleston, SC, a city I visit frequently. Siri told me it couldn't find any photos from Charleston. But look at the picture of this moment, and you'll notice the on-screen Photos widget is literally showing an album of photos from Charleston at the exact same time. Siri AI also struggled to find texts and emails from a contact with an oddly spelled name.

These are the kinds of frustrating and basic mistakes that make it hard to fully trust or recommend Siri AI yet.

The latest MacBook Pro retains the high-end build and classic Apple design of recent MacBooks, but it only suffers in comparison to the just-released MacBook Pro OLED laptop, which has an OLED display and upgraded speaker system.

So far, I haven't had any overheating issues or any problems at all from a design standpoint. The keyboard, trackpad, webcam, and Liquid Retina display are still rock solid.

While the latest MacBook Pro doesn't rate very highly on the "Wow factor," it's still a powerful laptop that can support professional workloads. Hopefully, the PROLED XDR Display becomes available with the regular MacBook Pro in the near-ish future, and I think it eventually will. That would be a non-iterative upgrade and a welcome one for many techies.

You can buy the new MacBook Pro for $1,999 at Apple, Amazon, and wherever Apple laptops are sold; it will be released on Nov. 6 alongside the new touch MacBook Pro OLED.

#3132. As Democrats Take Control of Congress, Warren Buffett Has a Timely Warning for Investors

The Democrats won control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate following the 2026 midterm elections.

The 2026 midterm elections was a decisive victory for Democrats, who won control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate. With Republicans retaining the White House, the election results bring a period of divided government starting in January.

Wall Street's initial reaction has been enthusiastic. As of this writing (Nov. 4), the Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI +3.03%) surged more than 1,500 points during morning trading, while the S&P 500 (^GSPC +1.58%) and Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC +1.44%) also rallied.

Beneath the broader market's gains, investors are undoubtedly repositioning their portfolios. Artificial intelligence (AI) hyperscalers like Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft, and Meta Platforms are surging, while many semiconductor stocks and data center operators are plunging.

The contrasting performance reflects uncertainty about how the election could affect AI and adjacent industries. For investors wondering whether to change their portfolios following the election, Warren Buffett's advice about mixing politics and investing is particularly relevant.

Warren Buffett: Image source: Getty Images.

During an interview in 2019, Buffett discussed how investors frequently allow their political views to influence financial decisions. The "Oracle of Omaha" noted that he had invested through 14 presidencies -- seven Republicans and seven Democrats. Despite the different administrations and their economic policies, Buffett continued investing.

His message was straightforward: "You do not want to have a political view in investing."

Buffett's point is that some investors become so concerned about election outcomes that they abandon otherwise attractive investments. Making portfolio decisions based primarily on which political party holds power can mean missing lucrative opportunities for long-term wealth.

In Berkshire Hathaway's 2016 annual shareholder letter, Buffett highlighted how the Dow Jones Industrial Average advanced from 66 to 11,497 during the 20th century, representing a capital gain exceeding 17,000%! That growth occurred despite wars, recessions, financial crises, and changes in political leadership.

Buffett's underlying message is that American businesses will continue innovating, generating profits, and creating shareholder value across different political administrations. While government policies certainly matter, investors shouldn't confuse political uncertainty with the disappearance of long-term economic growth.

Following the Democratic sweep, investors began to reassess the potential implications for AI infrastructure in particular. Shares of the cloud computing hyperscalers surged during morning trading on Nov. 4, while the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index declined about 4%. Data center operators and neoclouds endured even steeper losses, with Iren falling roughly 9% and Hut 8 plunging nearly 17%.

This divergence highlights an interesting development. Investors seem concerned that tighter oversight of AI infrastructure -- particularly data center construction and electricity consumption -- could complicate the industry's expansion.

However, big tech might benefit from a different dynamic. If expanding computing capacity becomes more difficult, companies with enormous infrastructure networks could gain a competitive advantage over smaller rivals attempting to enter the market.

This helps explain why investors are treating different pockets of the AI ecosystem so differently.

Buffett's investment philosophy provides a useful framework for investors navigating the post-election volatility. Consider semiconductor companies such as Nvidia and Micron Technology. Both companies are exposed to AI infrastructure spending, meaning delays in data center build-outs could affect demand for their products.

However, one election will not automatically eliminate the long-term need for advanced computing processors, high bandwidth memory (HBM), or networking equipment. Investors should examine whether these companies' earnings expectations, competitive moats, and valuations still justify their stock prices.

Similarly, data center operators experiencing plummeting stock prices could eventually offer attractive value opportunities. Of course, a falling stock doesn't necessarily mean it's undervalued. This is where Buffett's discipline becomes especially valuable.

Throughout his career, Buffett repeatedly observed that investors can benefit when widespread pessimism or emotionally charged selling pressure creates opportunities to purchase quality businesses at prices below their intrinsic value.

This is all to say that a political transition isn't a compelling reason to change a long-term investment strategy. Rather than panic-selling or blindly following momentum, investors should concentrate on business fundamentals, reasonable valuations, and diversification. That's the ultimate lesson Buffett reinforced through decades of consistent investing under both political parties.

TL;DR: Starbucks Red Cup Day 2026 takes place on Nov. 17. To get your free cup, buy any handcrafted holiday or seasonal beverage (hot, iced, or blended) in any size.

If your morning routine revolves around seasonal espresso shots and viral coffee tumblers, mark your calendar: Starbucks’ 2026 holiday menu officially launches on Nov. 5, bringing back fan favorites and fresh treats.

That's exciting news, but it's not the main draw for seasoned coffee lovers and cup collectors. The Peppermint Mocha is great and all, but it's not Red Cup Day. Starbucks hands out a free, limited-edition red reusable cup with every qualifying handcrafted holiday beverage order on this special day. And you guessed it: fans and collectors go wild.

Just be prepared for heavy app delays and long drive-thru lines on launch morning — mobile ordering at least 20 minutes ahead is non-negotiable if you want to dodge the rush.

#3130. MacBook Pro M6 review: A slight upgrade, but still the most accessible MacBook Pro

It's more of the same, but that's still pretty great.

When I reviewed the M5 Max MacBook Pro earlier this year, I predicted that it might soon feel out of date whenever Apple's fabled touchscreen MacBook Pros arrived. That's even more true for the new MacBook Pro with an M6 chip, which was briefly announced last week before the new touchscreen-equipped PROLED XDR MacBook Pros arrived. Those systems are clearly going to get most of the attention this holiday season from Apple's marketing team and deep-pocketed Mac-heads, so where does that leave the lowly entry-level MacBook Pro?

The M6 MacBook Pro is more of the same design we've seen for years, with a slightly faster chip. And yet, at $1,999, it's still a pretty compelling machine for anyone not crazy enough to spend an extra $900 for an OLED touchscreen and a slightly lighter system. Even Apple's leftovers are still miles ahead of most of the competition.

The biggest selling point of this MacBook Pro is Apple's new M6 chip, which we've already seen in the recent Mac mini. It's a 12-core CPU, 12-core GPU system-on-a-chip, which is slightly more powerful than last year's M5 chip and its 10 CPU cores and 10 GPU cores. The CPU is made up of two super cores for single-threaded work, four performance cores for more intensive multithreaded tasks and six efficiency cores for background tasks. The M6 chip also features dual 16-core neural engines for the first time, which helps to make it twice as fast at AI tasks compared to the M5 chip, according to Apple.

Apple's own benchmarks suggest otherwise modest gains for the M6 chip. The company claims that it's 11.7x faster at 3D rendering compared to the M1 MacBook Pro, while the M5 chip is 9.2x faster than that older system. The M6 is reportedly 3.2x faster while playing Cyberpunk 2077 compared to the M1 system, whereas the M5 was 2.5x faster. Basically, you don't need to throw out your M5 MacBook Pro anytime soon.

Just like with the Mac mini, you'll have to bump up to the M5 Pro or M5 Max chips if you want more power, as those have significantly more CPU and GPU horsepower. Those are the current top-end options since Apple hasn't yet launched faster M6 Pro or Max chips yet. You also get faster RAM performance by jumping to the M5 Pro or Max. The M6 tops out at 32GB of RAM running at 170 GB/s, while the M5 Pro can fit in 64GB at 307 GB/s.

Beyond the new M6 chip, the 14-inch MacBook Pro has all of the same hardware as the previous systems. There's the MiniLED Liquid Retina screen with a 120Hz ProMotion refresh rate, sturdy unibody case and healthy port selection (three Thunderbolt 4 USB-C ports, a MagSafe charging connection, HDMI, headphone jack and an SD card slot). At 3.4 pounds, it's not significantly different from the slimmer 3-pound 14-inch PROLED MacBook Pro.

Though we've seen most of this hardware before, I don't mean to dismiss it. There's certainty in battle-tested hardware designs, and for years Apple has schooled most PC makers when it comes to overall hardware quality.

I'll say this up front: The M6 MacBook Pro is yet another fast and reliable entry in Apple's lineup. Our review unit, which was equipped with 16GB of RAM and a 1TB SSD, flew through my daily workflow with no noticeable hiccups. But that's been true of every MacBook Pro for the past decade — this one is just ever-so-slightly faster than the previous model.

In the Geekbench 6 CPU benchmark, the M6 MacBook Pro scored 4,458 points for single-threaded work and 19,077 points for multi-threaded tasks. Last year's M5 14-inch MacBook Pro was only a bit slower with 4,310 single-threaded points and 18,003 multi-threaded points. The M6's more powerful graphics capabilities shined in the Geekbench 6 GPU test, though, scoring 64,115 points compared to the M5 system's 48,840 points. I saw similarly better gains in Cinebench R24, where the M6 MacBook Pro was around 30 percent faster than the M5 in multi-threaded performance.

I was already pretty impressed with the M5 MacBook Pro's gaming performance, and the M6 chip just pushed things a bit further. Lies of P ran between 90 and 100 fps while playing at the highest resolution (3,024 by 1,890) with graphics settings cranked to the max. That's a 25 fps gain from the M5 system, but it's not something I'd actually notice during gameplay.

It's also worth noting that I didn't miss the PROLED XDR MacBook Pro's touchscreen one bit. Apple's large touchpad remains far easier to reach for scrolling through web pages and documents. The M6 MacBook Pro's MiniLED screen isn't as bright as the PROLED system's, but it still looks great while viewing photos and videos. And most importantly, it's bright enough to use outside in direct sunlight.

Battery life remains great, as well. The M6 MacBook Pro lasted 11 hours and 35 minutes while running the MacBatteryBenchmark script, which simulates real-world programming workflows. In my testing, the battery reached 50 percent after six hours of continuous work, which involved juggling dozens of browser tabs, editing images and hopping on video calls.

While it's a shame that its price jumped from $1,599 to $1,999 in the last year, the 14-inch M6 MacBook Pro remains the cheapest Pro-grade laptop Apple currently sells. Unless you're willing to gamble on the used or refurbished market (something I wholeheartedly support), this is the MacBook Pro most people should consider. The M6 MacBook Pro is fast enough to handle content creation, gaming and demanding tasks that would make the MacBook Air sweat.

Your decision making becomes more complicated if you're considering upgrading to the M5 Pro chip, which costs $2,499. At that point, you might as well spend a bit more to get the redesigned $2,899 PROLED MacBook Pro, which also has an M5 Pro chip and a lighter design.

It's unclear how long Apple is going to juggle multiple MacBook Pro models, but personally I've always been a fan of the base 14-inch MacBook Pro. It's always been fast enough for most people, and it's a significant leap up from the MacBook Air thanks to its fast ProMotion MiniLED screen, active cooling and bevy of ports. The M6 MacBook Pro doesn't bring much new to the table, but it remains one of the best laptops you can buy today.

#3129. Eagle Materials: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Capital spending peaks at Laramie, so the bigger test is whether the expected cash flow step-up arrives on schedule once construction ends.

On its second quarter of fiscal 2027 earnings call, held on Nov. 4, 2026, Eagle Materials (EXP +2.82%) reported record quarterly revenue of $653 million. Heavy investments in plant modernizations aim to expand margins once capital spending drops. Three things management said stand out.

Upgrading the Mountain Cement plant in Laramie, Wyoming, replaces equipment from the 1960s. Completing this project marks the peak of capital expenditures, which are investments in physical assets, before free cash flow expands.

Elevated diesel fuel prices pushed up freight expenses across every product line during the quarter. Management is responding by raising cement prices early next year to protect profitability.

The market for aggregates, which are crushed stone, sand, and gravel, remains fragmented across the country. Management is actively pursuing mergers and acquisitions (M&A) that fit its low-cost operating model.

Public infrastructure projects and data center construction are driving cement demand, giving management tailwinds despite high mortgage rates weighing on residential housing. Eagle Materials relies on its long-term raw material reserves and low-cost footprint to manage cost swings while keeping an eye on freight rates and pricing discipline.

Disciplined capital investments during market troughs set up the company to capture higher margins whenever demand rebounds.

The Motley Fool recommends Eagle Materials. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#3128. MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display review: Lighter, brighter, but the touchscreen doesn't add much

It’s a notable evolution of the MacBook Pro at a much higher price.

The least interesting thing about Apple's new touchscreen MacBook Pro is the touchscreen. The new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, as it's awkwardly called, is better seen as a total redesign of Apple's premium laptops. Both models are slimmer and lighter on every front: The 14-inch model weighs 3 pounds, down from the standard MacBook Pro's 3.7 pounds, while the 16-inch model goes from 4.7 pounds to 4 pounds. It also marks the first time the MacBook Pro has been graced with OLED screens, which are gloriously colorful in all the ways OLEDs tend to be.

Oh yeah, these new machines are also significantly more expensive. The 14-inch starts at $2,899, $900 more than the standard MacBook Pro. The 16-inch PROLED model will cost you $400 more than the regular version at $3,399.

In a time when computers already cost more, thanks to the AI-driven price increases for RAM, storage and other components, it seems odd for Apple to unleash its most expensive laptops yet. But I'm sure there's a crowd who will pay anything to have the sleekest MacBook Pro around. I just hope that Apple keeps its non-touchscreen MacBook Pros around for a long time (and maybe even brings those prices back down).

As you can tell from their name (which really should be something along the lines of the MacBook Pro Ultra), the PROLED XDR screen is the real selling point of these computers. And, at the very least, the display is impressive enough for Apple to create an entirely new marketing buzzword. Both the 14-inch and 16-inch revamped MacBook Pros have OLED screens that are slightly larger than the standard models (14.2-inches and 16.3-inches), which, together with thinner bezels, makes them feel a bit more immersive. They can reach up to 2,000 nits of peak HDR and 1,000 nits of sustained full-screen brightness, making them the brightest OLED screens we've ever seen in laptops. They also sport an insanely high 10,000,000 to 1 contrast ratio.

Being OLED displays, where every pixel is turned on and off individually, they can reach pure deep blacks right alongside very bright elements. As someone who spent hundreds of hours staring at Apple's previous Mini LED-equipped MacBook Pros, which were already incredibly bright, I found it a bit hard to see the difference between the two screen technologies during normal usage. But when I was watching a movie with a dark background, which occasionally erupted into a bright scene, the PROLED XDR MacBook Pros looked more realistic. Watching the final scenes of F1: The Movie, where fireworks erupt against-black night sky for several minutes, felt absolutely revelatory on these screens.

The MacBook Pros with PROLED XDR also sport a Dynamic Island at the top of their screens, which houses their webcams and serves as a new home base for Spotlight and Live Activities. In practice, it works just like the Dynamic Island on iPhones — the displays morph around the black oval to reshape it for various tasks. It's slightly less noticeable than the notch on the standard MacBook Pros, but it ultimately doesn't make a huge visual difference.

For all of the attention Apple paid to its new OLED screens and thinner design, it's surprising that the company has taken a very basic approach to bringing touchscreen support to macOS. The PROLED XDR touchscreens work as you'd expect: You can swipe on the screen to scroll through articles or manipulate 3D objects or other media. Touch interactions just register as mouse clicks, so you can use it for everything in macOS, and Apple also has plenty of creative application partners like Adobe and BlackMagic who plan to fully support the touchscreen. There's no Apple Pencil support, though, so if you actually want to draw you'll still need an iPad.

Both PROLED XDR MacBook Pros look almost the same as the standard models, but there are plenty of hidden refinements that have led to a significant weight reduction. The 3-pound 14-inch model feels closer to a MacBook Air than a MacBook Pro, while the 16-inch MacBook Pro now feels more like the standard 14-inch model, which weighs between 3.4 and 3.6 pounds. Apple was able to shave off the fractional pounds by moving to the lighter OLED displays, as well as reworking the MacBook Pro's cooling design and internal components. I don't have a huge problem with the weight of the standard MacBook Pros, but given that PC competitors are aggressively making their machines lighter, it's nice to see Apple following along.

Beyond the screen and a new case design, the PROLED XDR MacBook Pros also feature a slightly redesigned audio system with six speakers. Apple already had the best speakers I've ever heard in a laptop, and now they're just better with enhanced low end for boomy bass. I was able to crank up the 14-inch model while playing music in my backyard, and there was no distortion or loss of clarity. It simply sounded great as I tried to fill my neighborhood with the sounds of Jungle's Tiny Desk concert.

Under the hood, Apple's new MacBook Pros are running the same M5 Pro and M5 Max chips as the previous models, so there shouldn't be any performance differences. Nothing has changed with the keyboard or trackpad either, but given that they're among the best we have already, I'm not complaining. Thankfully, Apple didn't make the same sacrifices as it did with the slim TouchBar MacBook Pros a decade ago. These PROLED XDR models all have the same ports as the standard MacBook Pros, including three USB-C Thunderbolt 4 ports, HDMI, a headphone jack, a MagSafe power adapter and a full-size SD card slot.

Even without opening up these MacBook Pros, it's obvious that they're more refined. You can immediately feel how much lighter they are than before. And once you get working, the slightly bigger screens and the ability to just touch them whenever you want becomes wonderfully convenient. None of the upgrades are compelling enough to throw out your MacBook Pro if you have a recent M-series model, but they're nice to have if you're willing to pay a premium.

I'll reiterate, though, that the actual touchscreens from these systems aren't anything special. It's nice being able to casually scroll through the web and documents like I can on most Windows PCs, but it's not exactly a game changer. Games like Angry Birds Reloaded and Powerwash Simulator also work seamlessly with the touchscreen, though there are occasional issues, like not being able to trigger specific Angry Bird powers. Powerwash Simulator was also much more accurate using the MacBook Pro's touchpad (I'd wager it's just not optimized fully for touchscreens yet).

While we've had Windows laptops that can twist and turn in all directions to make better use of their touchscreens, Apple has avoided doing anything too crazy with these MacBook Pros. The hinges are a bit more stiff to withstand you touching the screen, but that's about it. If you want a touchscreen Apple device that can move between laptop and tablet modes, you'll still need to get an iPad with a keyboard case. There were rumors that the company was working on some sort of "hybrid" touchscreen interface for macOS, but there's no sign of that here.

Maybe Apple didn't call these systems "MacBook Pro Ultra" because they're basically just MacBook Pros with nicer screens and slimmer cases. They're not exactly changing any computing paradigms. And given that these models are running existing Apple chips, their benchmark performance also comes as no surprise. Our 14-inch review unit, which featured an M5 Pro chip and 48GB of RAM, delivered a single-core Geekbench 6 score of 4,217 points, in line with what we've seen from the rest of the M5 family. That single-core figure is one of the highest we've seen this year, bested only by the ridiculously powerful Mac Studio with the M5 Ultra chip and the MacBook Pro with an M5 Max.

The 14-inch MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display lasted around 12 and a half hours on my workflow, which mostly involves juggling tons of browser tabs, Slacking, image editing, writing, video chatting and occasionally taking some video breaks. Apple claims the 16-inch model can get up to 24 hours of runtime with light web browsing and 1080p video streaming. In my testing, the 16-inch PROLED MacBook Pro lasted for 10 hours and 15 minutes while running a benchmark script replicating real-world coding work.

Given the huge price jump, these aren't systems I can easily recommend to casual buyers. If you're a professional who demands the best quality screen available, or if you travel a lot, it may be worth the significant premium for a PROLED XDR MacBook Pro. At the moment, the 16-inch model seems like the better value, since it's only $400 more than the standard 16-inch MacBook Pro. Spending $900 more just to get a touchscreen OLED 14-inch MacBook Pro just doesn't make much sense, unless you're aiming to get the lightest MacBook Pro possible.

It's hard not to look at the MacBook Pros with PROLED XDR Displays and avoid getting angry about skyrocketing hardware prices. Earlier this year, the 14-inch MacBook Pro started at $1,699, while the 16-inch model went for $2,699. But the price hikes in June pushed them up to $1,999 and $2,999, respectively. Now, Apple is pushing its lineup even higher just for a redesign and better screen.

The obscene prices are unfortunate, but if you're eager to get your hands on the best MacBook Pros around, you'll have to suffer through them. Maybe Apple will actually lower its prices in a few years once RAM and SSD demand stabilizes, but by that point you can likely also save a ton from buying a used or refurbished model. At these price levels, we'll have to start thinking about buying computers like we do cars, where it rarely makes sense to buy something new.

The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Displays isn't exactly revolutionary for Apple, but it shows there's still plenty of room for the company to refine its designs even further. Both the 14-inch and 16-inch models feature OLED screens that are so beautiful to watch, you won't notice that the actual touchscreen experience is fairly basic. If you've already spent a ton on a recent standard MacBook Pro, though, there's no need to rush out and upgrade. Those systems still have great screens and they perform just as fast.

#3127. The Austin Powers steamroller: How to trade CoreWeave's slow moving crisis

In Austin Powers: International Man of Mystery, a Virtuocon guard famously stands in front of a commandeered steamroller, screaming "No!!" three times before being run over. The joke, of course, is that the hazard moved so slowly he had ample time to step out of the way.

For months, equity traders holding CoreWeave (CRWV) have played that guard. Despite credit markets flashing warnings, equity holders essentially just stood there. Now, after a shocking 27.5% drop from last Friday's close to this Thursday morning's 52-week lows, followed by a whiplash 17% rebound, equity investors, if not squashed like Dr. Evil's henchman, are dazed and confused. Shares are down another 5% today.

With earnings just a few weeks away, massive leverage, a heavily split sell-side, and 15.4% short interest, the stock remains primed for explosive volatility.

The hazard approaching CRWV equity wasn't hidden. The AI cloud infrastructure platform essentially didn't exist five years ago and has accumulated $51.6 billion in debt (~$46 billion net of cash) against a backdrop of zero historical profitability. That was well known, but the CEO's comments that the company aspired to be investment grade so it could borrow "unlimited sums", even as investors already anticipated nearly another $60 billion in debt in the next 18months, spooked folks. (Trick or Treat!) Especially since the debt issued only in June had already fallen 20% since.

From an options trader's point of view, it was hard to reconcile deteriorating credit and rising leverage with falling options premia; as recently as last week, they were in the 6th percentile, 1.5 standard deviations below the one-year mean. At 72%, options weren't cheap in absolute terms, but given everything going on, they should have been higher. The stock also looked somewhat complacent, with the equity chopping around historical support levels dating back to May 2025. The credit side was on tilt:

Because CRWV is levered by more than 2:1, a 10% move in enterprise value translates to a nearly 22% swing in equity value.

Despite the dire credit picture, equity sentiment remains fiercely divided, driving this week's 17% bounce from the lows. For example, HSBC maintains a Sell rating with a $39 price target, essentially calling for the stock to be cut in half. Conversely, banks like BNP and Cantor Fitzgerald (my former employer) suggest these fears are overblown and the stock should more than double from here.

It's not just bankers defending the company either. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang downplayed systemic concerns, and ARK Investment stepped in to buy 192,000 shares. BofA argues that CRWV's ability to bring active power online at scale, combined with higher pricing from Nvidia's upcoming Vera Rubin deployments, will drive faster-than-expected revenue growth. They described execution risk as a bigger concern than financing; I'm not sure those who bought the 2032 8 1/2s at par would agree.

With CRWV's credit heavily distressed but its equity heavily defended by high-profile dip-buyers, going outright long or short into earnings carries excessive directional risk. A November/January Call Diagonal, currently trading for just under $6 per spread. Almost 9% of the current stock price. Normally, that's a lot, but given this stock has fallen 27.5% and then gained 17% in the past 5 sessions, it isn't.

#3126. These 6 Stocks Make Up a Big Share of the S&P 500

Six tech stocks make up nearly a third of the S&P 500. Here's how AI spending is shaping each one's results.

Nvidia (NVDA -3.17%), Microsoft (MSFT +6.68%), Apple (AAPL +5.31%), Amazon (AMZN +6.12%), Alphabet (GOOG +3.25%) (GOOGL +3.18%), and Meta Platforms (META +1.44%) walk into an index fund. They take up about a third of the room.

As of Nov. 2, 2026, these six stocks make up 30.8% of the S&P 500 (^GSPC +1.58%). Line up the index's 428 smallest companies, and their combined weight still looks small by comparison.

That share has held roughly steady in recent years. In October 2024, the same six stocks made up about 30.2% of the S&P 500. Most of the added concentration since then has come from further down the list, as Broadcom, Tesla, and Eli Lilly gained ground. The index's 10 largest companies now account for 39% of its weight, up from about 36.4% two years ago.

The group of six mega-techs has still outperformed, though. The Roundhill Magnificent Seven ETF (MAGS +2.24%) owns these six plus Tesla in equal doses and rebalances every quarter. It gained 41.9% over the last two years. The Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO +1.62%) managed a 31.7% increase. That's a respectable result, just not a particularly magnificent one.

Here is a closer look at each tech titan at the top of the S&P 500 index.

Every gold rush needs someone selling shovels, and Nvidia makes the sharpest and shiniest ones. Its AI chips sit inside the data centers the other five companies keep building, and the stock rose 49.3% over two years. That's good enough for a 7.1% slice of the S&P 500.

That position cuts both ways. Nvidia's best customers are the four big spenders on this list, and several of them design their own chips. That's a bit like each of your biggest clients opening a shovel factory in their backyards. Guidance points to roughly 89% year-over-year sales growth in the upcoming Q3 2027 report. That's down from 106% in Q2 but still an impressive velocity. Nvidia is fine as long as the digging for AI gold continues.

Microsoft got to the AI party early, and now it's stuck with the catering bill. The stock gained 23.6% in two years, trailing the index, and its weight slid from 6.4% to 5.5%.

Azure remains one of the largest cloud platforms, and the OpenAI partnership gave Microsoft an early lead in AI software. But investors have grown more cautious about the cost. Microsoft spent $39.4 billion on capital expenditures last quarter, largely on AI data centers and the computing hardware in them. On the upside, the company is financing it with incoming cash flows rather than new debt or stock sales. The open question is how quickly Copilot subscriptions and Azure AI revenue can justify that spending.

Apple, meanwhile, essentially skipped the AI spending spree and still ended up as the biggest company in the S&P 500, at 7.2%. The stock rose 51.9% over two years. Believe it or not, that's a slightly better showing than Nvidia's over the same period.

This company's capital spending is pocket change next to its peers', at just $3.2 billion in Q4 2026. It has partnered with others for some AI features rather than building every artificial brain in-house. I admire the thrift. Still, if AI reshapes how people use their phones, Apple could end up renting key AI technologies from the same rivals it competes with.

Amazon's 24.2% gain in two years is within shouting distance of the S&P 500's increase. Its weight crept from 3.5% to 3.9%.

Amazon Web Services rents computing power to everybody else, which makes Amazon both a big AI spender and a landlord to other AI spenders. It even builds its own chips, called Trainium, so it doesn't have to buy every shovel directly from Nvidia. Capital spending hit $77.3 billion last quarter. That's a lot of shovels in three months, and Amazon is taking on costly debt to pay for them. AWS growth tells you whether the landlord is filling the units.

Two years ago, many investors thought AI chatbots would eat Google Search for lunch. Alphabet apparently didn't get the memo. In last week's Q3 2026 report, Search posted 12% year-over-year revenue growth amid the highest query growth in five years. The stock has risen 63% since November 2024, the best on this list, and its S&P 500 weight climbed from about 3.6% to 4.9%.

Alphabet builds its own AI chips, runs a growing cloud business, and spends like the rest of them, with $51.4 billion in capital spending last quarter. But all that spending pushed free cash flow to negative $9 billion, and the stock fell about 10% after the Q3 report. Investors liked the receipts right up until they started showing more cash going out than coming in. Even so, Alphabet remains the clearest case on this list of AI spending that has paid off for shareholders.

Meta Platforms trails the group. The stock rose just 7% over two years, and its index weight fell from 2.5% to 2.3%. Tesla now ranks ahead of it in the S&P 500.

Meta is spending heavily on AI, at $34.9 billion last quarter, but it has no cloud business to rent that capacity to other companies. The returns have to come from Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp, mainly through better ad targeting and new AI products. The ads are still working, judging by Meta's double-digit growth in both ad impressions and average ad prices. Investors just aren't sure the rest of the bill makes sense yet.

Anders Bylund has positions in Alphabet, Amazon, Nvidia, and Vanguard S&P 500 ETF. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Meta Platforms, Microsoft, Nvidia, and Vanguard S&P 500 ETF. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#3125. Apple iMac M6 review: Faster, more expensive and deeply in need of a refresh

Most buyers would be better off with a Mac mini and a bigger external display.

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

With its new iPhone Duo and MacBook Pro touchscreen models, Apple is finally embracing change and shaking up its product mix. Unfortunately the new iMac M6 all-in-one — once one of Apple's most revolutionary products — has not been a beneficiary of that new ethos.

It is faster than ever thanks to the new M6 chip and updated memory. But the design, which hasn't changed since the 2021 iMac M1, is getting stale. The 24-inch display's small size is more of an issue than ever, considering that 27- and 32-inch monitors are now the norm. It's still a solid computer for consumers or business users, but at a $1,499 starting price ($200 more than before), there are better options — including other Macs.

I tested the iMac M6 in a pretty, pale blue color, with the higher-end 12-core CPU, 12-core GPU (with a dual 16-core neural engine) and 16GB of memory. After recently reviewing a Mac Studio M5 Ultra with 256GB of RAM, I was curious to try a Mac model configured with the least amount of memory possible.

Apple didn't release a new iMac last year, so the biggest change from the 2024 model is an upgrade from the M4 to the M6 processor. The new chip adds two extra cores to both the base and high-end models, with the latter offering up to a 12-core CPU and 12-core GPU instead of 10 cores for both as before. Apple says that memory bandwidth is higher as well at 170GB/s max, compared to the previous 120GB/s. The new model also comes with Apple's latest N1 wireless chip, so it now supports Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6, compared to Wi-Fi 6E and Bluetooth 5.3 on the iMac M4.

Otherwise, the new iMac is the same old iMac. It still comes with a 24-inch 4.5K (4,480 x 2,250) 500-nit IPS display, available with and without a nano-textured coating that reduces glare (a $200 option). The elegant stand still has a tilt but not a height adjustment, and it offers four Thunderbolt 4 ports on the higher-end model and two on the base version. Other features carried over from before include the magnetic power connector, 3.5mm headphone jack and sharp 12-megapixel webcam introduced on the last model.

The iMac is available with the same seven color options as before, including blue, green, pink, yellow, purple, orange and silver, with accessories (the mouse, keyboard and cables) in matching shades. The colors on the front are subdued, but they're more saturated on the back.

Since the iMac skipped the M5 chip, the M6 model is noticeably quicker than before. Apple claims it's up to 50 percent faster for productivity apps like Microsoft Excel compared to the last model, while offering a similar speed bump for things like photo and video editing.

The M6 chip is particularly proficient for AI, with Apple claiming five times faster on-device performance in LM Studio compared to the M4 model. However, keep in mind that AI models work best with plenty of memory and the iMac only offers 16GB, 24GB or 32GB configurations — tied with the MacBook Air for the least of any Mac product.

In my tests, performance largely lived up to Apple's claims. The iMac M6 scored 4,552 and 20,363 points on Geekbench 6's single- and multi-core CPU tests, around a 20 percent bump from the previous model. It did even better on Geekbench 6 GPU (metal) with a mark of 88,276, more than double the previous model. Cinebench 2024 scores were also up 38 percent on the GPU side and 25 percent/40 percent in single/multi-core tests compared to the iMac M4. Finally, the M6 iMac scored 81,050 on Geekbench AI ML, a significant increase from 50,704 before.

Disk speeds are key for low-memory computers, and fortunately, the iMac M6 didn't disappoint here. Those were more than double the previous model, with 12.4GB/s write and 6.76GB/s read speeds — right up there with the Mac Studio M5 Ultra's pace.

Benchmarks are one thing, but I was keen to test the new iMac for quotidian tasks like content creation, gaming and AI. As a machine for school or corporate work, it's great, with minimal lag and zippy performance for spreadsheets and video calls. It's also nice for entertainment, thanks to the bright and colorful (but too small) display with 4K HDR. The six-speaker setup with two force-canceling woofers and Dolby Atmos support also provides decent sound for an all-in-one (AIO) PC.

For some chores, though, my machine was impeded by its relatively meager RAM allocation. Blackmagic Design's DaVinci Resolve is a great test for creative work, and though the iMac did better than I expected, I saw a few issues. I was able to play back a mix of 4K MP4 files from a DJI drone and 6K RAW Nikon files without any issues. However, after adding effects, extra tracks and completing more edits, I saw some interface lag and playback skipping. For basic TikTok and YouTube editing, though, the iMac M6 performed well for me.

Gaming's not a strong point, though. With Cyberpunk 2077, I saw just 50 fps at 1080p with the default graphics settings, and was only able to achieve 60 fps dialing down the quality. Other games like Resident Evil Biohazard and Baldur's Gate 3 had similar performance issues, with 1080p resolution the maximum possible for playable frame rates. With an extra 8GB of RAM, my colleague Devindra Hardawar saw slightly better performance when gaming on a Mac mini with the same M6 chip.

When it comes to AI work, my machine definitely needed more RAM. I tested it using LM Studio with the quen3.5-9b model that matches well to this Mac. It ran at around 30 tokens per second for translation and other prompts, which isn't amazing for a machine at this price. Due to its small model limitations, it also produced some inaccuracies, so the iMac M6 won't be the AI computer of your dreams unless you upgrade the memory.

In my last iMac review, I said that the 24-inch display was "ample" for most work, but I'm no longer of that mind. With extra speed that makes the iMac more useful for AI and creative work, the display is simply too small and that Apple needs to offer at least a 27-inch screen on future models.

Though its design is getting dated, there's still a lot to like about the new iMac M6. It's a good productivity and entertainment machine, and it can even handle light gaming and creative work. The main problem, for me, though, is that you no longer get enough for your money. The base model starts at $1,499 with 10-core CPU and 10-core GPU, but the sweet spot is the version with the 12-core CPU and GPU and 24GB of RAM — more speed and two extra Thunderbolt ports. All of that pushes the price up to $1,899.

Here's the problem: You can purchase a Mac mini with the same M6 chip and 24GB of RAM for $1,099, leaving you $800 to buy a bigger and brighter display with a height adjustment, like LG's 27-inch 5K Ultragear Mini-LED model. Or, you could get a cheaper monitor and spend less.

With that said, if you really want an AIO computer for its simplicity and ease of setup, the iMac is the best one out there. It outperforms Windows models like the Lenovo Yoga AIO 27 for a similar price, particularly in the areas of productivity and content creation. If you don't mind a couple of extra cables, though, the Mac mini with a bigger display is a better option for most people.

#3124. 2027 Chevrolet Silverado 1500 First Drive: Big displays meet big V8s

Chevy's new Silverado needs a few updates before it's ready for prime time.

Global fuel prices are spiraling out of control and smaller, more efficient engines are powering more and more cars, but don't tell that to Chevrolet. The new 2027 Silverado 1500 features a pair of new, bigger V8 engines that make more power and torque, delivering better towing and hauling, but sucking down more fuel in the process.

The bigger story, though, is what's going on in the cabin. A wholly new, Android-based infotainment experience with both Android Auto and Apple CarPlay runs across the entire dashboard, powering up to three displays plus a heads-up display above. Add on a fold-out workspace plus integrated 5G connectivity in a cabin bigger than most Manhattan apartments, and you have a potentially excellent mobile workspace.

It even has hands-off driving and a suite of new features and cameras that make towing a cinch. It's a compelling truck in the making, but as I learned after spending a few days wheeling several different trucks across and around Tucson, Arizona, things aren't quite fully baked.

We'll get the numbers out of the way first, since performance figures sell trucks. For 2027, Chevrolet offers four different engines in the Silverado 1500. The smallest and most efficient of the bunch is a 2.7-liter turbocharged engine, which may sound underwhelming in a truck this size. But, with 350 horsepower and 455 pound-feet of torque, it's only lightweight compared with the rest of the lineup.

That now includes a new 5.7-liter V8, replacing the previously available 5.3. Power and torque step up to 402 horsepower and 428 pound-feet. The last gasoline-powered option is also new: a 6.6-liter V8 that delivers 481 horsepower and 501 pound-feet. That's the most powerful, but it's actually the 5.7 that enables the 1500's maximum tow rating of 13,700 pounds.

The fourth option is Chevrolet's Duramax diesel, with a 3.0-liter displacement, 305 horsepower and a whopping 495 pound-feet of torque. This is the most fuel-efficient of the bunch, with Chevrolet promising 900 miles out of the 34-gallon tank. This was formerly the economical choice, but the soaring prices of the stuff at the pump these days make this a little less appealing.

Chevrolet has seven trims available for the 1500, with the cheapest, the basic Work Truck trim starting at $41,395. From there, as you add on features like locking differentials, uprated suspension and luxurious interior touches, prices quickly climb. The base price on a top-trim, off-road-focused ZR2 is $79,995 after the $2,795 destination charge.

The new 1500 doesn't look radically different from last year's model, but it has seen some substantial design changes that make it look a little less busy and a little more sophisticated than in years past. It's perhaps not the most exciting-looking truck, but it is at least good-looking, something you couldn't necessarily say about the past few years' worth of Silverado.

Much more substantial changes are inside. For 2027, a 16.3-inch central touchscreen is standard, taking up much of the middle of the dashboard and is conjoined to a second display: a 12.2-inch unit that makes up the digital gauge cluster behind the steering wheel.

That includes services like Disney+, Hulu and YouTube, plus iHeartRadio and Amazon Music. You can even bring your own video thanks to an HDMI input. Combine that with the available three-prong outlet, and if you pack your PlayStation 5 you could get some quality GTA VI time in from the passenger seat.

My biggest disappointment, though, is how little you can do with that display. It's for streaming, and that's about it. To me, the most useful feature of passenger displays is letting your co-driver search for destinations and scroll around the map without taking over the driver's navigation view. You can't do that here, and while the Silverado does have an AI-powered co-driver onboard that can do some of that for you, in my testing it didn't always work.

Chevrolet's new Android-based experience has plenty to be happy about, not least the massive display, which is bright, clear and generally easy to reach. Performance of the interface is also quite good, and I appreciate having Google Maps built right into the truck. It's my preferred way of figuring out which way to get where I'm going, and not having to rely on my phone is a bonus.

That said, it's extra nice to use my phone when I want to. Chevrolet has happily excluded support for both Android Auto and Apple CarPlay from most of its EVs, but the new Silverados have thankfully been saved from that misguided decision. Both services work here and wirelessly, even.

That's good, because I didn't love everything going on in the rest of the interface. While the bulk of it is clean and easy, vehicle settings are spread across a few different areas, with many of them hidden behind a quick-access panel accessible only via a tiny icon on the lower-left of the display.

Other frequently used features, like the truck's 360-degree camera view (something you will definitely need for parking), are also accessible via more tiny icons arrayed along the top of the display. Given the size of, well, everything in the new Silverado, I'm not sure why they're so small. Hitting one while on the go is a genuine challenge.

Those cameras aren't just useful for successfully wedging your 5,800-pound, six-plus-foot-long truck into a parking space. Chevrolet puts cameras beneath the truck on its ZR2 model, so you can see whether your rear differential is about to shed its vital fluids upon a rock on the trail.

Cameras are also essential for many of the towing-centric features that make trailering a lot easier than it used to be. You can buy wired, remote cameras to mount on, and even in, whatever you're trailering. The truck can then create a "transparent trailer" mode, enabling you to see what's behind you when you're backing up as if your payload weren't there. You can also get a view inside of the trailer, useful if you have a nervous pony stomping around back there.

The Super Cruise hands-free driving system has also been optimized for towing, and I got a chance to go hands-free on a bumpy, narrow road with a 4,300-pound trailer behind. The system made it easy, keeping the truck perfectly centered without issue.

However, Super Cruise wasn't always perfect. On a later stretch of highway, driving trailer-free in a different Silverado, Super Cruise tried to automatically change lanes right into a motorcycle that was in the midst of passing me. I had to grab the wheel to stop the change. It was a surprising gaffe from a safety system that, in my experience, has been near bulletproof in the past.

So the interface isn't perfect, and Super Cruise isn't either, but those are issues that can hopefully be quickly and easily addressed via a software update. What about the rest of the truck, the parts that won't be so easy to address? I was quite impressed.

I got to sample three out of the four engines, and all proved quite capable for towing and general driving. Yes, the 6.6-liter V8 was strong and had plenty of torque to drive the ZR2 model I tested up and over every obstacle in its way. But honestly, the 5.7 felt very nearly as strong on the road, and I have to imagine for everyday use the four-cylinder will be plenty.

Out on Tucson's highways and byways, the Silverado 1500 was surprisingly pleasant. Its ride quality has just enough of a harsh edge on it to remind you that you're driving a box-frame truck with live axles at either end, but not so punishing that you'll hate your life over every concrete separation joint. It's even reasonably quiet at highway speed, and the interior is so massively roomy on the Crew Cab that you won't have to worry about your kids in the second seat getting in each other's faces.

The new Silverado is an impressive package already, though it'll need a software update or two to reach its full potential. Until then, the inclusion of wireless CarPlay and Android Auto is very appreciated, especially with the dual magnetic Qi chargers. The Super Cruise implementation here clearly still has a few kinks to work out, but otherwise the truck has a lot to offer.

That said, driving something like this is quite a commitment, both in terms of how much space it'll take up in your life and how much it'll drink. While Chevrolet doesn't post fuel economy figures for these trucks, I averaged 16.2 mpg in a 5.7-liter V8-equipped truck. And with that Trail Boss-trim truck coming in at $76,100 after destination with the options you see above, gas won't be the only thing you're paying for.

#3123. Too Late to Buy CrowdStrike Stock? Here's the 1 Thing to Watch.

CrowdStrike is riding AI-driven demand for cybersecurity, but the stock is richly valued. Here's the one number that will show whether the valuation can be supported.

CrowdStrike (CRWD -1.50%) stock has climbed about 83% over the past year as of Nov. 2, 2026, and that's after a recent 10% slip from its October high. Whether it's too late to buy may come down to one number: how fast it adds new subscription revenue.

This was the year cybersecurity became a must-have for companies adopting artificial intelligence (AI). CrowdStrike's Falcon platform protects devices and cloud systems, and its advantage lies in its data. It analyzes about 7 trillion security events a day, a "data moat," as CEO George Kurtz calls it, that trains its AI.

"The world's adoption of AI is rapidly expanding the attack surface," Kurtz said. Net new annual recurring revenue (ARR), the yearly subscription value CrowdStrike added in the latest quarter, hit a record $333 million, up 51% -- a meaningful acceleration over the 32% growth reported in the previous quarter.

CrowdStrike now expects to reach $10 billion in ARR by fiscal 2030 (ending January 2030). From the roughly $6.6 billion expected by the end of this fiscal year, that implies about 15% annualized growth.

Competition is one risk, with Microsoft its biggest rival. But in the near term, the bigger risk for investors is valuation. The stock trades at about 198 times forward earnings estimates, the cash left after investing in the business, while analysts expect long-term earnings growth of roughly 29% a year.

That makes net new ARR the one thing to watch. It drives future cash flow, and at this price, investors need it to not only rise but accelerate. If AI demand drives a sharp acceleration in net new ARR, the valuation could prove justified; otherwise, the share price may be hard to support. The next check is the quarterly report expected around the end of November.
