Silver trust outflows from India's import duties and rule changes sit beside gold inflows, a split that tests whether Sprott's diversification can hold steady.

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 4, 2026, Sprott (SII +7.22%) reported average assets under management, or fee-earning client capital, of $58.8 billion. Operating leverage converts higher average asset levels into expanding free cash flow. Three takeaways from management detail the strategic trajectory.

Sprott increased its regular quarterly dividend by 25%, marking its third straight year of double-digit dividend growth. Operational efficiency and zero balance sheet debt support continuous capital returns to shareholders.

Strategic energy metals provide balance against price swings in precious metals sentiment. Building dedicated strategies in uranium and rare-earth elements gives Sprott long-term exposure to physical supply deficits.

Import duties and regulatory changes in India restricted physical silver purchases, causing net outflows in silver trust products. Net additions in gold products offset silver weakness during a volatile period.

Persistent government spending deficits and tight physical supply in strategic commodities create clear tailwinds across precious metals and energy transition assets. On the distribution side, specialized product offerings and an expanding platform position the business to capture institutional capital allocations. And management continues to monitor international trade policies as they evolve.

With accelerating cash flow generation and zero balance sheet leverage, the company has room to continuously reinvest in new strategy launches, fund seeding, and opportunistic share repurchases.

Fears around the artificial intelligence trade and higher pressure on oil prices are weighing on global markets, but a few stocks offer investors solid growth prospects even in choppy times.

Investors with a long-term horizon can look beyond the ongoing volatility and track the recommendations of top Wall Street analysts to pick attractive stocks with strong long-term growth potential.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Health insurer UnitedHealth delivered better-than-expected results for the third quarter of 2026. The company also raised its full-year earnings outlook, reflecting continued progress on its turnaround plan.

"UNH's beat & raise reinforces turnaround momentum, with improving MA [Medicare Advantage]/Optum Health supporting a higher '26 EPS baseline & upside to '27 consensus," said Wright.

The five-star analyst added that better-than-expected performance in the UnitedHealthcare and Optum Health businesses supported another upgrade to the company's 2026 adjusted earnings per share outlook to at least $20.50. Wright noted that UNH raised the earnings guidance despite incremental investments planned for the fourth quarter of 2026.

Heading into Q3 earnings, Guggenheim analyst Michael Morris maintained a buy rating on Meta stock and increased his price target to $850 from $700, reflecting higher estimates for 2027. He expects Muse usage momentum and engagement levels to shape investor sentiment into the Q3 earnings call.

Specifically, Morris highlighted that, according to Apptopia, Muse reached 1.3 million daily active users in five weeks versus 300,000 in the first week. Given that Muse's current adoption represents less than 0.05% of Meta's 3.6 billion daily active user base, the analyst expects management to prioritize boosting usage over near-term monetization.

"Over time, we believe Muse monetizes primarily through businesses paying to reach consumers through their agents, consistent with the economics of Meta's core advertising business, rather than consumer wallets," said the five-star analyst. While XPU drove most of the nearly $1.5 billion Custom revenue in FY26, Svanberg expects Marvell's XPU Attach business to grow substantially through the end of the decade, leading to a more balanced mix in this business. At the Investor Day event, the company raised its FY29 Custom target from more than $10 billion to over $12 billion, mainly driven by strength in the XPU Attach business.

Svanberg said that another key topic in the roadshow was whether Marvell can secure enough capacity to meet its raised targets. Management said that it met with suppliers ahead of Investor Day to share its five-year goals and received commitments to support these targets. The analyst believes that Marvell's supply chain commitments give it a competitive edge over rivals as customers seek reliable partners for large-scale infrastructure buildouts.

Yesterday NASA announced the latest addition to its X-series of experimental aircraft that have included the Bell X-1 that first broke the sound barrier nearly 80 years ago, and the more recent X-59 quiet supersonic demonstrator. The new X-70 Fractal is designed to be a “high-performance, highly adaptable research platform” that NASA can use as a testbed for the development and testing of next-generation aviation technologies.

The agency only released an AI-generated image of the X-70 shrouded in smoke and shadows, but confirmed several of the plane’s capabilities. It will be a crewed aircraft with a cruising speed of Mach .75 that can reach altitudes of up to 45,000 feet and will provide an “operational range exceeding about 1,726 miles.” The X-70 will be able to carry up to 2,000 pounds of experimental equipment either inside or outside the aircraft, and will feature “advanced, rapidly reconfigurable flight-control technology that will allow NASA to explore aircraft maneuverability in ways never before demonstrated in crewed flight.”

“The X-70 Fractal gives NASA a crewed, high-performance platform to test advanced flight-control, maneuverability, and other cutting-edge technologies in real flight,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “Its modular design and ability to rapidly swap internal and external payloads will keep our teams flying, learning, and moving quickly from one experiment to the next. We expect her first flight under the NASA banner within the next two years, and X-70 is just one part of this new beginning for aeronautics.”

#3115. Could Buying Micron Stock Today Help Set You Up for Life?

The memory market's impressive prospects make Micron Technology stock worth buying and holding for the long run.

If you'd invested $10,000 in shares of Micron Technology (MU -7.00%) three years ago, the value of your investment would now be worth almost $118,000, suggesting that this semiconductor specialist has made investors significantly richer in a short period.

Importantly, Micron isn't done growing yet. The company is on track to benefit from the multi-year growth in the memory market. In fact, buying Micron stock as part of a diversified portfolio could help investors achieve their long-term goals of retiring comfortably or becoming millionaires.

Micron's terrific surge in recent years has been triggered by the incredible demand for memory chips from artificial intelligence (AI) data centers. AI chips are equipped with specialized memory, known as high-bandwidth memory (HBM), which helps transport enormous amounts of data in AI chip clusters and data centers.

HBM plays a critical role in AI data centers by feeding data sets quickly to graphics cards and custom processors. As a result, these accelerators don't sit idle, wasting time and power. Not surprisingly, the HBM market's revenue could hit a whopping $641 billion in 2030, according to Bloomberg Intelligence. For comparison, the HBM market was worth just $4 billion in 2023.

What's more, Bloomberg has significantly increased its HBM estimate for 2030. The firm was anticipating $130 billion in HBM revenue for 2030 in January 2025. This massive uptick in HBM growth estimate points to a long-term tailwind for Micron. That's because HBM is manufactured by stacking multiple conventional dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) chiplets

According to one estimate, HBM consumes around 3x the wafer capacity of conventional DRAM, suggesting that the ongoing memory shortage won't be going away at least until the end of the decade. Moreover, Micron is poised to capitalize on additional AI-related applications, such as humanoid robots and self-driving cars.

These markets can substantially improve Micron's total addressable market (TAM), ensuring that the healthy financial growth the company has been enjoying continues.

Micron will release its fiscal 2027 first-quarter results next month, according to Yahoo! Finance. The company expects non-GAAP earnings per share (EPS) of $38.15 on revenue of $61.5 billion. Those numbers point to a massive jump over the year-ago period's revenue of $13.6 billion and EPS of $4.78.

Micron trades at just 12 times earnings and 8 times sales despite the phenomenal growth it is poised to deliver. Moreover, we have already seen the reasons why Micron is built for robust long-term growth. So, I won't be surprised to see shares of this memory specialist trade at a premium valuation in the future, which could pave the way for significant upside in the stock given its exponential earnings growth.

So, investors looking to buy a long-term winner that trades at an attractive valuation should consider adding Micron to their portfolios, as its upside potential could make them significantly richer.

Tech CEO hearings. Tougher AI and data center guardrails. Investigations of Elon Musk’s DOGE cuts. The gates are open for Democrats once they regain control of committee gavels come January after a historic win of majorities in both the House and Senate on Tuesday.

“LAWYER UP,” the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee wrote on X in a message aimed at the Trump administration as well as “corporate corruption” shortly after networks like NBC News projected Democratic control of the House. “Subpoenas,” Senate Finance Ranking Member Ron Wyden (D-OR) posted. It’s clear tech executives will also be caught in Democrats’ crosshairs. “They are going to need to plant new forests for all of the subpoenas we’ll be printing,” Sen. Ed Markey (D-MA) posted in response to a comment that asked, “Live televised trials of Big Tech executives when?”

“They are going to need to plant new forests for all of the subpoenas we’ll be printing”

Democrats have already used their position in the minority to signal what would be at the top of their committee agendas. House Judiciary Committee Ranking Member Jamie Raskin (D-MD), for example, held a “shadow” hearing earlier this year after the Trump administration’s Justice Department settled its Live Nation-Ticketmaster antitrust trial, which state attorneys general who continued to litigate went on to win.

At the time, Raskin told reporters that it was important to get a head start on administration oversight. “The corruption permeates the administration so much that we have to start building the record because it’s such an overwhelming task,” he said. “We will be using the products of all of these shadow hearings to figure out where to go.” More recently, Raskin demanded information from Amazon, Google, Meta, and Oracle about nondisclosure agreements for public officials considering data center proposals.

“AI company CEOs should be called to testify under oath”

Democrats are also itching to investigate Tesla and SpaceX CEO Musk over all manner of issues. Musk spent record-breaking amounts trying to elect Republicans this cycle and held an unprecedented role in the second Trump administration as the public face of the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), responsible for slashing federal jobs and eliminating the country’s soft diplomacy arm, USAID. Powerful Democratic lawmakers recently told Politico they’re eyeing issues like Musk’s role in DOGE, his alleged conflicts of interest, and his role in reportedly disrupting Starlink service to Ukraine.

Rep. Sam Liccardo (D-CA), a lawmaker from Silicon Valley who just won reelection, says while he’s all for probing things like DOGE, he also doesn’t want his party to get lost in endless calls for tech CEOs to testify without significant legislating to back it up. “I think what is imperative for Democrats is to come to the table with solutions, not with slogans. Not with a lot of performative ranting, but actual solutions,” Liccardo tells The Verge in an interview.

With full control of Congress by a significant margin, Democrats may be able to push forward legislation that would have otherwise been difficult to pass under current Republican leadership. They will still likely run into vetoes by President Donald Trump over things like more heavy-handed AI safeguards that the president has resisted. TD Cowen’s Washington Research Group wrote in a note Wednesday that it still firmly believes Trump “will veto any AI safety bill passed by Congress that would slow the AI model releases cycle.” The group also anticipates that Democrats will take another stab at tech antitrust legislation, which has been more or less on hold for years, but suspects those efforts will either stop short of a floor vote or get vetoed.

Liccardo thinks AI safety rules should be at the top of Democrats’ tech agenda, followed closely by data centers and AI’s impact on jobs. Despite Trump’s aversion to many AI safeguards, he says Congress may be able to get Trump’s signature if they can muster enough bipartisan support. “Pushing Trump out of the way requires that we show strength,” Liccardo says. “We saw that in the past with, for example, the Epstein files.” When some Republicans broke away from him, Liccardo says, Trump realized “that he had to get out of the way of the train because he was not going to stop it.”

Trump told The New York Times on election night he’d at least aim to work with Democrats, which could indicate a potential path for measures with a broad coalition of bipartisan support. The Kids Online Safety Act (KOSA), for example, passed overwhelmingly in the Senate in 2024, but was blocked by Republican leadership in the House. While Trump has not endorsed the Kids Online Safety Act, which was cosponsored by his ally Sen. Marsha Blackburn (R-TN), it’s conceivable it could pass the House if given the floor time, and Trump could consider signing it should it pass both chambers. “Big Tech’s lawless disregard for our children and our communities will be among my top priorities this Congress,” KOSA cosponsor Richard Blumenthal (D-CT) said in a statement. “Whether it’s the industry trading kids’ lives for greater profits or its wealthiest leaders trying to buy influence from a corrupt Trump Administration, Big Tech’s reign of impunity must come to an end. Frankly, this issue has always been bipartisan, and I’m hopeful that I’ll have strong partners on both sides of the aisle as we pursue a strong oversight agenda.”

Rep. Jake Auchincloss (D-MA) says Democrats should pass bills like those he’s introduced to make app stores responsible for imposing age requirements and keep kids under 16 off of social media to give parents back a sense of control. “Democrats should give voice to parents who feel powerless against social media corporations that treat their children like free labor for the dopamine economy,” he says in a statement.

Data center developers are also likely to hit obstacles and have to slow their breakneck pace. “For tech investors the big focus is will these mid-term elections slow the pace of the planned 800 to 1,000 datacenters across the US fueling the AI Revolution…the answer in our view is a clear YES,” Yorkville Ives analysts wrote in a note on Wednesday. “There is no way to sugarcoat that Democrats taking control especially over the Senate will create some major hurdles for AI and tech legislation in the Beltway over the next 2 years. While Trump will likely veto any major draconian AI safety or regulatory laws, this will force the tech industry (Big Tech CEOs) to the negotiating table to try to come up with compromises around legislation in Congress surrounding AI related legislation.”

“Democrats taking control especially over the Senate will create some major hurdles for AI and tech legislation”

Center-left tech policy coalition Chamber of Progress is already warning Democrats not to “confuse an anti-Trump wave with an anti-tech mandate,” with CEO Adam Kovacevich saying that Democratic governor candidates who opposed data center bans won at higher rates than supporters. Liccardo says “it’s not a secret that data centers poll about as well as measles, mumps, and rubella, but I don’t think that’s what suddenly drove the midterms.” He hopes to leverage the data center buildout to make developers pay for needed investments in the energy grid.

One company that could get a slightly warmer welcome in Congress may be Anthropic, which notably stood up to the Trump administration when the Pentagon demanded it agree to let it use Anthropic’s AI for domestic mass surveillance and autonomous weapons. The company is still likely to face many of the same questions and skepticism about its AI safety proposals as other leading AI companies, but its positioning over the past several months may help differentiate it from peers.

Democrats’ recent messaging has promised a Big Tech and AI crackdown. Between 2020 and 2024, the party spent about $2 million to run six political ads that referenced keywords relating to the tech industry, according to public policy group Reset Tech; between 2025 and 2026, they ran 387, spending more than $100 million to do so. If the results from Tuesday are any indication, the rewards for following through with that message could be high.

#3112. Agentic AI Is Shipping Code. Who Owns The Risk?

Andrea Scaduto is co-founder and CEO of SecureFlag, a secure coding training platform.

Not long ago, much of the discussion in software engineering circles was about whether developers should use AI to write code. Now, the focus is on agentic AI and agents that run commands with minimal human direction.

Gartner put agentic AI at the top of its 2026 cybersecurity trends, warning that the technology is creating new attack surfaces as employees and developers adopt it, and that no-code platforms and vibe coding are speeding up the spread of unmanaged agents, unsecured code and potential compliance violations.​​

Before AI agents, development gave organizations a fairly clear path to accountability. A developer makes the change, a reviewer checks it and the service team owns what reaches production.

The chain is now more complicated when an AI agent takes a feature request and turns it into code for a developer to review. For example, a product manager provides the instructions, the agent generates the change and the developer approves it. If that change exposes customer data, who owns the decision to ship it?

The most practical answer, I’d argue, is the person who approves the merge. Agent-written code becomes the organization’s code once a developer approves it, so that approval can’t be a formality. If the person signing off can’t explain what a change does and why it’s safe, it shouldn’t be deployed.

Customers won’t accept “the AI wrote it” as an explanation, and neither will auditors or regulators. The EU’s Cyber Resilience Act makes this clear by placing responsibility on the organizations that put products on the market.​

It’s certainly beneficial that teams can now produce more software faster, but they don’t automatically gain the capacity to assess it all. More output also means more changes to approve, and less time to give each one proper attention.

Research from The Consortium for Information & Software Quality estimated that the cost of poor software quality in the U.S. was approximately $2.41 trillion in 2022, with accumulated technical debt tracked separately at around $1.52 trillion. As teams produce more code, even a low rate of flawed code can create more technical debt than they can keep up with.

Some of that debt is also security debt, as security vulnerabilities found in production can become entry points for attackers and cost more to fix in the long run.​

​Any approach to governing agentic AI has to start with knowing where it is being used. Gartner’s research mentioned above recommends identifying both sanctioned and unsanctioned AI agents, establishing controls for each and preparing incident response plans for agent-related risks.

It’s harder than it sounds, as agents work in integrated development environment extensions, command-line tools, CI/CD pipelines and business-user platforms. Calling them all “AI coding assistants” can obscure how differently they operate. An agent that proposes a change for review has a very different level of access and autonomy from one that can modify a repository or deploy code. These differences should determine how each agent is governed.

For each agent, security and engineering leaders should know who uses it and what it is allowed to do. ​

Agents should have only the permissions they need, with human approval reserved for higher-risk actions, such as merging changes to protected branches or modifying authentication and sensitive data.

Routine changes can use the same security checks as human-authored code, with agent-generated changes clearly identified so teams can see where they came from. Some of these checks have limits, though. In my experience, scanners are effective at finding known patterns but much less reliable when a vulnerability depends on business logic or application context.

As co-founder and director of SecureFlag, a company that provides hands-on developer security training, I’m particularly interested in how developers build the skills to work securely with AI agents and review the code they produce. This focus informs my views on agentic AI, though I recognize that training is only one part of governing how these agents are used.​​​

It’s developers who need to find the issues scanners miss, but general awareness training doesn’t necessarily equip them to do so. Instead, Gartner recommends adaptive programs that include AI-specific tasks, and I’ve found hands-on practice in real development environments can help to build the skills to do this.​​

​Organizations can only take responsibility for agents if they know whether the controls around them are working and developers have the skills they need.

The most useful measures come from the code itself, such as comparing vulnerability rates in agent-authored and human-authored changes, and tracking that difference to see if risk goes down. Remediation time and recurring vulnerability classes can also show where problems continue to occur.

It’s also worth tracking how often teams catch problems in agent-authored changes before merge. A rising catch rate could mean controls are working better or agents are producing more problematic code, and it’s important to know which. These measures give a better view of how the organization is managing the risks of agentic development.​

Securing agentic development has two sides. The agent itself needs to be secured, with limits on what it can access and change. The software it produces also needs to be secure, which depends on someone understanding what the agent was asked to do and whether the result matches that intent.

Developers are at the center of both. In many organizations today, agents operate with some of the same access as the developer using them, meaning developers often influence what agents can access without making a deliberate choice. They are also accountable for the changes they approve.

Leadership is responsible for the conditions around that work, including setting boundaries for what agents can access and making sure developers have the skills to configure agents securely and review what they produce. The organization carries the risk either way.

As agents take on more of the development process, organizations need to define where human responsibility lies. Waiting for an incident to establish those boundaries is a costly way to find out.​

#3111. 3 Stocks Yielding Triple the S&P 500 to Buy in November

Not every dividend stock's yield has been pared back amid the broad market's moves.

A fund or ETF that mirrors the performance of the S&P 500 Index (^GSPC +1.58%) is almost always a smart, all-weather growth investment.

There is one exception, however. That is, if you specifically need income. With a trailing dividend yield of only 1.1%, the S&P 500 just doesn't generate much of it.

There are still great alternatives, though. Here's a rundown of three dividend payers with yields that are not only at least three times bigger than the S&P 500's current yield, but yields based on dividends that have been paid and raised like clockwork for years now.

For most investors, beverage giant Coca-Cola is the go-to choice as an income holding from the consumer goods space. And it's still a good one to be sure. That's certainly not been the case for rival PepsiCo (PEP +3.75%) of late, however, which is down 28% from its 2023 peak mostly due to the company's struggle with inflation.

Both camps have arguably overplayed their hands, however. KO stock is up 50% for the past two years as investors clamored for the safety it offers, dragging its forward-looking dividend yield down to a multiyear low of 2.2%. Conversely, PepsiCo shares' prolonged weakness has pumped its dividend yield up to 4.2%.

A strong yield alone isn't necessarily enough reason to purchase a stock, even as high as this one may be. PepsiCo also brings all the rest of what it needs to bring to the table, though, including an impressive dividend pedigree as well as evidence that it's finally on a turnaround track.

Not only has this beverage (and snack) outfit now raised its per-share dividend for 54 consecutive years, but it's looking for full-year organic revenue growth of around 3% following Q3's top-line improvement of 3.1%, accelerating last year's tepid growth of only 1.7%. It's evidence that initiatives like its prebiotic cola and protein-enriched snack chips are getting traction.

Just don't tarry if you're interested. PEP stock has bounced 12% since reporting its third-quarter numbers in early October. The crowd's starting to believe in it again.

There will come a time when the tobacco business is no longer a tenable industry. Blame/credit successful smoking-cessation efforts, mostly.

That end isn't on the near-term horizon, however. Although the Center for Disease Control reports more than two-thirds of U.S. smokers say they want to kick the cigarette habit, only a little more than half actually tried to quit in the past year, while less than 10% successfully did so. That leaves 11.6% of a still-growing (albeit slowly) U.S. population that continues smoking. Meanwhile, the use of vaping continues to rise as means of delivering nicotine to craving consumers, offsetting much of the progress made on the tobacco-smoking cessation front.

Enter Altria Group (MO +1.39%), parent to U.S. cigarette company Philip Morris (which makes Marlboro cigarettes), but also vaping brand Njoy and oral nicotine pouch maker Helix Innovations. Although the company's sold nearly 3% fewer cigarettes through the first three quarters of 2026 than it did through the first nine months of last year, organic revenue is still up more than 3% thanks to a combination of higher prices and growth of its other product lines.

Perhaps most important, per-share earnings of $4.33 through the first three quarters of 2026 are up 5.1% from last year's comparison, supporting and extending 61 increases in its dividend payment over the course of the past 57 years.

Again, it can't last indefinitely. It's likely going to last longer than most people might expect it to, however, making this stock's forward-looking dividend yield of nearly 5.8% well worth it even without knowing exactly when in the future will be the right time to make your exit. That will become clearer as the time approaches.

Last but not least, add oil and gas pipeline owner/operator Enbridge (ENB -0.33%) to your list of high-yielding dividend stocks to buy while you can step into its yield of 5.6%.

Like the tobacco industry, there will come a time when the world just doesn't need fossil fuels like crude oil and natural gas. Also like the tobacco business, though, that time is well into the distant future. The International Energy Agency's latest outlook suggests demand for oil will continue rising every year all the way through 2050, from a little more than 100 million barrels per day now to 113 million per day then. There's plenty of money to be made in the business in the meantime.

And Enbridge is perfectly positioned to turn this demand into reliable dividends regardless of the price of oil or natural gas. That's because it gets paid a flat fee for the usage of its 18,586 miles of crude pipelines and 19,373 miles' worth of gas pipelines. As long as demand for both remains robust -- and it is -- this company will continue reliably collecting cash. That's why it's not only been able to pay a quarterly dividend like clockwork for decades, but raise its annual payout for 31 consecutive years -- and counting.

That being said, the company is being proactive about preparing for its eventual future, even if the industry's inevitable change is years down the road. Namely, Enbridge is investing in power-related projects like an offshore wind farm in Courseulles, France, and a solar farm near San Antonio, Texas. While these may be outside of the company's wheelhouse right now, it's smart to establish roots that position Enbridge for any and all possible future scenarios.

James Brumley has positions in Coca-Cola. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Enbridge. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#3110. What Midterms Mean for Your Stocks

Fool analysts weigh in on how Democratic control of Congress could affect your portfolio.

Democrats won control of Congress in Tuesday’s midterm elections, and you may be wondering what such a reshuffle means for your investments. We asked our analysts how a Democratic Congress could affect the parts of the market they follow most closely, from healthcare and energy to artificial intelligence (AI) data centers.

For quick background, Republicans will keep the White House for another two years while Democrats will take majority control of both the House and the Senate. When power splits this way, major legislation becomes harder to pass, so investors face fewer surprises from Washington. Markets usually welcome this stability, which helps explain why stocks rose Wednesday morning.

So what happens once the new Congress gets to work? A few themes stand out across our analysts’ answers:

Stocks of the major cloud operators rallied on Wednesday, after the Democratic Party swept control of both the House and the Senate and its candidates won important gubernatorial races. Amazon (AMZN +6.12%), Microsoft (MSFT +6.68%), and Alphabet (GOOG +3.25%) gained 7.2%, 6.5%, and 4.1%, respectively, as of this writing.

That reaction might seem counterintuitive, since there’s been a groundswell of public opposition to data centers. Furthermore, there were an eye-opening 50 data-center-related ballot measures across 10 states, with many supporting moratoriums or stricter regulations in the space.

Gina Hinojosa, the new Democratic governor-elect for Texas, championed freezing data center construction until the state’s lawmakers can assess the impact on water, electricity, air quality, and property rights. This could delay further development until mid-2027.

According to research firm SemiAnalysis, Texas will make up roughly 41% of new data center capacity slated for 2028. Ohio, Georgia, and Arizona also elected Democrats to top offices, and each is a hotbed of data center construction and could face similar hurdles.

Hyperscalers might benefit from stricter regulations, as it could hinder additional competition. It could also serve to slow the massive capital expenditures that have big tech investors on edge.

Democrats just got some political capital, but only a few places to spend it. Drug and biotech companies have largely thrived under Trump 2.0 while healthcare more broadly has been a mixed bag. Investors were initially fearful of huge tariffs and “most-favored nation” pricing, but ultimately realized that the policies mostly allow for business as usual. Don’t expect big changes there–Democrats are unlikely to unwind the price cuts Trump has negotiated. Instead, they will use MFN as a bargaining chip for other goals.

What goals? “Medicare for All”–the favored approach of some left-leaning Democrats–is a non-starter. The most likely goal of Congress will be to restore ACA subsidies and maybe provide some Medicaid relief. It will be a careful dance, though, since any proposals will have to overcome a veto threat.

For investors more interested in development-stage biotech, a bigger issue than policy will be interest rates, since plentiful, patient capital is required to make new drugs. That’s largely outside the hands of lawmakers. Stabilizing the grant process of the National Institutes of Health (NIH) may be an achievable goal, however.

Every election, investors try to pick winners and losers based on who’s in charge. Energy stocks show why that rarely works.

U.S. oil production boomed after Barack Obama took office in 2009—the shale revolution didn’t wait for Washington. Yet energy was the worst-performing sector of his presidency, partly because the industry was so successful it pumped too much oil and prices collapsed in 2014-2016.

Pro-energy Donald Trump took office in 2017. Energy was the worst-performing sector of his first term.

Joe Biden took office in 2021 and signed the Inflation Reduction Act, packed with clean-energy incentives, into law. Oil & Gas stocks were the best-performing sector of his presidency. Clean energy stocks plummeted more than 60%.

Trump returned in 2025 ready to “Drill, Baby, Drill.” Energy was the worst performer in his first year back, then surged in 2026 as the war in Iran sent oil prices soaring. We’ll see where it ends up.

The point is that business fundamentals, valuations, and macro trends matter far more than who’s in office. That’s true for energy, and probably most industries. If presidents can’t steer a sector, a new Congress probably won’t either.

Gaming publisher Take-Two Interactive (TTWO +7.13%) reports results on Monday, but most casual observers are looking out to the week after. That’s the launch of Grand Theft Auto VI, a game that fans have been speculating about for well over a decade.

Take-Two is a three-time Rule Breakers recommendation, going back almost two decades, and all three are beating the market by triple digits. But Take-Two has been lagging the broader market for over five years, and the stock is down around 25% year-to-date. If you think you’ve missed the new GTA cycle, it’s perhaps worth another look.

Our successes came from two distinct theses, both of which proved correct.

GTA 5 is proof that revenue from game IP can continue long after depreciation and amortization charges push down reported earnings. Expectations for GTA 6 aren’t low, but investors may still not fully appreciate the potential for long-term cash flow.

Now that post-midterm market moves are underway, do you plan to buy or trim any stock, or wait for the market to cool down?

Discuss with friends and family, or become a member to hear what your fellow Fools are saying!

#3108. This Janus Henderson fund manager owns CoreWeave debt — here's why he's sticking with it

CoreWeave can overcome the market's skepticism about its debt.

That isn't the consensus view — some Coreweave debt remains deeply distressed with yields above 15%. But Coreweave should power through this tough stretch, according to John Lloyd, global head of multi-sector and corporate credit at Janus Henderson.

"It's a little bit of overreacting," Lloyd tells CNBC, referring to the sell-off in Coreweave bonds, which have tanked along with its equity.

Lloyd owns Coreweave 9.75% bonds due in 2031 in the firm's Multi-Sector Income Fund. The yield to maturity on the debt is now 15.97%, a more than 70% jump since its issuance in April. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.

"Bond prices are lower, spreads are wider, yields are wider, and I don't see a huge fundamental change in the ecosystem right now that would warrant that, other than their higher cost of financing, which I think they can get creative with," Lloyd added.

CoreWeave has taken on a massive amount of debt to fund its data center buildout. The company has roughly $51.6 billion in total debt, including about $35 billion in notes, bonds and loans.

The market is getting nervous about how CoreWeave will be able to keep financing its data centers, and at what cost. Its stock has tumbled 20% over the past week, while the spread on its five-year credit default swaps is nearly 1,081 basis points — lower than earlier in the session but up 13% week over week. Spreads of 1,000 basis points and above are generally a sign of credit distress.

CoreWeave shares moved roughly 2% higher on Tuesday, after tumbling over the past several days and hitting a 52-week low earlier in the session. Its bond yields and spreads remain highly elevated.

Lloyd believes the selloff is a bump in the road for the neocloud company.

The market has been spooked by the jump in Treasury rates, which pushes up funding costs for companies, he explained. The focus largely turned to companies like CoreWeave that have refinance risk when rates move higher, he said.

CoreWeave leverage is high with a debt-to-equity ratio of 702%, up from 290% a year ago. Moreover, CoreWeave will spend an estimated $36.4 billion on capital expenditures this year against Ebitda of $7.5 billion, according to consensus estimates.

Revenue and Ebitda will ramp up next year, hitting $26.5 billion and $16.7 billion respectively, analysts estimate. But capex will hit $47.9 billion, indicating the company may need to finance its data center buildout with more equity issuance and/or debt.

Lloyd isn't necessarily worried about CoreWeave's ability to finance its capital expenditures, despite the fact that its capex outweighs its free-cash flow.

"Next year … they're going to be generating operating free-cash flow that'll support some of that capex need," he said.

The company can also turn to other methods of funding, like more GPU financing, which will allow it to borrow against its graphics processing units or rental contracts, he noted. In addition, CoreWeave could ask its biggest customers — including Microsoft, Meta Platforms and OpenAI — to increase their prepayments, he added.

"They can probably get creative enough where they don't even need to come to the high-yield market," Lloyd said.

The company also doesn't have any near-term maturities, which means it isn't facing a refinancing risk anytime soon, he added.

Meanwhile the supply/demand dynamic should remain tight across the AI compute landscape. Overall adoption rates within the ecosystem are running above consensus demand curves, he said. Add to that a bottleneck in supply, with chips and memory power sold out, and it's a nice set up for CoreWeave.

"All data point to the business model functioning very, very well," Lloyd said. "CoreWeave is one of the best-in-class at getting data centers up and actually running them," he added, noting that CoreWeave's financials have been improving throughout the year.

Another turning point could come if Anthropic goes forth with an IPO, expected in November, followed by OpenAI. Successful IPOs for the frontier labs could soothe market nerves and help support the neocloud operators.

"You just need more of those data points where people become more comfortable with the AI demand side," Lloyd said.

CoreWeave still needs to convince markets it can handle higher market rates and get through the financing bottlenecks.

Lloyd sees the company making it, albeit with some bumps along the way. The bonds should recover, he says, "just not in that straight line."

#3105. Greif: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Greif is shutting its Sweetwater mill to exit coated recycled board, pulling capital toward higher-margin polymer containers and closures.

On its fourth-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 4, 2026, Greif (GEF -5.60%) announced that structural cost reductions drove higher profitability in fiscal 2026. Long-term shareholders benefit as management converts these operational gains into reliable cash flow and balance sheet strength. Three takeaways stand out for long-term investors.

Management completed its original $100 million run rate cost reduction target a year ahead of schedule. The company raised its goal to $150 million by the end of fiscal 2027 to expand profit margins through the economic cycle.

The company shut its Sweetwater mill to exit coated recycled board, which is paperboard made from recycled fibers. This decision follows prior divestitures in containerboard and timberlands as management concentrates capital on higher-margin polymer containers and closure products.

Industrial demand dropped across major product categories like metal and polymer containers during the fourth quarter. Greif countered this market contraction by capturing new customer accounts across growth sectors like data center chemicals and cosmetics.

Industrial activity remains depressed across major regions, forcing a conservative baseline for the coming fiscal year.

That said, low debt levels and global scale give Greif a durable foundation to expand high-return packaging lines. Management is prioritizing network efficiency and pricing discipline to compound value regardless of where the broader economy goes.

#3104. Why Communication Equity Matters In A Global Workforce

Shawn Zhang is Co-Founder & CTO at Sanas, a provider of an AI-powered real-time speech understanding platform.

Today’s employees now collaborate across countries, time zones and cultures as a matter of routine. Companies recruit expertise regardless of location and support customers around the world.​ Yet, many still evaluate communication the same way they did years ago, with a far less global workplace.​

When communication becomes difficult, the burden often falls on the speaker. A candidate needs stronger communication skills. An employee should be more articulate. A customer service representative needs to build better rapport. Sometimes, those assessments are justified. Often, they assume the challenge lies with the individual rather than the interaction itself.​

From hiring to customer interactions, communication shapes how organizations evaluate people and exchange information. When organizations misinterpret communication challenges, they risk overlooking expertise, limit contributions and create barriers that have little to do with an individual’s ability to do the job.​

As co-founder and CTO of Sanas, I’ve spent the last several years building real-time speech technology that helps people understand each other across accents and languages. That work has shown me how often good people get misjudged because of how they sound rather than what they know or how hard they work. In this article, I’ll explain why communication gaps are a business problem, not just a personal one, and share practical steps leaders can take to find hidden talent, strengthen global teams and improve customer conversations.​​

As work has become more distributed, the number of variables affecting communication has increased as well. Language differences, cultural norms, accessibility needs and technology all influence how information is understood and acted upon.​

Research on global virtual teams found that communication practices, cultural differences and language-related challenges affect how teams collaborate and share knowledge. Yet communication challenges are still commonly treated as individual problems rather than shared challenges shaped by people, processes and technology.​ Employees are expected to adjust their communication style, improve language proficiency or adapt to workplace norms. Those efforts can be valuable, but they can also obscure the fact that communication is shared.​

Accent bias provides one well-documented example of what happens when organizations fail to make that distinction. Researchers at the University of Queensland reviewed 27 studies involving more than 4,500 participants and found evidence of hiring discrimination tied to certain non-standard or foreign accents, despite no connection between accent and an individual’s ability to perform a role. People should be hired based on their talent, intelligence, experience and work ethic, not on their accent.​​​

The consequences of these communication barriers are rarely obvious.​ They surface in delayed decisions, weaker collaboration and promising ideas that fail to gain traction. When communication becomes a barrier to participation, businesses gain a less accurate view of the talent and expertise already inside their workforce.​

This has implications for customer experience as well. Organizations spend significant resources trying to reduce friction in customer interactions, yet many continue to rely on communication systems that place the entire burden of understanding on one participant in the conversation.​

Progressive organizations recognize that communication is an operational issue that influences productivity, collaboration and business outcomes.​

Communication equity doesn’t mean lowering the bar. It means making sure the bar measures what really matters. The suggestions below combine technology, leadership behavior and simple process changes that any organization can start on this quarter.​

Advances in real-time language translation, accent translation and other voice technologies are making it easier for people to understand one another without requiring them to change how they speak. These tools help improve understanding within the interaction itself. Increasingly, they can be deployed directly within the communications platforms organizations already use, helping improve conversations without introducing additional complexity for employees or customers.​ When adopting these technologies, organizations will also need to maintain appropriate safeguards for sensitive information.​​

As companies build global workforces, leaders should examine how communication influences hiring decisions, performance evaluations and advancement opportunities. They should ask whether expectations are tied to the actual requirements of a role or whether familiarity is being mistaken for competence. They should consider whether communication challenges are being addressed solely at the individual level when systems, processes and technologies may be equally important parts of the solution.​​

Modeling this starts with small, visible habits. Leaders can ask clarifying questions instead of letting a misunderstanding pass. They can summarize decisions in writing after meetings so that people working in a second language have something to refer back to. They can rotate meeting times so the same time zone isn’t always taking the late call. And when giving feedback on communication, they can point to the specific outcome that suffered, such as a missed requirement or an unclear handoff, rather than to how someone sounds. If a leader can’t name the business impact, that’s a sign the feedback may be about familiarity, not performance.

At Sanas, our teams are spread mainly between the San Francisco Bay Area and Bangalore, with researchers in Europe as well, so we deal with this every day. When we build an interview loop, we decide up front which skills each stage is testing and what a strong answer looks like, and we score candidates against that rubric rather than on overall impressions. A candidate is judged on how well they solve the modeling problem in front of them, not on whether their delivery matches the interviewer’s. Some of our strongest researchers would have been easy to underrate in a less structured process.

Companies have never had greater access to talent or relied more heavily on collaboration across borders, cultures and languages.​ But hiring globally means little if employees must still sound local to be heard, trusted or promoted.​

Trade time and a little extra thought to enhance gifts this holiday season.

Each month, NerdWallet suggests one wallet win to help you feel more confident about your money. This month’s topic is making holiday gifts feel more valuable, and we’re going to show you ways to elevate a gift without overspending.

Making an inexpensive gift feel fancy is a winter challenge I relish.

As a relatively frugal person who often gets sticker shock when shopping for gifts, I’m always looking for creative ways to save money without diminishing the present. Over the years, I’ve developed a few strategies to make a $50 gift feel like it’s worth at least double that.

In the spirit of the season, I’m sharing these strategies with you. I hope you — and your recipients — find them as celebratory as I do.

What does your gift recipient love to do? It helps if they have a favorite hobby, sports team or other interest.

Let’s say your recipient likes to fish. Giving a gift card to a niche fishing store makes it feel far more valuable than the standard Amazon card because it shows that you considered who they are. And there are specialty stores for every hobby these days.

Maybe gift cards aren’t your go-to. You can easily enhance other gifts, too.

Paying $5 extra to engrave or embroider their name on the gift — whether it’s stationery, jewelry or a backpack — makes the item feel far more valuable than its price tag because it’s customized to the individual.

If you choose a gift that couldn’t have been given to anyone else, it increases its value.

Time required: A few extra minutes to think about your recipients’ preferences and apply them when shopping.

A vintage or thrifted scarf can be a wrapping paper alternative that also functions as a gift. Similarly, you could wrap a gift in tea towels, artwork or online prints that can be reused by the recipient.

Another idea: Wrap a gift in printed sheet music that contains a special meaning for the recipient.

Customizing the presentation of the gift elevates it without adding much to the expense.

Time required: Since you have to wrap the gift anyway, this method doesn’t need to take extra time. You’ll just need to find the cloth or paper you plan to use.

One of my favorite gifts in recent memory involved turning a family photograph into a Jane Austen-era image set on a bucolic English estate with the empire-waisted gowns to match. My mom is a big fan of Jane Austen, so I knew she would appreciate seeing the family in a Regency-style photo.

I hired an Etsy artist to transform my original image, but you may be able to do it yourself with a photo app. Similarly, you could create a custom song, illustration or other form of art made specifically for your recipient.

Adding your own creative spin on a gift shows you spent extra time thinking about the recipient to make something extra special for them.

Time required: Applying your own creativity can be time-intensive, but the process is enjoyable so it goes quickly.

I like to call this technique the hybrid gift approach: You buy something, then get crafty to transform the gift into something one-of-a-kind.

One of my favorite ways to do this is with a photo. I’ll buy a nice but inexpensive frame and then put a photo of the recipient, or the recipient alongside loved ones, inside it.

If the person you’re buying for posts on social media, you might not even have to ask them for a photo in advance. Instead, you can find a favorite one that they already shared and surprise them.

The options are endless, especially with online tutorials to help hone your crafting skills. Adding your own customization to a purchased gift makes it feel special, but doesn’t have to cost much.

Time required: Baking, crafting or creating can take several hours, but again, it’s an enjoyable process.

Experiential gifts tend to go over well, and you may even get to have some fun, too.

One year, I gave my mom a membership to a nearby art museum and tacked on an offer to attend an exhibit with her. We had something on the calendar to look forward to together, and she got the option to visit more times throughout the year.

My parents have given me memberships, too. More recently, they gave me one to a local nature center. It’s great because I can visit on my own or attend kid-friendly events at a discounted rate. It makes me feel part of the community, and I love supporting an organization that helps kids learn more about nature.

Another option is to donate to charity in a loved one’s name and then make plans to volunteer at the organization together.

Experiential gifts help create more family memories together, which is one of my favorite ways to celebrate the holidays.

Time required: Setting aside time to visit a museum or other destination can take an entire day, but it’s time well spent.

The bottom line is that giving a highly personalized gift adds value without eating too far into your own budget. Spend $50. Make someone feel like a hundred bucks.

If you’re following along with us on this monthly financial challenge, start by testing out the tips we shared today over the next few weeks. We’ll be back again next month to learn about setting money goals for the new year. And if you missed last month’s edition, take a look back at how to shop the holiday sales.

#3102. American Express vs. PayPal: Which Financial Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

American Express commands premium margins and a closed-loop advantage, while PayPal trades at a significant valuation discount despite stronger profitability metrics.

The payments landscape is evolving rapidly as traditional financial giants face off against digital-first innovators. Investors must decide if the premium resilience of American Express (AXP +2.18%) or the digital reach of PayPal (PYPL +3.42%) offers better value today.

American Express caters to high-net-worth individuals and corporate clients through a unique integrated model. PayPal remains a leader in online transactions and mobile payments, processing trillions in volume. Comparing their growth and risk profiles helps clarify which fits a 2027 investment horizon.

American Express operates a unique integrated payments model, acting as both the card issuer and the network operator. This closed-loop system allows it to capture the full value of every transaction while gathering proprietary data on high-spending consumers and businesses. A key pillar of its growth strategy is its partnership with Delta Air Lines (DAL +7.16%), which serves as its largest strategic partner. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business, but it also provides a steady stream of premium, loyal cardholders.

Financial performance remains robust as the company expands its merchant network and refreshes its card offerings. In fiscal 2025, revenue reached nearly $80.5 billion, representing growth of approximately 8.4% compared to the prior year. The company reported net income of roughly $10.8 billion for the period, resulting in a net margin of 13.5%. These figures highlight a consistent ability to generate profit from its high-fee credit products and merchant discount revenue.

The balance sheet reflects the specific requirements of a large financial institution. As of Amex’s December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio -- which measures total debt divided by shareholder equity -- was roughly 1.7. Its current ratio, a metric that tracks the ability to cover short-term debts with short-term assets, was approximately 0.3. In fiscal 2025, the company generated roughly $16 billion in free cash flow, which is cash from operations minus capital expenditures.

PayPal maintains a massive two-sided network that connects roughly 439 million active accounts across more than 200 global markets. The company provides essential digital tools for both consumers and merchants, including its namesake checkout service and the popular Venmo app. It is a dominant player among fintech stocks, focusing on making digital money movement simple and personalized. Its merchant solutions include branded and unbranded checkout options that help businesses of all sizes accept global payments.

Top-line growth has continued as the company prioritizes high-margin transaction services and cost discipline. In fiscal 2025, revenue reached approximately $33.2 billion, reflecting nearly 4.3% year-over-year growth. The company delivered net income of close to $5.2 billion, achieving a net margin of roughly 15.8%. While its revenue growth rate is lower than some younger competitors, its high net margin indicates a mature and profitable business model.

PayPal maintains a healthy liquidity position to support its global operations. According to its December 2025 balance sheet, the company carried a debt-to-equity ratio of approximately 0.5. Its current ratio was roughly 1.3, suggesting a comfortable cushion for meeting its immediate financial obligations. For fiscal 2025, the company produced close to $5.6 billion in free cash flow, providing ample capital for share buybacks or further product innovation.

American Express faces intense global competition from other payment networks like Visa (V +3.84%) and Mastercard (MA +3.94%), as well as emerging alternative payment providers. It deals with significant dependence on key business partners, particularly its co-branded relationship with Delta Air Lines. Geopolitical instability and trade wars also pose risks, as these events can disrupt global travel and reduce the billed business volume from its premium cardholders. Additionally, as a highly regulated financial institution, it must manage ongoing compliance costs and strict data protection requirements.

PayPal must navigate a landscape of sophisticated cybersecurity threats and potential system outages that could damage its reputation and lead to financial loss. The company faces stiff competition from established tech giants like Amazon (AMZN +6.12%) and new disruptive technologies that could change how consumers pay. Extensive global regulatory and licensing requirements add complexity to its operations, particularly regarding anti-money laundering laws. Furthermore, its credit product offerings expose the company to potential borrower defaults and legal challenges regarding how it manages those receivables.

PayPal currently appears significantly cheaper than American Express based on both earnings and sales multiples, suggesting the market is pricing in slower growth for the digital payment pioneer.

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

PayPal's valuation is clearly lower than Amex's; investors evidently don't see the former growing much from here. While I don't think historical stock performance necessarily dictates future stock performance, I kind of understand why investors are willing to give American Express a premium valuation relative to PayPal.

Over the past 10 years, Amex has outperformed PayPal by more than 250 percentage points. Worse yet, PayPal hasn't even kept pace with the broader market, trailing the S&P 500 badly in that time frame. Indeed, PayPal's returns barely outpaced inflation over the past decade. The payments specialist has been a pretty terrible investment.

I concede that Amex's single-digit revenue growth is not super exciting in and of itself. Its net margin is also just fine. But I will take a good-enough company over a stagnating stock any day. American Express gets my vote for 2027.

#3101. If You'd Invested $1,000 Alongside Warren Buffett in Coca-Cola, Here's How Much You'd Have Today

Coca-Cola has stood the test of time as an investment, and remains one of Berkshire Hathaway's largest stock holdings.

Coca-Cola (KO +1.05%) is one of Warren Buffett's most famous investments. By the time he stopped picking up more shares of the beverage company in 1994, the position had grown to dominate Berkshire Hathaway's (BRKA +3.93%) (BRKB +3.95%) marketable equity portfolio, accounting for more than a third of its value. Today, Coca-Cola remains one of Berkshire's largest stock holdings, though it has been more than 30 years since the conglomerate last bought shares.

Everyday investors had the opportunity to invest right alongside Buffett. He disclosed the purchases in the company's quarterly SEC filings and detailed his reasoning for them in his annual shareholder letters. If you had invested just $1,000 in Coca-Cola at around the time Buffett started accumulating shares, your position today would be worth a nice chunk of change.

Buffett first bought Coca-Cola for Berkshire Hathaway's portfolio in 1988. That year, he paid a total of $592.5 million for just over 14 million shares. His average purchase price was $41.81 per share. He added to the position the following year, paying an average of about $47 per share to bring Berkshire's total share count to 23.35 million. Over the following years, Coca-Cola split its shares twice, bringing Berkshire's share count to 93.4 million by the end of 1993. In 1994, Buffett made his final purchase of Coca-Cola shares, adding another 6.6 million shares at an average price of $41.66 to bring Berkshire's total share count to a round 100 million.

If you'd invested $1,000 in 1988 at the same price as Buffett, you'd end up with 24 shares (assuming you were willing to invest just a few bucks over $1,000 to get that final share). Since then, Coca-Cola has split its stock four times, moves that would have turned those original 24 shares into 384 shares. Those shares would be worth nearly $37,000 at today's price.

But that understates the total return of the investment by a wide margin. Among the factors that attracted Buffett to Coca-Cola are its strong free-cash-flow and earnings growth, which have supported its reliable annual dividend increases. An investor who bought 24 shares of Coca-Cola in 1988 would have collected $7.20 in dividends each quarter from the company. Last month, that investor would've collected a total of $203.52 in dividends. Since 1988, the total value of the dividend payments on that original $1,000 investment would add up to $12,581.76.

Adding the value of the shares and the total dividend payout would bring your total return on investment to about $49,500. But if an investor had opted to reinvest the dividends into Coca-Cola stock, they'd now own over 960 shares worth over $92,000. Either way, that's a fantastic return on a $1,000 investment.

Coca-Cola has what Buffett calls a wide moat: a competitive advantage that protects its business against both rivals and macroeconomic forces. In this case, the moat stems from its strong brand portfolio, which has enabled it to continue raising prices and maintain a dominant market share in the soda business for decades. Management has strategically added to the company's beverage brand portfolio via acquisitions and product development, and it now sports 32 brands with at least $1 billion in annual sales. Those strong brands enable it to charge premium prices and maintain margins even amid periods of high inflation or macroeconomic turbulence.

The company's scale also gives it leverage to drive down bottling costs and control more shelf space in grocery aisles. The latter advantage allows it to easily introduce new products or boost the visibility of newly acquired brands. The result has been steady revenue growth and margin expansion. Coca-Cola's organic revenue climbed 7% in the third quarter while its comparable operating margin expanded by 1 percentage point to 32.9%.

Coca-Cola's stock price has climbed significantly in 2026. Its strong operating results and steady free cash flow may have attracted investors looking to diversify away from cash-burning AI stocks. Trading near 28 times expected forward earnings, the stock looks somewhat expensive, so investors looking to put $1,000 to work in Coca-Cola stock may be better off waiting for a better entry point. That said, there's nothing about the company's recent results or management's outlook that should give investors any reason to sell the stock.

#3099. The Most Undervalued Asset In Critical Infrastructure

Christopher Guttman-McCabe leads Anterix‘s regulatory and spectrum agenda, advancing private broadband for critical infrastructure.

Over the past 18 months, tens of billions of dollars in announced transactions have involved spectrum licenses. Yet most conversations about spectrum focus on what it costs rather than what it enables. ​That’s a mistake.

Spectrum is no longer simply a communications input. For more and more organizations, it’s become a strategic infrastructure asset that shapes resilience, operational control and long-term flexibility.

I’ve watched this conversation change dramatically. What has not changed is that we still tend to think about spectrum too narrowly. We debate auction results, compare license valuations and measure holdings in megahertz. Those metrics tell us surprisingly little about what spectrum is actually worth to the organizations that depend on it.

Spectrum has monetary value. It also has strategic value. Owning spectrum determines how much control an organization has over its own communications and, increasingly, over its own operations.

The buyers are not all looking for the same thing. They are looking at spectrum through different lenses and for different applications. What they have in common is that they are placing a very high value on access to a resource that cannot simply be manufactured when demand increases.

There is a tendency to treat spectrum as though a megahertz is a megahertz. It is not.

Low-band spectrum is a good example. Below 1 GHz, signals travel farther and penetrate buildings, foliage and other obstacles more effectively than higher-frequency spectrum. That matters when you are trying to connect equipment spread across a large geographic area, reach into buildings or maintain connectivity in environments where coverage is difficult.

You cannot simply substitute another frequency and get the same result. The physics do not work that way.

There are only so many opportunities to acquire meaningful amounts of high-quality low-band spectrum. Once those opportunities are gone, creating more spectrum with the same characteristics is not an option. ​Wireless operators need spectrum for terrestrial networks. Satellite companies are pursuing direct-to-device connectivity and looking at how terrestrial and satellite networks can work together. Our company and Lynk Global, for example, are testing satellite direct-to-device service on our 900 MHz spectrum under an FCC experimental license. Beginning with Ameren in 2020, utilities are using 900 MHz to connect more devices, automating more of the grid and asking their communications networks to do more.

What I find most interesting about the transactions we have seen recently is not the dollar value; it’s the diversity of buyers and what they are trying to accomplish.

A satellite company may see terrestrial spectrum as part of a broader connectivity architecture. A critical infrastructure operator may value spectrum because it can provide control over a network that supports operations where communications cannot be treated as an afterthought. Those are very different investment decisions, but they point to the same market reality.

A spectrum auction can tell you what the market was willing to pay under a particular set of circumstances. A strategic acquisition can tell you something different.

For an infrastructure operator, the value of spectrum may have very little to do with whether it could be sold tomorrow. It may be reflected in what the network enables every day.

Consider what is happening on the electric grid. Utilities are deploying intelligent devices, sensors and automated equipment across increasingly distributed networks. The grid is becoming more digital and more dependent on the ability to move information quickly and reliably.

Take a power line that breaks and begins to fall. Sensors can detect the break and de-energize the line in about a second, before it reaches the ground. In dry country, in high wind, that second is the difference between an outage and a wildfire. But the detection only matters if the information reaches the system quickly and reliably enough to act on.

The value of the spectrum supporting that connection is not captured by the price of the license. It is reflected in the capability of the network: better visibility, faster response, greater automation and more control over critical operations.

For any infrastructure provider, spectrum is not simply a communications asset. It becomes part of the infrastructure itself.

There is another part of spectrum’s strategic value that is harder to quantify: optionality.

Consider satellite connectivity. Direct-to-device technology is creating the possibility of satellite connectivity extending the reach of terrestrial networks and providing another layer of coverage and resilience. For a critical infrastructure operator, terrestrial connectivity could remain the primary network while satellite provides an additional layer when and where it is needed. Owning spectrum can create those options. It can allow an organization to build a network today while preserving flexibility around how that network evolves tomorrow.

It is also one reason spectrum is different from many other infrastructure assets. A physical asset can depreciate as it ages. Spectrum does not wear out. Its usefulness can increase as more devices, applications and technologies depend on connectivity.

There is no single formula that captures the value of spectrum. Comparable transactions matter. Auctions matter. But they need to be considered alongside the characteristics of the spectrum itself, its scarcity, what it enables and the alternatives available to the potential user.

Strategic value belongs in that discussion as well.

Demand is expanding across terrestrial wireless, satellite and critical infrastructure, while the supply of high-quality low-band spectrum remains limited. As more industries depend on connectivity, the more consequential that scarcity becomes. Blocks of high-quality, low-band spectrum rarely become available. If you pass on one, you are not deferring the decision. Likely you are making it permanently.

​For organizations that depend on spectrum, value is measured not by what it can be sold for but by what it enables. That is a different way of thinking about an asset that has traditionally been measured primarily in megahertz. Spectrum is finite. The demand for what it enables is not.

To save money on holiday gifts this year, Americans are using these 5 strategies that require coordination with friends and family.

Gift giving can bust a budget, so some Americans plan to have conversations with friends and family this year about setting limits around holiday gifting.

This isn’t as Scroogey as you might think: 55% of holiday spenders plan to use at least one money-saving strategy that likely involves coordinating with loved ones, according to a new NerdWallet survey conducted online by The Harris Poll.

Money can be a taboo subject, especially among family and friends. But a focused discussion on gift boundaries could be the difference between staying within your budget and piling up debt this holiday season.

What other Americans are doing: 28% of holiday spenders plan to set a per-gift dollar limit with family or friends.

Why this works: It’s simple and easy to remember. Unlike some other ideas on this list, you can probably coordinate this one over text.

For best results: If you’re the one bringing up the topic, you should come with a dollar amount that would be reasonable for everyone in your gift exchange group, so no one feels excluded or overextended.

Your circle of friends and family has a lot of kids.

What other Americans are doing: 23% of holiday spenders plan to buy gifts for children in a family, but not the adults.

Why this works: Cutting out adult gifts altogether can rescue a gift budget that has undergone major “kidflation” as new children join the family.

For best results: If you still want to include adults, give a gift that’s fun for the whole family, like a board game or an experience. And make sure your kid-free loved ones are on board.

You traditionally exchange gifts one-on-one with a friend, but the last few gifts you’ve given — and received — were duds.

What other Americans are doing: 18% of holiday spenders plan to skip exchanging gifts with at least one friend or family member.

Why this works: If you’re feeling gift fatigue, there’s a chance they are, too.

For best results: Frame this as an improvement to the gift-giving tradition rather than a scaling back. Propose an alternative way to celebrate your friendship, like swapping out the $40 gift that’ll probably get shelved for a $7 coffee together.

What other Americans are doing: 16% of holiday spenders plan to do a secret Santa gift exchange, or another game that requires purchasing only one gift.

Why this works: 15% of holiday spenders list buying gifts for more people than they originally planned for as among the reasons they’re most likely to overspend this holiday season. This strategy keeps your list in check, even if the number of people playing grows.

For best results: There are bound to be people in your group for whom the rules to the game are important. If you’re the one organizing, be ready to answer questions — can you trade or steal gifts, for example, and, if so, how many times? Also, this works best for family or friend groups who aren’t likely to go rogue and buy extra gifts anyway.

You have no idea what your college friend’s kids (or spouse) are into.

What other Americans are doing: 12% of holiday spenders plan to give one shared gift per family instead of individual gifts.

Why this works: In addition to saving money, this avoids the awkwardness that comes with uninformed gift giving.

For best results: Presentation is key. Don’t sheepishly give an UNO game you clearly bought on the drive over. You may be cutting back, but enthusiasm is free.

Talking about the holidays and talking about money can be stressful conversation topics. About four in five Americans avoid discussing some money topics with family and friends, according to a 2026 survey by the CFP Board. So discussing both at once may seem daunting. But without a doubt, you’re not the only one thinking about them.

Nearly 9 in 10 (86%) holiday spenders plan to use at least one money-saving strategy this holiday season. Start with an icebreaker: “Hey, have you noticed how expensive everything is lately? Would you be open to talking about how we can do gifts this year while keeping spending under control?” This conversation might be the thing that’s secretly on everyone’s wish list.
