#3097. Could $10,000 Invested in ASML Set You Up for Life?

It could, but how profitable that position could be for you will likely depend on your time horizon and commitment.

ASML Holding (ASML -3.60%) has a competitive moat of a type that most companies can only dream about. It might be one of the best stocks to own in the world, given its competitive advantages.

But can an investment in just one company, no matter how dominant it is in its field, set you up for life?

Getting that sort of return on investment from a stock is a tall order, and to do so would require a strong commitment. Even then, it's a long shot. But if one stock could do that, ASML might have the best chance.

ASML is a Dutch company that is a major equipment supplier to the semiconductor industry. It makes the lithography machines needed to manufacture semiconductor chips, and it's by far the dominant player in its niche, with roughly 83% market share.

But more specifically, it is the only company that has the technological capability to produce extreme ultraviolet lithography (EUV) machines, which in turn are the only machines able to make today's high-performance AI chips. It literally enjoys 100% market share in EUV lithography machines, which are used by leading foundries such as Taiwan Semiconductor and Samsung.

In the third quarter, ASML's revenue increased by 26% to 11.7 billion euros from the previous quarter, not year over year. Net income was 5 billion euros, up 72% from Q2.

In Q4, it anticipates revenue of 14.2 billion euros and 15.2 billion euros, up 26% from Q3 at the midpoint. Net sales for fiscal 2026 are forecast to land between 44 billion euros and 45 billion euros, up 36% at the midpoint over fiscal 2025. Its gross margin is projected to be 56%, up from 52.8% in 2025.

And demand for its systems is only increasing as we head into 2027 and 2028 -- and beyond. The supply of machines it currently plans to manufacture in both 2027 and 2028 will not fully meet the demand, so the company is looking to boost its own production capacity for 2028 beyond the 30% increase already planned, ASML President and CEO Christophe Fouquet said.

"We are increasingly receiving orders for 2028, and customers are also expressing interest in placing orders for 2029 and even 2030," Fouquet added.

ASML is so well positioned because of its technological advantages.

Due to the complexity of making an EUV lithography system, ASML had to spend 30 years developing the technology before it was able to bring it to market. At this point, considering the state of the competitive landscape, it would take perhaps 10 to 15 years of development for a would-be rival to match the EUV machines that ASML currently has, according to analysts -- and by then, ASML -- which has continued to push the technology forward with its latest high-numerical-aperture (high NA) EUV machines -- will doubtless be working on even more advanced iterations.

Plus, ASML is a supplier to the entire industry, so it doesn't matter if foundry or manufacturer names change, or if new chipmakers gain ground; they all will have no choice but to come to ASML for equipment.

There aren't many stocks that have performed better than ASML has since it went public in 1995. The stock is up by about 47% over the past year.

It has a 10-year average annualized return of 32%, and over the past 20 years, it has posted an average return of 23%.

Since the company went public, ASML stock has averaged a 20% return.

So, assume that dominance continues for at least the next two decades, due to the unfolding AI boom, which Fouquet said could last 10 to 15 years, and ASML's massive technology advantages.

Suppose you invested $10,000 in ASML stock right now, reinvested your dividends, and held on for 20 years. If the stock matches the 23% average annualized return it has delivered over the past 20 years, you would have a stake worth about $628,000. And if you contributed $100 per month to that initial investment, in 20 years, you would have a stake worth about $983,000.

And if you held it for 30 years and averaged a 20% return, you would have about $2.4 million. With $100 per month contributed, that would jump to $3.9 million.

So, yes, investing in ASML could set you up for life. But you'd have to buy the stock, hold it for at least 20 years, and also be diligent about adding to your position every month. You would also be assuming returns similar to those it has had in the past. Given its strengths and the AI cycle that we are in, those high long-term returns are certainly in play.

#3096. BlackRock's Rick Rieder sees 'historic' opportunity in high-quality bonds

Investors may be wary of the volatility hitting parts of the bond market right now, but they have an "historic" opportunity to grab attractive yields in high-quality credit, Rick Rieder, BlackRock's chief investment officer for global fixed income, told CNBC in an exclusive interview.

Hypothetically, it's now possible for investors to build a diversified portfolio that yields more than 7% with less than three years of duration and an average credit quality of A-, he said. Duration is a measurement of a bond's price sensitivity to fluctuations in rates, and issues with shorter maturities tend to have lower duration.

"Not only is it historic in that these yields are where they are, but the only time these yields are ever here is when there's some problem, like an economic problem or default problem," Rieder said in an interview about his fourth-quarter outlook, released Wednesday.

That isn't the case now, where the economy remains strong, he said. "So you don't really have to worry about defaults of any significance."

While Rieder didn't specifically identify the credits in the aforementioned portfolio, the iShares Aaa - A Rated Corporate Bond ETF (QLTA) has a 30-day SEC yield of 5.68% and an effective duration of 6.48 years — higher than Rieder's low duration focus.

The iShares Flexible Income Active ETF (BINC), which is managed by Rieder, has a 5.66% 30-day SEC yield and three-year effective duration, but its portfolio extends beyond investment-grade credit.

Rieder sees the best opportunity right now in investment-grade corporate bonds — which he pointed out he hasn't said "in a really long time." Investment grade bonds are rated AAA through BBB- by S&P and Fitch, while Moody's rates them Aaa through Baa3.

That includes hyperscaler bonds, which have flooded the market with issuance this year as they ramp up their AI infrastructure. Alphabet, Amazon, Meta Platforms and Oracle have issued a total of about $228.4 billion in bonds year to date, as of Oct. 20, according to LSEG.

"They're very low leverage. They have tremendous amounts of cash flow coming in," Rieder said of the hyperscalers in general. "You're now getting to buy these entities which are higher quality, paying you a very attractive yield to get it."

Rieder's iShares Flexible Income Active ETF has upped its allocation to investment-grade corporates to 14.3% of its portfolio. In July, that stood at 8.5%.

That said, investors need to be patient and sit tight since rates could still move higher from here, he advised.

"Your starting point is by far your best barometer of what your return is going to be," he noted. "So if you get seven and a quarter, maybe you get eight, maybe you get six, but ... if your holding period is a year or longer, you're going to get that yield."

Caution should also be exercised outside of investment-grade credit, which requires more selectivity and deep research, he warned. That includes AI names.

"There's parts of the data center supply that's not hyperscaler guaranteed or hyperscaler backed," he said. "That we've been more cautious around, and we'll continue to be."

The bond market, particularly high-yield credit, has been rocked as investor concern grows over the massive amount of debt some companies are taking out to fund their artificial intelligence build-out.

Junk-rated CoreWeave has become the poster child, seeing its stock drop, bond yields jump and credit-default spreads widen. Oracle, which is sitting in the lower end of investment grade and is seen as a bellwether on the broader AI market, has also taken some hits.

Rieder is also keeping an eye on the Federal Reserve, which is expected to raise its federal funds rate again in December to combat inflation. The market is currently pricing in a nearly 90% probability that the central bank will hike at that time, according to the CME Group FedWatch tool.

The money manager expects that to happen, although he does not agree with it. Higher rates are hurting parts of the economy, like housing, while not having much of an impact on other areas — such as tech companies' capital expenditures, which have become a big driver of growth, he said.

"They're not borrowing off the overnight funds rate," Rieder noted. "There's a lot of floating rate finance in housing, credit card, auto loan finance, and you're seeing those areas already under pressure."

Instead, the market is and will continue to price the AI supply coming into the market, he added.

Rieder sees a number of possible risks ahead, including rising levels of government debt across the globe. In the United States, the budget deficit has grown to $2 trillion for fiscal 2026.

"The more the central banks raise the rates, the cost of debt to these to already indebted governments is something we've got to be careful about over time," he said.

Bond supply coming from AI companies should also be watched.

"With the amount of supply that's coming — data center, hyperscaler — there's some crowding-out effect that's taking place," he said. "With government rates moving higher, that is something that we just got to keep an eye on."

In the meantime, Rieder would just continue to reap the rewards of high investment-grade yields "and smile a lot," he said.

#3092. AI Will Make Code Cheap, But It Won’t Shrink Most Engineering Teams

As a leader in a technology company or role, you may be asking yourself: If agents are writing code, we’ll need a fraction of the engineers, right?

It’s a fair question. But my honest answer, for most enterprises, is probably not. Here’s why, and where I could be wrong.

In 1865, the English economist William Stanley Jevons published The Coal Question. Britain feared running out of coal, and many assumed more efficient engines would solve it. Jevons pointed out the opposite: As coal-powered work got cheaper, it spread into more industries, and the total coal use kept climbing. In his words: “It is wholly a confusion of ideas to suppose that the economical use of fuel is equivalent to a diminished consumption. The very contrary is the truth.”

That’s the Jevons paradox. Make something cheaper to use, and if enough demand is waiting, you end up using more of it.

I think code is going through the same thing.

It’s already happening one layer down. This summer, AI token prices fell by more than one-third while GPU rental prices held, according to market data compiled by Citadel Securities. Cheaper inference didn’t mean less compute. People used more of it.​​

Every enterprise I’ve worked with has two backlogs of projects. There’s an official one. Then, there’s a much bigger one that never got written down because nobody thought these were worth the money or time​.

• Needed Internal Tools That Were Put On The Back Burner: When you have approvals that run through a chain of emails or reconciliations that someone does by hand every month-end, you need a better process. But everyone is used to the manual fixes, so they make do.

• Modernization Efforts That Are Always Pushed Back To “Next Year”: You might have a core system on a database that’s full of stored procedures written by people who left a decade ago, but nobody wants to touch it.

• A Long Tail Of Spreadsheet Workflows: The operations analyst pulls reports, fixes them up in Excel and keys them into another system. There are thousands of these, but each are too small to justify a project.

The benefits are clear, but these needs didn’t justify the cost and the risk, so the business case was never made.

That’s changing. Across the modernization programs we’ve delivered over the last 18 months, engineering effort has come in about 70% lower than it used to. Not all of that is the tooling; good teams matter a lot. But modernization also changes which programs make sense.

And the demand is growing. At one of our clients, an agentic order-entry system built for one division worked well enough, and cheaply enough, that a second division funded its own program soon after. Work that used to be “nice to have, can’t justify” turns into “Why haven’t we started?”

That’s the Jevons moment for software: The forgotten backlog starts showing up as real demand, and someone has to build and run it.

Every piece of software you build is something you now have to maintain, secure and operate. That’s more access to manage, more dependencies to patch and more to monitor and support. The operations side doesn’t shrink because the build side got cheaper. It grows with it.

Much of that work will be agentic too. But someone still has to design those loops and decide what counts as an exception.​

If writing code isn’t the expensive part anymore, what is? It’s two things: deciding what’s worth building, and judging whether what got built is right.

Earlier this year, I wrote about how, once engineers start directing agents, value moves upstream to intent and downstream to validation. The danger is shipping more things nobody validated.

So, the work I see growing is specification, validation and architecture. Someone has to know the business rules well enough to write them down. Someone has to decide how a new service fits with the 20 others around it. Someone has to own it when it breaks at 2 a.m.

Agents can generate the code. They can’t be accountable for it.

Jevons isn’t a law of nature. It only holds when demand grows faster than the cost falls.

And the bar is high. If a program takes 70% less delivery effort, a company has to build more than three times as much software just to keep the same number of build hours. A backlog proves there’s demand. It doesn’t prove there’s three times more of it.

My bet is that most enterprises will clear that bar. But some will build the same portfolio with a smaller team, and that’s a legitimate choice.

The other caveat is about people. Total demand for engineering can grow while specific roles shrink. Coal use rose in Jevons’ time, but that didn’t help every worker tied to the old way of doing things. More software doesn’t automatically mean a better job for every engineer.

Back in 2023, I wrote about skills with different half-lives. Some are perishable, such as a specific framework or syntax. Others are durable, like understanding how a business process works and judging quality. The durable ones are exactly what companies need.

When a CIO asks me how many engineers they’ll need, I ask a different question first: What would you build if building were cheap? Most have been carrying that list for years. Go back through the ideas you turned down, and give each one an owner who’ll run it, not just build it.

Cheap code doesn’t shrink the work. It shows you how much you left undone.​

#3091. Champion Homes: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Factory-built housing is winning first-time buyers, but material cost inflation is squeezing margins before price increases catch up.

On its second-quarter fiscal 2027 earnings call, held on Nov. 4, 2026, Champion Homes (SKY +11.35%) reported net sales growth of 6.2% over the prior year. For long-term investors, the company's expansion into company-owned sales centers provides higher average selling prices and direct access to homebuyers. Three key takeaways from the call highlight how management is steering the business.

Management is expanding captive retail, which refers to company-owned sales centers that sell directly to homebuyers rather than through independent dealers. Controlling these outlets lets Champion Homes capture higher retail margins and strengthen customer engagement across its footprint.

Input costs for steel and petroleum-based materials accelerated late in the quarter. Management is using targeted price increases and sourcing efficiencies to offset those expenses. But price realization tends to lag raw material cost hikes, so margins feel the squeeze in the near term.

Elevated mortgage rates and expensive site-built housing are pushing new buyers toward factory-built alternatives. Champion Homes is meeting that demand by updating home aesthetics and expanding digital marketing leads to reach buyers who might not have considered manufactured housing before.

Orders are expanding across multiple channels, and management expects third-quarter revenue growth of 8% to 10% year over year despite persistent macroeconomic inflation.

The business relies on its captive retail scale, backlog lead times, and cash position to navigate input cost swings. And management continues to execute on strategic acquisitions alongside organic growth.

#3090. The CIO Playbook That Worked For 20 Years Is Breaking

Sue Odle is CEO of StorMagic, where she helps organizations simplify on-site virtualization for distributed IT environments.

​For years, infrastructure planning was predictable. CIOs knew their vendors, understood licensing models and could plan around standard hardware refresh cycles. That predictability has changed as hardware costs and availability fluctuate, vendor models change and AI creates new infrastructure demands while organizations continue to manage centralized and diverse distributed IT operations.​

Many CIOs are slowing down, not because they lack urgency but because they understand that the way IT planning has been governed for the last 20 years is no longer reliable. The old playbooks assumed a level of stability that many organizations don’t have anymore.​

​Hardware is one of the clearest examples of how infrastructure planning has changed. Many organizations historically followed a three-to-five-year refresh cycle and treated it as a standard part of IT planning. Now, CIOs have more reason to question whether every scheduled refresh is really necessary.​

Hardware is more dependable today, while costs and supply are harder to predict. According to a July 2026 report from TrendForce, server DRAM contract prices were expected to rise 13% to 18% quarter over quarter in the third quarter, while there was still a hardware shortage. As a result, some organizations are extending the life of existing hardware and looking more closely at what they own before committing to a replacement.​

That decision isn’t only about preserving budget. Hardware cost has a trickle-down effect on modernization plans, software choices and the pace of innovation. It’s a risk factor, not just a line item. Refresh cycles should increasingly be driven by workload and business requirements rather than simply by the calendar. If existing hardware still supports the business, keeping it in place often makes sense.​

​When conditions are difficult to predict, long-term commitments can carry more risk than they once did. A longer agreement may create cost certainty, but it can also limit flexibility if pricing, licensing, support or business needs change before the contract ends.​

That doesn’t mean long-term planning should disappear. It means CIOs need to be more deliberate about where the business can comfortably make a long-term commitment and where a shorter scope gives the organization more room to adjust.​

Vendor history, stability and behavior are now a part of infrastructure risk. CIOs aren’t only evaluating whether a platform works today. They’re also evaluating whether the licensing model, support experience and vendor relationship can be trusted over time.​

​Cloud-first strategies have shaped IT modernization for years, but a one-size-fits-all approach is becoming harder to justify as infrastructure and workloads spread across more locations. The cloud remains important, but some workloads need to operate closer to where data is created and where the business is running.

Retail locations have different requirements than centralized data centers. Many retailers run transaction, inventory and security applications locally, where connectivity and onsite IT support vary. Relying entirely on centralized infrastructure can increase operational risk.

Healthcare, manufacturing and other distributed industries face similar challenges. Healthcare organizations may run systems locally to support patient care, while manufacturers may keep applications onsite to maintain production when connectivity fails. Latency, availability, regulatory requirements, data sovereignty and data movement costs can determine whether workloads run in the cloud, at the edge or across both.

This is where CIOs need to be careful not to apply data center assumptions to edge environments. The edge isn’t simply a smaller data center. It has different constraints around space, staff, connectivity, cost and uptime. Treating those environments the same can lead to unnecessary complexity or infrastructure that exceeds what the location actually needs.​

AI is creating new pressure on infrastructure decisions, but AI readiness isn’t only a GPU issue. Before committing a significant budget to new compute resources, CIOs need to understand where AI will be used, what data it depends on and whether the workload needs to run centrally, at the edge or both.

Some AI use cases may require specialized infrastructure. Others may be supported by existing CPU-based servers, especially in early-stage or edge environments where the objective is to process data closer to where it’s created. The point is to avoid assuming every AI use case requires the same infrastructure strategy.

CIOs should connect AI infrastructure planning to data maturity, workload placement, governance and operational requirements. AI investments should be tied to what the business can truly use, support and scale.

​There’s still pressure on CIOs to move quickly as the C-suite pushes for modernization, AI efforts and measurable returns. Taking more time can be interpreted as hesitation, but a slower decision isn’t always a weaker one.​

CIOs are weighing rising costs, changing vendor models and infrastructure needs before committing resources. Some projects can move forward now, while others may be better phased or delayed.​

CIOs also need to explain that reasoning to the rest of the C-suite. If a delay reduces unnecessary cost or operational risk, that context matters. Careful sequencing can protect the business from overcommitting to technology, contracts or hardware before the requirements are clear.​

​CIOs need to build more flexibility into the decisions they’re already making. That means looking more closely at whether existing hardware can continue doing the job before refreshing it, choosing vendors and contracts that leave room to adapt as conditions change and matching infrastructure to the workload rather than defaulting to one environment.

​The old playbook assumed more predictability than CIOs have today. Hardware cycles, vendor models, cloud strategies, data sovereignty and AI requirements are all changing at once. CIOs can’t control what the market does next, but they can build infrastructure strategies that give the business more room to adapt.​

TL;DR: Mortgage rates kicked off the week with a drop, but they’re still above 7%.

Mortgage rates are cooling off as we roll into November. However, they’re still above the 7% threshold.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage dropped to 7.07% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is 11 basis points lower than yesterday and 13 basis points lower than a week ago. (See our chart below for more specifics.) A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.

This week’s employment data could potentially push mortgage rates one way or the other — more on that below the graph.

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

This week, the Nerds will be watching the October jobs report, which comes out on Friday, Nov. 6. If it shows that employment remained steady (or even improved), that will build a stronger case for the Federal Reserve to raise overnight borrowing rates again at their next meeting on Dec. 8-9.

While the Fed doesn’t directly set mortgage rates, it does set the federal funds rate, which is the fee that banks must pay to borrow from one another (which is how they fund mortgages). Lenders raise mortgage rates any time they think that the federal funds rate is about to go up.

Central bankers hiked the federal funds rate in September, so a relatively steady jobs report would suggest the labor market could withstand higher rates.

The Fed has a dual mandate to control inflation while supporting maximum employment, and raising the federal funds rate is their main tool for bringing inflation down. If they can work to lower inflation without hurting employment too badly, central bankers may feel more confident to act.

The September Personal Consumption Expenditures price index (PCE), the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, was released last Thursday. The data shows inflation was 3.6% year-over-year in September, up from 3.4% in August.

September’s federal funds rate hike came in the middle of the month, so October’s inflation data will really capture its effect on inflation. The October PCE report will come out on Nov. 25.

» Learn more: How the Fed affects mortgage rates

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

With rates where they are right now, you may want to start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.57% or higher — but there just aren't too many people for whom that's true.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

» Time to refi? Compare refinance rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

#3088. China's Rare-Earth Export Pause Expires Nov. 10. Here's What It Means for USA Rare Earth and MP Materials.

The U.S. government is making major investments to rebuild domestic rare-earth mining and processing capabilities, marking a sharp break from decades of Western dependence on China.

After decades of aggressive state subsidies and undercutting competition, China has taken control of rare-earth mining and processing. According to research from The Motley Fool, China controls 70% of rare-earth element extraction and 90% of processing.

This strong position has given China the upper hand in trade negotiations and has been a strong point of contention between the two countries. In October 2025, China's Ministry of Commerce significantly tightened control over rare-earth supply chains.

In November 2025, the U.S. and China came to a bilateral trade truce that put these measures on pause for about a year. The sides announced an extension of the broader trade truce in late September, extending the deadline to Jan. 10, 2027. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says the extension covers China's broader rare-earth controls. However, China has yet to publish a formal notice, and the legal suspension on rare-earth will end on Nov. 10 without it.

The U.S. is taking steps to reestablish a domestically controlled supply chain for mining and processing rare-earth elements, with companies like MP Materials (MP -5.08%) and USA Rare Earth (USAR -5.86%) leading the way. Here's what the export pause means for these miners and what comes next.

The U.S. government is investing heavily to reestablish rare-earth mining and processing, a fundamental shift that reverses decades of Western reliance on China for these elements.

MP Materials was naturally among the first companies to benefit from U.S. spending to establish rare-earth supply chains. The company owns the Mountain Pass mining and processing site in California, the only large-scale rare-earth mining and processing facility in North America.

Last year, MP entered into a historic partnership with the Department of Defense. As part of this, the DOD provided a 10-year, 100% magnet offtake commitment and a 10-year price floor mechanism guaranteeing $110 per kilogram for all neodymium-praseodymium (NdPr) products. The DOD also agreed to purchase 100% of magnets produced at MP's upcoming 10X facility.

USA Rare Earth has a bigger uphill climb. Late last year, it acquired Less Common Metals, a U.K.-based company that can convert separated rare-earth oxides into refined metals and specialized strip-cast alloys. Earlier this year, it secured up to $1.6 billion in funding from the CHIPS and Science Act to establish its own "mine-to-magnet" supply chain.

The company also acquired Serra Verde Group in September 2026, a Brazil-based rare-earth operation and the only one outside Asia that produces all four critical magnetic rare-earth elements. On top of this, it is investing heavily in the resource-rich Round Top mine in Texas and expanding its manufacturing and processing capabilities.

China's potential export restriction on Nov. 10 doesn't change the story for rare-earth miners like MP Materials and USA Rare Earth. While the two sides could extend the truce, China's export controls are fundamentally bullish for domestically based rare-earth miners in the long term.

For investors considering these stocks, USA Rare Earth is establishing itself, integrating its acquisitions, and expanding its production capabilities, and is a more aggressive long-term play in reestablishing U.S. supply chains. Meanwhile, MP Materials is the top domestic rare-earth miner, is actively fulfilling customer agreements, and has government backing that others cannot match.

Courtney Carlsen has positions in MP Materials and USA Rare Earth. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends MP Materials. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#3086. Casey's General Stores Has Fallen 10% Since Reporting Earnings. Is It a Buy in November?

Casey's General Stores' same-store sales disappointed, but that didn't change the big problem with the stock.

Casey's General Stores (CASY +1.42%) is a fast-growing convenience store chain, but investors weren't particularly excited by its fiscal first-quarter 2027 earnings results. Even after regaining some ground, the stock is still down 10% from its pre-earnings level as of this writing. That's probably not enough of a decline to make this stock worth buying as November gets underway. Here's why.

Casey's General Stores' business didn't fall off a cliff in the fiscal first quarter of 2027. Earnings rose 27% year over year, with same-store sales (excluding gasoline) up 3.2%. That's not exactly bad, given that consumers are increasingly watching their budgets, but the same-store sales growth rate was lower than a year ago and the lowest in five quarters. Meanwhile, gallons of gasoline sold fell slightly year over year, which is notable because fuel sales are what get people into a Casey's store.

But a 10% price drop may still seem a bit extreme. Until you take valuation into consideration. Even after that drop, Casey's General Stores' price-to-sales ratio is 1.3x compared to a five-year average of roughly 0.8x. Its price-to-earnings ratio is 32x, compared to a five-year average of 26x. Basically, this retailer's stock still looks expensive, suggesting the drop was driven more by investor sentiment than anything else.

So the bigger issue is really that investors clearly have high expectations for Casey's General Stores. Falling short in the slightest way can turn into a negative event in such situations. That dynamic was on clear display when the company reported its fiscal first-quarter 2027 earnings. Perfection is often the only way to keep an expensive stock moving higher, but perfection is an impossible expectation of any company. Casey's is still growing its business, with plans to open or acquire 120 new locations in fiscal 2027. However, it is clear that investors are increasingly concerned that too much good news has been priced into the stock.

Casy's General Stores' yield is a paltry 0.4%, so income investors won't be interested. As noted above, the stock looks expensive historically, so value investors won't like it either. That leaves growth investors, but the post-earnings price drop suggests even they are getting worried that the company's growth prospects won't live up to expectations. In other words, only the most ardent fans of Casey's General Stores will probably want to step into this stock in November.

Reuben Gregg Brewer has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Casey's General Stores. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#3085. How AI Is Changing The Playbook For Venture-Backed Companies

Nada Usina is CEO & Co-Founder of NU Advisory Partners.

​The question I hear most often in VC circles is whether the AI investment boom is a wave that will eventually crash. Will the flood of capital and climbing valuations prove to have sustainable traction and revenue? I’ve been at the forefront of several major technology shifts, from leading digital media companies through the dot-com era to working at the leading edge of mobile. Today, I’m building an AI-native, high-growth business. I’ve seen firsthand what happens when excitement gets ahead of fundamentals.

AI investment will continue well beyond 2026, but what interests me most is how AI is changing the way companies are built and led. Technology allows them to move faster with fewer people, challenging assumptions about what an executive team should look like.

The enormous amounts of capital being poured into AI make the market appear more mature than it is. Commercially, it is still early. A breakthrough in technology does not automatically create distribution, customer trust or a sustainable business.

AI can shorten that timeline considerably. We are seeing companies go from zero to $100 million in revenue at speeds that would have seemed extraordinary a decade ago. When a company can accomplish in a few years what once took 10, investors naturally start looking for the next one.

That speed can also lead to bad bets. Some companies will be swallowed by larger platforms while they are still small. Others will discover that an impressive product does not solve a problem customers urgently need to solve. It also raises a practical question for investors: What kind of leadership does a company need when it can grow this quickly with a much smaller team?

For years, companies approaching a new stage of growth often responded by adding people. Layers of vice presidents, senior vice presidents and functional leaders came in as the organization became more complex. With AI, companies can accomplish more with smaller teams, which means the people at the top have to be much closer to the actual business.

Leaders need to understand the product, the customer, the economics and how the business actually operates. They need to make decisions quickly, work across functions and know when technology can replace a process rather than simply adding another person to manage it.

As AI reduces the need for some layers of middle management, the expectations of the C-suite are getting higher. We are seeing investors look for leaders with the judgment and operating experience to work effectively in much leaner organizations. With fewer people between the C-suite and the work itself, the people at the top need to be able to run the business, not just oversee it.

For a portfolio company, I would ask: Is AI actually changing the business, or has it just been added to the product? The strongest companies are using it to improve the customer experience, make the product smarter through proprietary data or change the economics of the business. Calling something “AI-powered” does not tell an investor very much if the underlying business still operates the same way.

That can also point to a talent decision. A company may need a more commercially minded CEO, a different product leader or an executive who has already navigated a similar technology shift.

Public markets will make it easier to see which AI companies have built durable, profitable businesses and which have benefited primarily from the private-market environment. Investors will scrutinize revenue quality, retention, margins and the cost of maintaining the technology. They will also look at who is running the company.

I have seen strong technology companies lose momentum because their leadership team was built for invention rather than growth. The executives who made sense at $10 million in revenue may not be the right people at $100 million. Waiting too long to recognize that can cost a company valuable time.

My experience with frontier technology goes back to the early days of the internet and mobile media. At broadcast.com, I worked at a company that was among the first to stream live content over the Internet. Later, at Nokia, I worked with the music industry to bring music, games and video to mobile phones.

Both experiences showed me what happens when technology opens up a market before the infrastructure, business models and consumer expectations have caught up. AI presents a similar challenge: Leaders have to figure out what the technology makes possible while building a business that can actually take advantage of it.

We are applying the same thinking at our company, where we have built an AI-native executive search firm. We use AI throughout the search process while relying on human judgment to assess leadership, experience and fit.

We ask ourselves many of the same questions we ask our clients: Where can AI make a meaningful difference? Where does judgment still matter? And how do we make the best use of our team’s expertise for the complex advisory work our clients rely on us for?

AI investment will continue, but investors will become more selective. Companies will have to prove that their products solve urgent customer problems, their economics improve with scale and their growth can survive outside a generous funding market.

Technical credibility can earn a company its first check, but building a lasting business requires operating experience and commercial judgment. AI may allow companies to operate with fewer people and fewer layers, but that does not make talent less important. It puts more responsibility on the people at the top.

Investors should be asking not only whether a company has the right technology but also whether it has the right people to make the most of it.​

#3084. Biotech stocks are surging. How investors can play the new drug innovation boom

Moderna gave investors a scare as its stock plunged on Thursday. But it's still one of the hottest biotechs this year. And it's hardly alone – the sector is on a roll and looks poised for more gains.

The iShares Biotechnology ETF (IBB) is up 24% through October 23, building on a 28% gain in 2025. Two dozen of the ETF's 233 holdings have more than doubled year-to-date. Moderna leads the pack with a 587% surge — even after an 18% decline following a leak of clinical data for its cancer vaccine (which was actually positive).

Analysts say a new biotech cycle is underway, fueled by clinical trial results, M&A activity, and promising technologies such as genomics, mRNA — and AI.

"We're in the midst of a powerful innovation cycle," said John Hall, portfolio manager of the T. Rowe Price Biotechnology ETF. "What's super exciting is we're seeing newer modalities start to make it to market." Companies "understand the disease biology better," he adds, and that could ultimately lead to more novel drugs making it to market.

Investors are excited about technologies like mRNA and genomics, along with a steady stream of new drug approvals. The FDA approved about a dozen novel biologic drugs in 2025, out of 46 approvals in total. Roughly 66 novel drugs are in the pipeline for FDA approval, including potential blockbusters like Moderna and Merck's cancer drug for melanoma, and a next-generation obesity drug from Eli Lilly.

Analysts say AI could also lead to more approvals as companies deploy the software to speed up drug development.

"Biotech is a phenomenal application for artificial intelligence and machine learning," says Piper Sandler analyst Ted Tenthoff. "You can set up exciting predictive models that, frankly, can do things that we've never been able to do in the space in terms of novel drug discovery."

Granted, the industry is recovering from a fallow period. The sector's last strong performance was during the Covid era when ultra-low interest rates encouraged investment in early-stage drug developers, and mRNA vaccines fueled a revenue surge for companies like Moderna, Pfizer and Biontech.

The sector then went cold as many early-stage companies fizzled. Demand for Covid vaccines evaporated, and surging interest rates put a chill in IPOs and M&A.

The risks haven't evaporated – this is still a sector whose products take years to develop, resulting in far more failures than successes. But analysts say the outlook is healthier now. While that's reflected in strong performance and richer valuations, there's still good reason to invest.

Recent clinical trial results are stoking excitement that novel drugs in the works could tackle some of the toughest problems in medicine.

Moderna and Merck's melanoma drug, for instance, uses mRNA to trigger an immune response in patients, targeting tumors that have been surgically removed and genetically analyzed. It's not a preventive vaccine, but it uses a similar immunology mechanism and showed a 42% reduction in cancer recurrence or death (used in conjunction with Merck's cancer drug Keytruda).

While the Phase 3 results disappointed Wall Street, oncologists say the outcomes were still highly positive. And they see the technology as a potential game changer, ushering in an era of personalized treatments for cancers. Moderna and Merck have said they aim to submit the drug for FDA approval and get it launched in 2027.

Inflammation treatment is another promising area. AstraZeneca and Amgen recently released positive Phase 3 results for another use for their drug Tezspire, an injectable approved for nasal polyps and asthma. In clinical trials, it showed that it successfully relieved swallowing symptoms and healed microscopic and visual tissue damage in patients with severe throat inflammation.

Roche, meanwhile, notched a win after the FDA approved its drug Enspryng, a therapy to treat rare inflammatory and autoimmune diseases. It became the first and only at-home injection for adults with thyroid eye disease.

Obesity drugs are also advancing beyond the first generation of GLP-1s. Eli Lilly's retatrutide, a "triple agonist" targeting three different hormone receptors, cleared two more clinical trials over the summer. The drug produced 28%-30% weight loss at the highest doses in the study, Lilly said. The company plans to submit the drug for FDA approval in the first quarter of 2027.

Much of the innovation isn't just happening in drug-making – it's also in areas like gene sequencing, mRNA, and high-tech instruments.

Illumina has more than doubled this year. The DNA and gene sequencing company is seeing accelerating demand for its NovaSeq X high-end sequencing platform. Pharmaceutical companies including Bristol-Myers Squibb, Merck and Kura are working with Illumina to develop precision oncology solutions.

Another big winner is 10x Genomics, up more than 300%. The biotech firm offers its lab instruments to help scientists research cancer, immunology and neuroscience. The company's Atera platform is helping produce data sets to train AI models, a process that helps accelerate personalized therapies.

On the AI front, companies are using the technology for more efficient drug discovery, says Shreefāl Mehta, president of Guidant BioTherapeutics. Using AI, "you can now bring a drug to clinical trials with less capital. More investment is also going into companies that are demonstrating that," he said.

Global AI in drug discovery will grow from a $20 billion market in 2025 to more than $160 billion by 2035, according to forecasts by Towards Health, a research and consulting firm.

One other catalyst for the sector could be M&A. Dealmaking for biopharma hit $134 billion in the first half of 2026, up from $112 billion for all of 2025, notes Jeet Mukherjee, biotech analyst at BTIG. That's a positive signal, indicating more drugs in development are showing clinical promise.

It also helps that Big Pharma has a "patent cliff" ahead. Products representing $180 billion of revenue will lose exclusivity by 2030, according to research firm RTW Institute. Companies with looming expiries "are looking for novel products and innovative products to put into their pipeline," Mehta says.

GLP-1 blockbusters have also left some companies flush with cash for acquisitions. Eli Lilly alone has completed 10 acquisition deals in 2026 worth $25 billion.

ETFs can capture the investing theme, though they aren't all alike. The iShares Biotech ETF is one of the lower cost funds. It tracks a market-cap weighted index of biotech stocks, led by companies like Gilead Sciences, Amgen, Vertex Pharmaceuticals, and Moderna.

The State Street SPDR S&P Biotech ETF holds stocks in equal weight, offering more exposure to small- and mid-cap names. Its top holdings are Moderna, Natera, Twist Bioscience and Halozyme Therapeutics.

Piper Sandler calls Illumina and 10x Genomics the "primary infrastructure plays" in the life science arena, saying their technologies are "driving the next generation of precision medicine."

Piper analyst David Westenberg has a buy rating and $305 target on Illumina, implying 14% gains from recent prices around $267. He has a hold rating on 10X with an $80 target, above recent prices around $70.

Twist Bioscience is another name to consider. The company makes customized synthetic DNA and sells DNA sequencing tools. Twist has partnered with Eli Lilly's AI and machine-learning platform and linked up with Anthropic in August to start testing its AI model, Claude, for protein development.

Twist isn't expected to turn an EPS profit until 2029, according to consensus forecasts. But revenue is expected to go from $572 million in 2027 to $833 million in 2029. Analysts have an average target of $168 on the stock, implying 21% returns from recent prices around $138.

In the small-cap space, Piper Sandler's Tenthoff likes Monte Rosa Therapeutics, a pioneer in protein degradation that selectively destroys disease-causing proteins.

The firm has partnered with Novartis to develop a drug for inflammatory conditions and autoimmune diseases. The companies announced a Phase 2 clinical study in September for an autoimmune disease treatment, which has been "triggering milestones to Monte Rosa," Tenthoff said.

Tenthoff has a buy rating and $37 target on the stock, which recently traded around $10.70.

Also in the small-cap arena, BTIG's Mukherjee recommends Faeth Therapeutics.

The biotech is developing a novel two-drug regimen to treat breast cancer and other tumors. The regimen "has the potential to address safety and dosing limitations of another recently approved drug for breast cancer," he says. And it could become "a mainstay of the future breast cancer treatment paradigm and other cancers."

Faeth is a clinical-stage company that has yet to bring a drug to market. Yet the stock is up 93% year-to-date on positive clinical trial results, trading around $18. Mukherjee has a $55 target on it.

Kymera Therapeutics is worth considering too. The company is developing an oral version of the blockbuster drug Dupixent (made and co-developed by Regeneron Pharmaceuticals and Sanofi). Dupixent is an injectable, however, and oral agents "are frequently preferred by patients," Mukherjee says. "The drug has the potential to not only take share from patients taking Dupixent for numerous immunological diseases but also expanding the market to those not taking systemic biologic drugs," he tells CNBC.

Kymera has said it doesn't expect a patent fight over Dupixent because its drug is distinct, not a biosimilar or biologic copy.

T. Rowe's Hall also likes Kymera for its potential "to unlock disease targets that have been classically considered un-druggable." The stock is the second largest holding in T. Rowe's Biotech ETF, accounting for 4.2% of the portfolio.

#3082. Should You Buy C3.ai Stock After Its 93% Decline? The Answer Might Surprise You.

C3.ai is proof that not every artificial intelligence stock is a winner.

C3.ai (AI +3.64%) went public in December 2020, and its stock quickly set a record high of $177. It has trended lower ever since, with the downside reaching a crescendo after its founder and chief executive Thomas Siebel announced he was stepping away to deal with health issues last September.

Siebel always played a central role in the sales and customer relationship management processes, so his departure led to a dramatic decline in C3.ai's revenue. Fortunately, he returned to lead the company in May, and he's now trying to right the ship.

C3.ai stock remains 93% below its all-time high, so could this be a buying opportunity as Siebel puts his turnaround plan in place? The answer might surprise you.

Developing AI software from the ground up requires a considerable amount of financial and technical resources, which the average business simply doesn't have. C3.ai developed a portfolio of turnkey applications covering a range of different industries, and they can be tailored for the specific needs of almost any customer, giving enterprises a more practical way to tap into the power of AI.

However, C3.ai is expanding its addressable market by becoming a platform provider. It launched the C3 Agentic AI Platform last year, which builds a deep understanding of every existing process, relationship, and data set within the enterprise, allowing managers to create powerful agents that can make operational decisions and even automate tasks. In essence, it serves as an intelligent operating system for the enterprise.

The C3 Agentic AI Platform integrates with leading cloud platforms like Microsoft Azure and Amazon Web Services, so it can ingest operational data from across the entire enterprise in real time.

C3.ai's decision to become a platform provider will be critical to its future success because AI will eventually be at the center of every enterprise, so catering to those deploying just one or two applications was simply the wrong strategy for the long term.

C3.ai delivered $250.3 million in revenue during its 2026 fiscal year (ended April 30), a 35% decline from the prior year. The company then delivered $52.4 million in revenue during its fiscal 2027 first quarter (ended July 31), a 25% decline from the year-ago period.

The negative results were directly attributable to Siebel's departure, but better times might be ahead now that he's leading the company again. According to management's latest guidance, C3.ai could generate up to $240 million in total revenue during fiscal 2027, which would represent a much smaller decline of 4% compared to fiscal 2026. Plus, Siebel thinks a return to sales growth could be in the cards within the next two quarters.

C3.ai has significantly cut costs across the board to right-size the business in light of its shrinking revenue. It was a necessary step, because the company lost a staggering $470.4 million at the bottom line during fiscal 2026, an increase of 63% from the prior year. It lost a further $92.8 million during the first quarter of fiscal 2027, but that was a 20% improvement from the year-ago period, so things are starting to move in the right direction.

Shortly after C3.ai went public in 2020, its price-to-sales (P/S) ratio briefly climbed to over 100, which was a ludicrous valuation. For some perspective, the technology-heavy Nasdaq-100 index has a P/S ratio of just 6.3. Investors were expecting rapid revenue growth from C3.ai that simply never came, hence the prolonged decline in its stock over the last six years.

The stock is now trading at a more reasonable P/S ratio of 7.2, which is a steep discount to its average of 14.1 since going public. However, given the company's revenue is expected to decline in fiscal 2027, its forward P/S ratio is actually slightly higher at 8.3.

In other words, C3.ai is more expensive when valued against its future potential financial results, whereas a healthy, growing company would actually look cheaper on a forward basis. Shrinking businesses tend to destroy shareholder value over time, which is exactly why investors try to avoid them.

With that said, C3.ai saw a 73% quarter-over-quarter increase in its gross bookings during the third quarter, which typically reflects the value of signed contracts for services that haven't been delivered yet. Bookings can be a good predictor of future revenue, so this supports Siebel's expectation of a return to sales growth in the next two quarters.

However, I wouldn't buy C3.ai stock right now. I would prefer to wait until the company actually does start delivering consistent revenue growth, because any further declines could leave shareholders exposed to steep losses.

Anthony Di Pizio has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Amazon and Microsoft. The Motley Fool recommends C3.ai. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.
